suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(ggplot2))
options(digits = 3, scipen = 0)

big <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)   # 5,130,000
pal <- c(charcoal = "#33393F", slate = "#5A6470", silver = "#D9DCE0", brick = "#8C3B2E", blush = "#F2E6E3", offwhite = "#F3F4F5", pencil = "#C9CBCE", ink = "#1A1A1A",
         steel = "#2E5F8C", mist = "#E3EBF2", denim = "#6A9ACB", rose = "#C8837C")   # figure palette (all plots); steel/mist are the blue pair matching brick/blush; denim/rose the mid tones; literals below are these values
year_axis <- function(y0, y1, date = FALSE, ...) {                # time axes: tick marks at every year-end, the year label centred between them
  if (date) scale_x_date(breaks = as.Date(sprintf("%d-07-02", y0:y1)), labels = y0:y1, minor_breaks = as.Date(sprintf("%d-01-01", y0:(y1 + 1))), guide = guide_axis(minor.ticks = TRUE), ...)
  else scale_x_continuous(breaks = y0:y1 + 0.5, labels = y0:y1, minor_breaks = y0:(y1 + 1), guide = guide_axis(minor.ticks = TRUE), ...) }

This notebook derives the numbers printed in Table 3.1, §4.4 and Sections 5–6 of the paper (the few it does not are listed in §S.8) from the data snapshots in `data/` and a small number of stated inputs. Most of the snapshots are Epoch AI's (CC BY 4.0); the two curated lists of named owners and the two customs extracts are described where they are used (§S.6.4, §S.6.5). Each section gives the adopted value, the inputs and their sources, the calculation, the judgment calls it rests on, the cross-checks that reach the same quantity by another route, and the direction in which each choice is conservative. "Conservative" throughout means *regime-unfavorable*: a smaller fleet for the regime to police ($F_E$, $F_B$) or a larger exposure on a state's ledger. A reference such as §6.2.2 is to a section of the paper; §S.1.2.3 is section 1.2.3 of this supplement. Knitting the notebook recomputes every value and figure.

**Order.** §S.1 measures the world as it stands on the eve of a pause: the frontier training trajectory, the accelerator fleets (world, United States, China, and the leading lab), and what that hardware costs. Nothing in it assumes a treaty. Everything after it does: §S.2–§S.3 set the treaty thresholds, §S.4–§S.5 derive the two violator fleet sizes, and §S.6–§S.8 assemble the ledgers.

# S.0 Conventions and units

```{r units}
h100e.peak  <- 989e12                    # FLOP/s: one H100 SXM, dense FP16/BF16 with FP32 accumulate (paper fn 15)
secs.per.yr <- 365 * 24 * 3600
h100e <- function(flops.per.sec) flops.per.sec / h100e.peak       # peak FLOP/s -> H100e
h100e.years <- function(flop) flop / (h100e.peak * secs.per.yr)   # FLOP -> H100e-years at peak
```

* **H100e.** One H100 = `r sci(h100e.peak)` FLOP/s dense 16-bit (NVIDIA n.d. lists 1,979 TFLOP/s "with sparsity"; halved for dense operation). Epoch AI's H100e is defined on dense **8-bit** throughput (1.98e15 OP/s per H100). A chip whose 8-bit rate is twice its 16-bit rate, as it is for the H100 and for the Blackwell chips, counts for the same number of H100e on either convention, so Epoch's fleet figures are used directly; only the FLOP/s per H100e differs (by 2×). What does differ is the *rating* of a Blackwell chip, for which NVIDIA publishes two figures: the 72-GPU liquid-cooled GB200 rack is listed at 360 PFLOP/s 16-bit with sparsity, which is 2.5e15 FLOP/s dense per GPU or 2.53 H100e (NVIDIA n.d.b), and the eight-GPU air-cooled B200 system at 72 PFLOP/s 8-bit with sparsity, which is 4.5e15 dense per GPU and so, at half the 8-bit rate, 2.25e15 FLOP/s dense 16-bit or 2.28 H100e (NVIDIA n.d.c). Epoch's data take every B200 and B300 at the first (2.53 H100e in `data/ai_chip_sales_timelines_by_chip.csv`), and every fleet in this notebook follows them. The Astra back-of-envelope of §S.1.1.2 takes the second, the lower one.
* **Thresholds** ($C_F$, $C_T$, $C_E$) are *total training FLOP* of the final run, pretraining plus post-training, matching Epoch's database convention and the paper's §3.2.2 definition.
* **Judgmental inputs and derived quantities.** Every number in this notebook is one or the other. A *judgmental input* is a value the authors chose on the evidence and state as a round number ($C_F = 2\times10^{27}$, $\beta_T = 10^{-3}$, $\beta_E = 10$, the blind-leap increment $\delta = 1/3$, $T_E = 5$ yr, the 2.41×/yr growth of the world flow, the 0.75 U.S.-located share, the 100M consumer cards, the discount factors $\pi$ and $\tau$); each section says which of its inputs are judgmental and what evidence brackets them. A *derived quantity* is computed from the inputs and the data, carried at full precision into downstream calculations, and rounded to two significant figures only when printed. So $F_E$ enters the §6.4 percentages at full precision (§S.4.4), not at its two printed figures, and $K_0$(Consumer) enters as 3.03M, not 3M. Some inputs are published estimates rather than round numbers, such as the frontier research overhead $\rho_F = g^{-4/12}/0.096 \approx 6.3$ (a 9.6% final-run share, adjusted for a four-month lag; §S.4.2); they too are carried at full precision.
* **Fleets** ($F_E$, $F_B$, $F_P$) are *peak* throughput in H100e, "at present-day utilization": the fleet a frontier lab would need. An evader achieving utilization $\tau \cdot U_F$ relative to a frontier lab needs $F/\tau$ actual chips.

# S.1 The pre-pause trajectory

Everything in this section measures or projects the world as it stands at the end of 2026, before any treaty. It supplies three things the rest of the notebook needs: the frontier training threshold $C_F$ and the utilization $U_F$ of a frontier run (§S.1.1); the size and growth of the accelerator fleets a treaty would have to govern, globally and for the United States, China and the leading lab (§S.1.2); and what that hardware is worth in dollars (§S.1.3).

Only the first of these feeds the treaty thresholds. The fleets and the dollar figures are the base against which every ledger in §S.6–§S.8 is compared, and none of them depends on a treaty parameter.

## S.1.1 The training trajectory

**Adopted: the frontier threshold $C_F = 2\times10^{27}$ FLOP, the total training compute of a frozen-frontier model at year-end 2026; the historical growth rate $g = 4.5$ per year; and the frontier utilization $U_F = 0.21$.**

$C_F$ is the quantity every treaty threshold is indexed to: the compute ceiling $C_T$, the covert evasion threshold $C_E$ and the overt breakout threshold $C_B$ are all multiples of it. It is estimated two ways — by extrapolating Epoch's fitted trend through published frontier runs, and by a back-of-envelope on the largest run whose hardware is known — and §S.1.1.3 sets the adopted value.

### S.1.1.1 Epoch’s frontier-compute trend

Data: `data/frontier_ai_models.csv` from Epoch AI's *AI Models* hub (frontier subset; snapshot ~2026-09-05; CC BY 4.0). Epoch's headline is "training compute of frontier models has grown 5× per year since 2020"; their regression gives 4.5×. Two readings of "the frontier" are fitted below: all frontier-flagged models (the typical frontier model) and the running-maximum record-setters (the single largest run).

```{r trend-fit}
ep <- read.csv("data/frontier_ai_models.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
ep$C    <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(ep[["Training compute (FLOP)"]]))
ep$date <- as.Date(ep[["Publication date"]])
ep <- ep[!is.na(ep$C) & !is.na(ep$date), ]
ep$yr <- as.numeric(format(ep$date, "%Y")) + (as.numeric(format(ep$date, "%j")) - 1) / 365.25
ep <- ep[order(ep$yr), ]
T.anchor <- 2026 + 365 / 365.25                     # 31 Dec 2026

fit.trend <- function(d) {
  m <- lm(log10(C) ~ yr, data = d)
  pred <- predict(m, data.frame(yr = T.anchor), interval = "confidence", level = 0.95)
  data.frame(n = nrow(d), growth.per.yr = 10^coef(m)[["yr"]], r2 = summary(m)$r.squared, resid.sd.dex = summary(m)$sigma,
             at.end.2026 = 10^pred[1, "fit"], ci.lo = 10^pred[1, "lwr"], ci.hi = 10^pred[1, "upr"])
}
all.since.2020 <- ep[ep$yr >= 2020, ]
ep$runmax <- cummax(ep$C)
records <- ep[ep$C == ep$runmax & ep$yr >= 2020, ]; records <- records[!duplicated(records$C), ]
trend <- rbind("all frontier models since 2020" = fit.trend(all.since.2020),
               "record-setters since 2020"      = fit.trend(records))
trend
```

The figure below also shows the authors' back-of-envelope range for GPT-6 Astra (released 2026-09-03), derived in §S.1.1.2: 100.8k B200/B300-class GPUs (Epoch lists 100.8k of each type at Abilene; Astra's "more than 100,000" matches one block) for 3 to 6 months at 40% MFU, 16-bit arithmetic, 40% post-training share; mid = geometric mean of the two ends. It is not an Epoch estimate.

```{r astra-range}
astra.total <- function(gpus, months, mfu = 0.40, f.post = 0.40, chip.peak = 2.25e15)
  gpus * chip.peak * mfu * months * 30.44 * 86400 / (1 - f.post)
astra.gpus <- 100.8e3                                                     # Epoch AI 2026e: 100.8k B200 + 100.8k B300 at Abilene
astra <- data.frame(yr = 2026 + (246 - 1) / 365.25,                      # 3 Sep 2026
                    lo = astra.total(astra.gpus, 3), hi = astra.total(astra.gpus, 6))
astra$mid <- sqrt(astra$lo * astra$hi)
signif(unlist(astra[c("lo", "mid", "hi")]), 2)
```

```{r trend-figure, fig.cap = "Frontier training compute, Epoch AI data, with the OLS trend (dashed), its 95% confidence band, the adopted C_F with the thresholds C_T = β_T·C_F and C_E = β_E·C_F indexed to it, the overt breakout threshold C_B (an absolute level, six blind steps above C_F; §S.5), and the authors' back-of-envelope range for GPT-6 Astra (error bar: 100.8k GPUs for 3-6 months; not an Epoch estimate). Reproduces Epoch's '5x per year' chart; the fitted slope is 4.45x/yr."}
m.all <- lm(log10(C) ~ yr, data = all.since.2020)
grid <- data.frame(yr = seq(2020, T.anchor, length.out = 200))
ci <- predict(m.all, grid, interval = "confidence"); grid$fit <- ci[, 1]; grid$lo <- ci[, 2]; grid$hi <- ci[, 3]
ggplot() +
  geom_ribbon(data = grid, aes(yr, ymin = lo, ymax = hi), fill = "#D9DCE0", alpha = 0.45) +
  geom_line(data = grid, aes(yr, fit), colour = "#33393F", linetype = "22") +
  geom_point(data = all.since.2020, aes(yr, log10(C)), shape = 21, size = 2.6, fill = "#C9CBCE", colour = "#5A6470") +
  geom_errorbar(data = astra, aes(x = yr, ymin = log10(lo), ymax = log10(hi)), width = 0.12, colour = "#8C3B2E") +
  geom_point(data = astra, aes(yr, log10(mid)), shape = 23, size = 3, fill = "#8C3B2E", colour = "#1A1A1A") +
  annotate("text", x = astra$yr - 0.12, y = log10(astra$hi) + 0.02, hjust = 1, vjust = 0, size = 3, colour = "#8C3B2E",
           label = "GPT-6 Astra\n(our range)") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = log10(c(2e24, 2e27, 2e28, 2e29)), colour = "#8C3B2E", linetype = "dashed") +           # C_T, C_F, C_E, C_B (sections S.2, S.3, S.5)
  annotate("text", x = 2020.05, y = log10(2e27) + 0.08, hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = "#8C3B2E",
           label = "'Frozen frontier ' * C[F] == 2 %*% 10^27 ~ '(end of 2026)'", parse = TRUE) +
  annotate("text", x = 2020.05, y = log10(2e28) + 0.08, hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = "#8C3B2E",
           label = "'Covert evasion target ' * C[E] == 2 %*% 10^28 ~ '(' * beta[E] * C[F] * ')'", parse = TRUE) +
  annotate("text", x = 2020.05, y = log10(2e29) + 0.08, hjust = 0, vjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = "#8C3B2E",
           label = "'Overt breakout target ' * C[B] == 2 %*% 10^29", parse = TRUE) +
  annotate("text", x = T.anchor, y = log10(2e24) + 0.08, hjust = 1, vjust = 0, size = 3.2, colour = "#8C3B2E",
           label = "'Treaty compute ceiling ' * C[T] == 2 %*% 10^24 ~ '(' * beta[T] * C[F] * ')'", parse = TRUE) +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = 22:29, labels = function(v) parse(text = paste0("10^", v))) +
  year_axis(2020, 2026, expand = expansion(mult = c(0.01, 0.02))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "Training compute (FLOP)",
       title = "Frontier training compute since 2020") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + year_theme + theme(panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank())
```

Footnote 64's "$1.7\times10^{27}$ at year-end 2026" is the all-models trend (`r sci(trend$at.end.2026[1])`). The record-setter trend is `r sci(trend$at.end.2026[2])`. Individual frontier models scatter about the trend with a standard deviation of `r round(trend$resid.sd.dex[1], 2)` dex, so the *next* record run at end-2026 is not well pinned down by the fit: the 95% band on the trend itself is `r sci(trend$ci.lo[1])`–`r sci(trend$ci.hi[1])`.

### S.1.1.2 GPT-6 Astra back-of-envelope

Facts used (fn 64): Astra was pretrained on "more than 100,000 GPUs" at OpenAI's Stargate Abilene campus (Lardinois 2026); Epoch's data-center directory lists Abilene at ~100.8k B200 + ~100.8k B300 as of May 2026 (Epoch AI 2026e), i.e. roughly 200k chips were physically there. A B200/B300 is taken at 2.25e15 FLOP/s dense 16-bit, 2.28 H100e; this is the lower of NVIDIA's two ratings for the chip, and at the higher one (2.5e15, the rating Epoch's fleet data use; §S.0) every figure in this section would be 11% larger. Pretraining MFU is taken at 40% (Llama-3 reported 38–43%; Epoch uses 30–50%).

```{r astra}
b200.peak.16 <- 2.25e15
astra.gpus   <- c("100k GPUs" = 100e3, "200k GPUs" = 200e3)
astra.months <- c(3, 4, 6);  mfu <- 0.40;  f.post <- 0.40      # post-training share of total FLOP (implied by Epoch's GPT-5 medians)
pre16 <- outer(astra.gpus * b200.peak.16 * mfu, astra.months * 30.44 * 86400)
colnames(pre16) <- paste(astra.months, "mo")
list("pretraining FLOP, 16-bit, 40% MFU"          = signif(pre16, 2),
     "total FLOP (pre + post) at f_post = 0.4"     = signif(pre16 / (1 - f.post), 2),
     "total FLOP if the run was FP8 (x2)"          = signif(2 * pre16 / (1 - f.post), 2))
```

Footnote 64 quotes the pretraining-only row for 100k GPUs at 3–6 months ($6.9\times10^{26}$–$1.4\times10^{27}$) and a total of 1.2–$2.4\times10^{27}$ at a 40% post-training share; the upper end of that total is the 6-month case of §S.1.1.1's figure range (at 3–4 months the total is 1.2–$1.6\times10^{27}$). For 200k GPUs the totals would be 2.4–$3.2\times10^{27}$. Epoch had not published its own estimate for Astra when this notebook was prepared (mid-September 2026).

### S.1.1.3 The frontier threshold C_F: choice and sensitivity

```{r cf-choice}
C.F <- 2e27
grok4 <- 5e26; grok4.date <- 2025 + 190 / 365.25
c("C_F / all-models trend" = C.F / trend$at.end.2026[1],
  "C_F / record-setter trend" = C.F / trend$at.end.2026[2],
  "Grok 4 carried to end-2026 at 5x/yr" = grok4 * 5^(T.anchor - grok4.date),
  "C_F / Grok 4" = C.F / grok4)
```

**Judgment calls.**

* *Typical frontier model vs. largest run.* $2\times10^{27}$ is 1.2× the typical-frontier trend and 0.37× the record-setter trend. The thresholds are meant to describe the most capable models at the frozen frontier, which argues for something between the two.
* *Post-training share.* 40% (implied by Epoch's medians for GPT-5; §S.1.1.4), the same share that enters the blended utilization $U_F$ (§S.1.1.4) and the reinforcement-learning (RL) fine-tuning remark of §6.2.5.
* *Arithmetic precision.* The paper rates all hardware in dense 16-bit (fn 14). If Astra's pretraining ran in FP8 the chips delivered twice the operations per second, so the run used twice the FLOP shown in the Astra table and $C_F$ "should" be twice as high. But this does not change $F_E$ once it is converted to H100e: an evader training in the same precision gets the same 2× from its own chips, so the chip-count $F_E = \rho_E \cdot \beta_E$·(Astra's chip-time)/$T_E$ is invariant to the precision convention. Basing $C_F$ on Astra's hardware-time is what makes $F_E$ robust to this concern.
* *What "training compute" counts.* Epoch derives FLOP as chip-seconds × peak × an assumed 30–50% utilization, which overstates useful FLOP for RL-heavy runs. A treaty would need to fix a counting convention (e.g. 6·N·D plus counted RL FLOP) rather than GPU-hours × MFU.

**Direction of conservatism.** $F_E$, $F_P$, $C_T$ and $C_E$ scale linearly with $C_F$; $F_B$ does not (§6.2.3). A smaller $C_F$ means a smaller covert-evasion fleet to police, so rounding *down* is the regime-unfavorable, conservative side.

### S.1.1.4 The post-training share f_post, and the blended utilization U_F

A frontier training run has two parts: pretraining, the large next-token-prediction run, and post-training, which today consists mostly of RL, in which the model generates long outputs that are then scored. Let $f_{\mathrm{post}}$ be the share of the final run's total FLOP that goes to post-training. It is a judgmental input, and it enters this notebook in three places.

1. **The Astra total (§S.1.1.2).** The back-of-envelope in fn 64 counts only Astra's pretraining hardware, so the run's total FLOP is the pretraining FLOP divided by (1 − $f_{\mathrm{post}}$).
2. **The utilization $U_F$ (§6.2.1).** Pretraining runs at 30–50% of peak throughput (Epoch AI n.d.), and reinforcement-learning post-training at 5–20% (Denain and Wu 2026). Taking the mid-range of each gives 40% and 12.5%; Meta's reported 38–43% for Llama-3-405B corroborates the pretraining figure. The utilization of the whole run is the FLOP-weighted average of the two, which is a harmonic mean, and it falls as $f_{\mathrm{post}}$ rises. $U_F$ sets the covert evasion fleet through $F_E = \rho_E \cdot C_E$ / ($T_E \cdot U_F$), so a lower $U_F$ means a larger $F_E$.
3. **The RL fine-tuning remark in §6.2.5**, that an RL fine-tune of an existing model that stays below $C_T$ is a small fraction of the post-training compute already spent on that model.

**The evidence for 0.40.** The only estimate of $f_{\mathrm{post}}$ for a specific frontier run is Epoch AI's estimate for GPT-5, released in August 2025: a median of about $3\times10^{25}$ FLOP of pretraining and about $5\times10^{25}$ in total (Epoch AI 2025b), which leaves about $2\times10^{25}$ for RL, a post-training share of 40%. It is an estimate rather than a disclosure, and Epoch's range for GPT-5's final RL relative to its pretraining, 10% to 200%, corresponds to shares of 9% to 67%. Parity, 50%, has been suggested as a forward-looking value, because RL budgets have been growing faster than pretraining budgets (xAI described Grok 4's RL compute as comparable to its pretraining compute), but it has no single source.

The table below shows what each value of $f_{\mathrm{post}}$ implies, holding everything else fixed: the Astra total for 100k GPUs over four months, $U_F$, the resulting $F_E$ at $C_F = 2\times10^{27}$, and the size of an RL fine-tune at $C_T$ relative to the original model's post-training.

```{r fpost}
g.F <- 4.5; lag.rd <- 4 / 12                          # the historical growth rate g, and the R&D-to-final-run lag, both from section S.4.2 below
rho.F <- g.F^(-lag.rd) / 0.096; delta <- 1 / 3         # frontier research overhead and blind-leap increment, derived in section S.4.2 below; needed here for F_E
blind.steps  <- function(beta, dl = delta) pmax(1, log10(beta) / dl)                         # n = log10(beta) / delta, NOT rounded: every step is delta, the last may be partial
blind.factor <- function(beta, dl = delta) { n <- blind.steps(beta, dl); f <- (1 - 1 / beta) / (1 - beta^(-1 / n)); ifelse(rep_len(beta, length(f)) <= 1, 1, f) }
rho.E.of <- function(beta, rF = rho.F, dl = delta) rF * blind.factor(beta, dl)                                # rho_E = rho_F x blind-leap factor
U.blend <- function(f, U.pre = 0.40, U.post = 0.125) 1 / ((1 - f) / U.pre + f / U.post) # FLOP-weighted utilization, mid-range of each band
F.E.fpost <- function(f) rho.E.of(10) * 10 * C.F / (5 * secs.per.yr * U.blend(f)) / h100e.peak               # F_E at beta_E = 10, T_E = 5 for a given post-training share
f <- c(0.09, 0.30, 0.40, 0.50, 0.67, 0.75, 0.90)
astra.pre <- pre16["100k GPUs", "4 mo"]
data.frame(f_post = f,
           astra.total.FLOP = signif(astra.pre / (1 - f), 2),
           U_F = round(U.blend(f), 3),
           F_E.M.H100e = round(F.E.fpost(f) / 1e6, 2),                                          # rho_E beta_E C_F / (T_E U_F)
           RL.finetune.share = sprintf("%.2f%%", 100 * (C.F / 1000) / (f * C.F)))
```

Because the blend is a harmonic mean, it is pulled toward the lower RL utilization: at $f_{\mathrm{post}} = 0.5$ it is `r round(U.blend(0.5), 2)` rather than the arithmetic average of `r round(0.5 * 0.40 + 0.5 * 0.125, 2)`; at 0.4 it is `r round(U.blend(0.4), 2)`.

**Newer evidence that runs have become more RL-heavy.** The last two rows of the table cover a much more RL-heavy run, which the most recent evidence points toward, although that evidence does not measure $f_{\mathrm{post}}$ directly. SemiAnalysis's tokenomics model (Xie et al. 2026) splits the combined GPU capacity of OpenAI and Anthropic among three uses: pretraining, post-training and RL, and inference serving. It has the split moving from 40% / 24% / 36% in the third quarter of 2025 to 7% / 55% / 38% in the fourth quarter of 2026, the last two quarters being projections. Two things separate this from $f_{\mathrm{post}}$. It is a share of *hardware-time* for the whole company, across every model and every experiment, not the FLOP of one final run; and it is a model built by SemiAnalysis, not a disclosure by the labs. The two frames can be converted with the utilization figures above: an hour of RL hardware yields 0.125 / 0.40 of the FLOP that an hour of pretraining hardware yields, so a ratio of RL to pretraining hardware-time of r corresponds to a FLOP ratio of `r 0.125 / 0.40` · r.

The two frames can be compared in mid-2025, when both are available. GPT-5's final run had RL at 0.67 times its pretraining in FLOP, which is `r round(0.67 * 0.4 / 0.125, 1)` times in hardware-time; the lab-wide chart has RL at only 0.3 to 0.6 times pretraining over the same quarters. So a flagship run was several times more RL-intensive than the company's compute as a whole, presumably because most lab-wide pretraining capacity goes to experiments and smaller models rather than to the flagship's final run. Two conclusions follow. The chart cannot be read as $f_{\mathrm{post}}$ for a single run. And since flagship runs were more RL-heavy than the lab average when the comparison can be made, the chart's later lab-wide ratios, about 4 in the second quarter of 2026 and 8 in the fourth, are if anything low for a late-2026 flagship run such as Astra.

Taken at face value, those ratios would put a late-2026 run's post-training share at `r round(100 * (4 * 0.125 / 0.4) / (1 + 4 * 0.125 / 0.4))`% (ratio 4) to `r round(100 * (8 * 0.125 / 0.4) / (1 + 8 * 0.125 / 0.4))`% (ratio 8). $U_F$ would fall to `r round(U.blend(0.6), 2)`–`r round(U.blend(0.75), 2)`. The Astra total for 100k GPUs over three to four months would be 1.7–$2.3\times10^{27}$ at a 60% share and 2.8–$3.7\times10^{27}$ at 75%, rather than 1.2–$1.5\times10^{27}$. And because $F_E$ is proportional to a frontier run's total hardware-time (§S.1.1.3), which is (1 + r) times its pretraining hardware-time, the run would take `r round((1 + 4) / (1 + (0.4 / 0.6) * (0.4 / 0.125)), 1)`–`r round((1 + 8) / (1 + (0.4 / 0.6) * (0.4 / 0.125)), 1)` times the hardware-time that $f_{\mathrm{post}} = 0.40$ implies, and an $F_E$ anchored on Astra's hardware would be larger by the same factor: roughly `r round(F.E.fpost(0.4) * (1 + 4) / (1 + (0.4 / 0.6) * (0.4 / 0.125)) / 1e6)`–`r round(F.E.fpost(0.4) * (1 + 8) / (1 + (0.4 / 0.6) * (0.4 / 0.125)) / 1e6)`M H100e rather than `r round(F.E.fpost(0.4) / 1e6, 1)`M.

**Adopted: the post-training share of a frontier run's FLOP, $f_{\mathrm{post}} = 0.40$, and with it the frontier utilization $U_F = `r round(U.blend(0.40), 2)`$**, the fraction of peak throughput a present-day frontier training run sustains.

**Direction of conservatism.** The late-2026 value of $f_{\mathrm{post}}$ is not known: the one per-run estimate, from mid-2025, gives 0.40, and the lab-wide trend since then is consistent with anything from 0.6 upward for a single run. Every value above 0.40 raises the Astra total, and so $C_F$; lowers $U_F$; and raises $F_E$. A larger $F_E$ is the regime-favorable direction, because it means a larger covert fleet, which is harder to hide and easier to police. So 0.40 is adopted as the regime-unfavorable end of the range, not as a central estimate, and the paper's $F_E$ is a floor in this respect: on the lab-wide trend the true figure could be two to three times higher.

```{r ufe}
f.post <- 0.40
U.F <- U.blend(f.post)
c(U_F = U.F)
```

## S.1.2 The fleet trajectories

The world accelerator fleet, and the national and company fleets inside it, are used at four points: §4.4's transition timeline needs the stock at the start of Phase 2 and the rate at which it is being replaced; §6.4.2's transitional-service exposure needs the U.S.-located and Chinese fleets; §6.4.3's dark-compute residual needs the composition of the U.S. fleet; and the leading lab's own fleet is the yardstick $F_E$ is checked against in §S.4.5.

**One world model serves all of them.** Epoch's quarterly chip-sales data run out partway through 2026; the model fills the gap centrally, then grows the quarterly flow at a fixed rate. The national fleets are shares of that model or are built from the same source, so the pieces sum. §S.1.2.1–§S.1.2.6 build the world model; §S.1.2.7–§S.1.2.9 take the United States, China and the leading lab in turn.

**Adopted: a world fleet of 47M H100e at year-end 2026, of which three quarters (35M) is located in the United States and 3.1M is China's; and a leading lab at 6.4M H100e.**

**Adopted: the world accelerator fleet at year-end 2026, 47M H100e on a sold basis, produced by one world model that every later fleet quantity uses; and the Phase 2 duration of §4.4, that fleet divided by the model's own year-end installable flow of 2.9M H100e per month, about 16 months.**

The world accelerator fleet is the total number of AI accelerators in existence, measured in H100e. Several quantities in the paper depend on it: the size of the fleet at year-end 2026 that a treaty would have to register, the part of it located in the United States (§S.1.2.7), the length of Phase 2 (how long it takes to replace the fleet with inference-only hardware), and the share of it serving inference (§S.7.2). Rather than estimate each of these separately, this section builds one model of the fleet over time and every later section draws on it, so that all of these quantities are consistent with one another.

Two conventions govern the count. First, it is a *stock*: every accelerator ever sold and still counted, not the number shipped in a period. Second, it is counted on a *sold* basis, that is, at the point where the vendor recognises the revenue, which is somewhat before the chip is installed and running; §S.1.2.5 explains why that is the right basis for a registration regime.

The model has three pieces, described in the subsections that follow. Up to the end of 2025 it uses Epoch AI's cumulative count of accelerators by owner (§S.1.2.1). For the first half of 2026 it adds Epoch's quarterly shipment data, which are still incomplete for some vendors, with the missing rows filled in by the authors (§S.1.2.2 and §S.1.2.3). From the third quarter of 2026 onward, where there are no data, it assumes that the quarterly flow of new accelerators keeps growing at 2.41× per year, a judgmental input discussed in §S.1.2.4. The result is the fleet at year-end 2026 and, for the breakout calculation, its path through 2029.

### S.1.2.1 End-2025 stock

```{r fleet-stock}
Hcol <- "Compute estimate in H100e (median)"
own <- read.csv("data/ai_chip_owners_cumulative_by_designer.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
o25 <- own[own[["End date"]] == "2025-12-31" & own$Owner != "China (smuggled)", ]       # the smuggled row re-allocates chips already counted in the other rows (sales and owners totals agree without it)
by.owner <- tapply(o25[[Hcol]], o25$Owner, sum)
## A100s sold before 2022.  Epoch's chip-sales and owner data start in 2022, so these are added from its estimate of NVIDIA's installed computing
## power by generation (Emberson and Owen 2025): cumulative Ampere FLOP/s through 2021Q4, at 989 TFLOP/s per H100e, by quarter of sale.
nv <- read.csv("data/nvidia_flops_by_generation.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
nv <- nv[nv[["Chip type"]] == "Ampere" & nv$Period <= "2021Q4" & !is.na(nv[["Cumulative FLOP/s"]]), ]; nv <- nv[order(nv$Period), ]
a100.pre <- data.frame(t = as.numeric(substr(nv$Period, 1, 4)) + (as.numeric(substr(nv$Period, 6, 6)) - 1) / 4 + 0.125, h = diff(c(0, nv[["Cumulative FLOP/s"]])) / h100e.peak)
oq.a <- read.csv("data/ai_chip_owners_quarters_by_chip_type.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
oq.a <- oq.a[oq.a[["Chip type"]] == "A100" & substr(oq.a[["Start date"]], 1, 4) == "2022", ]
a100.mix <- tapply(oq.a[[Hcol]], oq.a$Owner, sum); a100.mix <- a100.mix / sum(a100.mix)                 # the A100's buyers in 2022, its first year in Epoch's data
by.owner[names(a100.mix)] <- by.owner[names(a100.mix)] + a100.mix * sum(a100.pre$h)
by.owner <- sort(by.owner, decreasing = TRUE); stock.2025 <- sum(by.owner)
data.frame(owner = names(by.owner), M.H100e = round(by.owner / 1e6, 2), share.pct = round(100 * by.owner / stock.2025, 1), row.names = NULL)
c("world stock, end-2025 (M H100e)" = stock.2025 / 1e6, "  of which A100s sold before 2022 (M)" = sum(a100.pre$h) / 1e6)
```

Source: Epoch AI 2026c, "Data on AI Chip Owners" (updated 2026-05-12). Epoch's published headlines are reproduced before the addition described next: about 20M sold, five hyperscalers 71%, Google about 25%, China "just over 5%". Epoch's per-firm 90% intervals are roughly −23/+29% (the "Other" bucket −33/+42%).

**Chips sold before 2022.** Epoch's owner and sales data begin in the first quarter of 2022, so the count above starts from zero then. Two groups of older chips are therefore missing. *A100s sold in 2020 and 2021* are accelerators of the class this analysis counts, and they are added: Epoch's estimate of NVIDIA's installed computing power by chip generation, built from NVIDIA's data-center revenue (Emberson and Owen 2025), puts the A100 generation at $2.2\times10^{20}$ FLOP/s through the end of 2021, which is `r signif(sum(a100.pre$h) / 1e6, 2)`M H100e at 989 TFLOP/s each. They are assigned to owners in the proportions in which A100s were bought in 2022 (`r round(100 * (1 - a100.mix[["Other"]] - a100.mix[["China"]]))`% the seven large firms, `r round(100 * a100.mix[["Other"]])`% other owners, `r round(100 * a100.mix[["China"]])`% China). That estimate assigns all of NVIDIA's data-center revenue to a chip generation, and for 2022 it shows about twice the A100-generation compute that Epoch's chip-sales data do, so it is the larger of the two readings and is used as the regime-unfavorable one. *Generations before the A100* (the V100, P100 and K80, about 0.11M H100e at their 2021 peak on the same estimate, nearly all of it V100) are left out: the cloud providers have retired them (§S.1.2.6), and a V100 is comparable to a high-end consumer card, so they belong with the consumer GPUs of §S.7.3.

### S.1.2.2 Quarterly flow in 2026, and the rows that are missing

```{r fleet-flow}
sal <- read.csv("data/ai_chip_sales_timelines_by_chip.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
sal$start <- as.Date(sal[["Start date"]]); sal <- sal[!is.na(sal$start), ]
sal$q <- sprintf("%s Q%d", format(sal$start, "%Y"), (as.integer(format(sal$start, "%m")) - 1) %/% 3 + 1)
sal$incomplete <- sal$Incomplete %in% c(TRUE, "True", "true", "Yes")
flow <- tapply(sal[[Hcol]], list(sal$q, sal[["Chip manufacturer"]]), sum, na.rm = TRUE); flow[is.na(flow)] <- 0
flow <- flow[order(rownames(flow)), ]
recentq <- c("2025 Q1", "2025 Q2", "2025 Q3", "2025 Q4", "2026 Q1", "2026 Q2", "2026 Q3")
cbind(round(flow[recentq, ] / 1e6, 3), total = round(rowSums(flow[recentq, ]) / 1e6, 2),
      any.incomplete = tapply(sal$incomplete, sal$q, any)[recentq])
c("check: Epoch's cumulative sales, 2022 through 2025, equal its owners-hub stock (M)" = sum(flow[rownames(flow) <= "2025 Q4", ]) / 1e6)
annual <- tapply(rowSums(flow), substr(rownames(flow), 1, 4), sum)
round(rbind("annual flow (M H100e)" = annual[c("2022", "2023", "2024", "2025")] / 1e6,
            "growth over previous year (x)" = c(NA, annual[c("2023", "2024", "2025")] / annual[c("2022", "2023", "2024")])), 2)
```

Source: Epoch AI 2026d, "Data on AI Chip Sales" (updated 2026-08-27). Read as listed, the 2026 flow looks flat (4.4M, 4.5M, 4.5M per quarter). It is not: the 2026 quarters have **no Huawei, Amazon (Trainium) or Cambricon rows yet**, the Q2 2026 Google row covers only about a month of the quarter (flagged Incomplete), and Q3 2026 has a partial Nvidia row only. Nvidia's rows, which are complete, grow about 16% per quarter.

### S.1.2.3 Gap-fill

Epoch's chip-sales data are complete through the end of 2025 and complete for Nvidia in 2026, but for four other vendors the 2026 quarters are missing or partial: Epoch had not yet published rows for Huawei, Amazon and Cambricon, and its Google row for the second quarter covers only part of the quarter. Left as listed, the first half of 2026 would understate the flow and make it look flat. Each missing quantity is therefore filled in with a single value derived from an outside estimate of the vendor's 2026 output where one exists (Huawei) and otherwise from the vendor's own recent rows (Amazon, Cambricon, Google). Together the fills add about 1.7M H100e over the two quarters, under 4% of the year-end 2026 fleet, so the fleet is not sensitive to the exact values.

**Huawei.** Epoch lists Huawei's Ascend 910B and 910C shipments at a flat 0.13M H100e in every quarter of 2025, and nothing for 2026. Somala (2026), Epoch's own study of Huawei's roadmap, puts 2026 production at a median of 1.5 million units, which "translates to 880,000 H100-equivalents", or about 0.22M per quarter, after allowing for the high-bandwidth-memory shortage that limits how many of those units are full-specification accelerators. The fill takes Somala's estimate at face value: 0.88M spread evenly over the year, 0.22M per quarter, rather than Epoch's flat 0.13M, because Somala's figure is a production estimate for the whole year while Epoch's rows record shipments as they are confirmed and tend to be revised upward later. Epoch's rate would add 0.18M less over the two quarters. The same rate is used for China's 2026 additions in §S.1.2.8, so the two sections share one assumption about Chinese production.

**Amazon.** Epoch's Trainium2 rows rise through 2025, from 0.14M H100e in the first quarter to 0.22M in the fourth, and stop there. The fill extrapolates that ramp geometrically: the growth rate per quarter over 2025 is the cube root of the ratio of the fourth-quarter row to the first, about 17%, and the two 2026 quarters continue the fourth-quarter rate at that growth, giving about 0.26M and 0.30M (the chunk prints the exact values). No outside estimate of 2026 Trainium output was found, so this is the one fill that rests on Epoch's rows alone; holding the fourth-quarter rate flat instead would add 0.12M less over the two quarters, a quarter of a percent of the year-end fleet.

**Nvidia** needs no fill: its rows are complete for the first two quarters of 2026 (and grow about 16% per quarter). Epoch's third-quarter Nvidia row is partial, but the model of §S.1.2.4 takes over from the third quarter, so it is not used.

**Cambricon.** Epoch lists Cambricon, China's other accelerator designer, at 0.005–0.008M H100e per quarter through 2025. The fill is 0.01M per quarter, a rounding of the recent rate; it is immaterial to the fleet and is included so that China's additions in §S.1.2.8 are complete.

**Google.** Google's TPUs are the second-largest flow after Nvidia. Epoch's row for the second quarter of 2026 is flagged as incomplete and totals 0.32M H100e, about 38% of the first-quarter total of 0.85M, consistent with covering roughly the first month of the quarter. The fill replaces it with a full quarter at 0.92M, the first-quarter rate with modest growth (8%; Epoch's rows show 2–4% growth per quarter into early 2026, and a new TPU generation was ramping), rather than adding to the partial row.

The chunk below applies these fills to the listed rows. The growth rate it reports, from the fourth quarter of 2025 to the gap-filled second quarter of 2026, is the realised pace of the flow at the point where the model of §S.1.2.4 takes over.

```{r fleet-gapfill}
huawei.q    <- 0.88e6 / 4                                            # Somala 2026: 880k H100e of Huawei output in 2026, spread evenly
tr <- flow[c("2025 Q1", "2025 Q4"), "Amazon"]; g.tr <- (tr[2] / tr[1])^(1 / 3)   # Trainium: growth per quarter over 2025, from Epoch's rows
trainium.q  <- tr[2] * g.tr^(1:2)                                    # Q1 and Q2 2026 by geometric extrapolation of the Q4 2025 rate
cambricon.q <- 0.01e6
gap.q <- huawei.q + trainium.q + cambricon.q                         # per quarter (Q1, Q2)
round(c("Huawei per quarter (M)" = huawei.q / 1e6, "Trainium growth per quarter over 2025 (x)" = g.tr, "Trainium Q1 2026 (M)" = trainium.q[1] / 1e6, "Trainium Q2 2026 (M)" = trainium.q[2] / 1e6), 3)
q4  <- sum(flow["2025 Q4", ])
q1f <- sum(flow["2026 Q1", ]) + gap.q[1]
q2f <- sum(flow["2026 Q2", ]) - flow["2026 Q2", "Google"] + 0.92e6 + gap.q[2]
g.q <- (q2f / q4)^(1 / 2)                                            # geometric mean quarter-on-quarter growth, Q4 2025 -> Q2 2026
round(c("Q4 2025 (M)" = q4 / 1e6, "Q1 2026 gap-filled (M)" = q1f / 1e6, "Q2 2026 gap-filled (M)" = q2f / 1e6, "growth per quarter (%)" = 100 * (g.q - 1)), 2)
```

### S.1.2.4 The world model: year-end 2026 and beyond

Past the quarters for which there are data, the world *flow* grows at **2.41×/yr**, a judgmental input equal to the product of the two trends in §1.1 of the AI 2040 compute supplement (Dean 2026a): AI capital expenditure about 1.72×/yr (Q3 2023 to Q4 2025, from Epoch's hyperscaler capex data) and cost-efficiency, H100e per dollar, about 1.4×/yr. That is the supplement's *naive baseline*, not its judgmental forecast, which re-forecasts capex from hyperscaler finances and throttles cost-efficiency with an EUV scarcity surcharge. The extrapolation picks up from the gap-filled Q2 2026 flow and the stock through Q2 2026.

```{r fleet-ye2026}
stock.q2 <- stock.2025 + q1f + q2f
g.flow <- 2.41                                                  # 1.72 (AI capex) x 1.40 (H100e per $): Dean 2026a, sec. 1.1
make.world <- function(g.flow, n.q = 18) {                      # quarter-ends Q2 2026 ... Q4 2030; t = years after end-2025
  fq <- q2f * (g.flow^(1 / 4))^(1:n.q)
  data.frame(t = 0.5 + 0.25 * (0:n.q), flow = c(q2f, fq), W = stock.q2 + c(0, cumsum(fq))) }
make.W <- function(wq) function(t) exp(approx(c(0, 0.25, wq$t), log(c(stock.2025, stock.2025 + q1f, wq$W)), xout = t, rule = 2)$y)   # log-linear between quarter-ends
world.q <- make.world(g.flow); W.of <- make.W(world.q)
adds <- c("2026" = q1f + q2f + sum(world.q$flow[2:3]), "2027" = sum(world.q$flow[4:7]), "2028" = sum(world.q$flow[8:11]), "2029" = sum(world.q$flow[12:15]))
round(rbind("world additions (M H100e)" = adds, "world stock, year-end (M H100e)" = W.of(1:4)) / 1e6, 1)
fleet.ye2026 <- W.of(1)                                         # the year-end 2026 fleet: derived, carried at full precision, printed as 47M
flow.q4.2026 <- world.q$flow[3]                                 # the model's Q4 2026 quarterly flow
us.frac <- 0.75                                                 # fraction of the fleet located in the U.S.: "about three quarters" (section S.1.2.7)
round(c("stock through Q2 2026 (M)" = stock.q2 / 1e6, "world fleet, year-end 2026 (M)" = fleet.ye2026 / 1e6,
        "monthly installable flow at year-end 2026 = Q4 2026 flow / 3 (M per month)" = flow.q4.2026 / 3 / 1e6,
        "  observed, gap-filled Q2 2026 / 3" = q2f / 3 / 1e6, "  observed as listed, Q2 2026 / 3" = sum(flow["2026 Q2", ]) / 3 / 1e6,
        "Phase 2 = fleet / monthly flow (months)" = fleet.ye2026 / (flow.q4.2026 / 3), "  at the observed gap-filled Q2 rate (months)" = fleet.ye2026 / (q2f / 3)), 2)
phase2.rate <- flow.q4.2026 / 3                                 # H100e per month installable in Phase 2: the world model's Q4 2026 flow, so stock and flow come from the same model at the same date (section 3.4)
phase2.months <- fleet.ye2026 / phase2.rate
round(c("Phase 2 = fleet / the Q4 2026 monthly flow (months)" = phase2.months, "Phases 1+2 = 26 months + Phase 2 (years)" = (26 + phase2.months) / 12), 2)
```

2.41×/yr is a central trend, not a conservative one, and it sits above the realized 2026 flow growth. Epoch's own figures give a slightly higher product: performance per dollar +49%/yr since 2023 (90% CI 1.36–1.66×; Epoch AI 2026a) and hyperscaler capex +72%/yr (90% CI 66–78%; Juniewicz 2026d), about 2.56×. There is no supply throttle here; the supplement's forecast has additions growing about 1.5× in 2029 where this path has 2.41×.

```{r fleet-figure, fig.width = 10, fig.height = 4.4, fig.cap = "Left: quarterly flow of AI accelerators by designer (Epoch chip-sales data), with the 2026 gap-fill in grey. Right: the cumulative stock through Q2 2026 and the world model's year-end 2026 value."}
library(patchwork)
fl <- as.data.frame(as.table(flow[rownames(flow) >= "2024 Q1" & rownames(flow) <= "2026 Q2", ])); names(fl) <- c("q", "designer", "h")
gap <- data.frame(q = c("2026 Q1", "2026 Q2"), designer = "gap-fill (authors)", h = c(q1f - sum(flow["2026 Q1", ]), q2f - sum(flow["2026 Q2", ])))
fl <- rbind(fl, gap); fl$designer <- factor(fl$designer, levels = c("gap-fill (authors)", "Cambricon", "Huawei", "AMD", "Amazon", "Google", "Nvidia"))
p.flow <- ggplot(fl, aes(q, h / 1e6, fill = designer)) + geom_col(width = 0.8, colour = "#5A6470", linewidth = 0.15) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("gap-fill (authors)" = "#F2E6E3", Cambricon = "#5A6470", Huawei = "#8C3B2E", AMD = "#C9CBCE", Amazon = "#E3EBF2", Google = "#2E5F8C", Nvidia = "#33393F"), name = NULL) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "M H100e per quarter", title = "Quarterly flow (sold basis)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank(), axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1), legend.position = "bottom", legend.key.size = unit(0.8, "lines")) + guides(fill = guide_legend(nrow = 1, reverse = TRUE))
cum <- sum(a100.pre$h) + cumsum(rowSums(flow)); cum <- cum[names(cum) >= "2023 Q4" & names(cum) <= "2025 Q4"]
qend <- function(q) as.Date(sprintf("%s-%02d-01", substr(q, 1, 4), 3 * as.integer(substr(q, 7, 7)))) + 30
stock.df <- rbind(data.frame(date = qend(names(cum)), h = cum), data.frame(date = as.Date(c("2026-03-31", "2026-06-30")), h = c(stock.2025 + q1f, stock.q2)))
p.stock <- ggplot() + geom_line(data = stock.df, aes(date, h / 1e6), linewidth = 0.9) + geom_point(data = stock.df, aes(date, h / 1e6), size = 1.8) +
  annotate("segment", x = as.Date("2026-06-30"), xend = as.Date("2026-12-31"), y = stock.q2 / 1e6, yend = fleet.ye2026 / 1e6, linetype = "22", colour = "#8C3B2E") +
  annotate("point", x = as.Date("2026-12-31"), y = fleet.ye2026 / 1e6, colour = "#8C3B2E", size = 3.2) +
  annotate("text", x = as.Date("2026-11-20"), y = fleet.ye2026 / 1e6 + 2.5, label = sprintf("year-end 2026: %.0fM", fleet.ye2026 / 1e6), hjust = 1, size = 3.5, colour = "#8C3B2E") +
  year_axis(2024, 2026, date = TRUE, limits = as.Date(c("2023-12-01", "2027-03-01"))) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "M H100e (cumulative, sold basis)", title = "World stock") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + year_theme + theme(panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank())
p.flow + p.stock + plot_layout(widths = c(1.15, 1))
```

### S.1.2.5 Judgment calls in the world model

* **Sold, not deployed.** You (2026) puts *deployed* capacity at 12–16M of the ~20M sold at end-2025; a deployed-basis year-end figure would be roughly 0.7–0.8 of the sold one. The sold basis is the right one for a registration regime (every sold chip must be accounted for) and the larger number for the breakout ledger.
* **No retirements.** Every chip sold is still counted: nothing is removed for failure or retirement. Chips sold before 2024, the oldest counted (A100s from 2020–21 and everything sold in 2022–2023), are about `r round(100 * (sum(a100.pre$h) + sum(flow[rownames(flow) <= "2023 Q4", ])) / stock.2025)`% of the end-2025 stock in H100e terms. §S.1.2.6 examines what this convention leaves out. Failures at the Delta rate measured on young chips would be about half a percent of the stock, and no cloud provider has retired a generation as young as the A100; but failure rates for chips three or more years old are not known, and on the Titan supercomputer they rose sharply once a defect emerged (Ostrouchov et al. 2020). The convention therefore overstates the fleet by an unknown but probably small amount. Overstating the fleet overstates every breakout exposure that scales with it, which is the regime-unfavorable direction, so the convention is conservative.
* **Phase 2 (§4.4).** Phase 2 is the period in which the pre-treaty fleet is replaced by inference-only hardware, so its length is the year-end 2026 fleet divided by the rate at which inference-only accelerators can be installed. The paper takes that rate from the same world model as the fleet: the model's Q4 2026 flow, `r round(flow.q4.2026 / 3 / 1e6, 1)`M H100e per month, so that stock and flow are measured at the same date. That gives `r round(phase2.months)` months, and with Phase 1's 26 months about `r round((26 + phase2.months) / 12, 1)` years. The observed shipment rate in Epoch's chip-sales data for Q2 2026 is lower, `r round(sum(flow["2026 Q2", ]) / 3 / 1e6, 2)`M per month as listed (`r round(q2f / 3 / 1e6, 1)`M with the §S.1.2.3 gap-fill), and would give `r round(fleet.ye2026 / (sum(flow["2026 Q2", ]) / 3))` (`r round(fleet.ye2026 / (q2f / 3))`) months; that is the regime-unfavorable reading, but it pairs a year-end stock with a mid-year flow. Phase 1's 26 months are derived in §4.4 of the paper, not here.
* **Direction of conservatism.** The fleet has no single conservative direction. A larger fleet raises every breakout exposure in §6.4.2, which is regime-unfavorable. It has no effect on the adopted $F_E$ or $F_B$, both of which are built from $C_F$ rather than from the fleet. So the world model is a central estimate rather than a conservative one. The uncertainty in it is comparatively small: the stock through mid-2026 is Epoch's data plus fills worth under 4%, and the only projection is two quarters of flow, so plausible alternatives for the second half of 2026 (a flat flow, or the first-half pace continued) move the year-end fleet by only a few million H100e, within about 5% of 47M.

### S.1.2.6 Failure and retirement by vintage, at year-end 2026

How much of the stock counted above has in fact left service by the time of the agreement, either because the chip failed or because its owner retired it as uneconomic? (What leaves service *after* the agreement is not a concern here: licensed operators must destroy retired chips verifiably.)

The failure rate is measured on the only public record of replacements in a production AI cluster: Delta, the Illinois NCSA machine, which reported 6 accelerator replacements over its A100 and H100 partitions. It is used again in §S.4.3, where hardware lifetime is a supporting argument for the covert evasion horizon $T_E$.

```{r delta-failures}
gpu.years <- (448 * 895 + 608 * 146) / 365
fail.rate <- c(low = qgamma(0.025, 6), central = 6, high = qgamma(0.975, 7)) / gpu.years      # replacements per GPU-year; exact Poisson 95% interval on 6 events
round(c("GPU-years observed" = gpu.years, 100 * fail.rate, "A100 alone (%/yr)" = 100 * 4 / (448 * 895 / 365), "H100 alone (%/yr)" = 100 * 2 / (608 * 146 / 365),
        "Llama-3 interruption rate, for contrast (%/yr)" = 100 * (148 + 72) / 16384 / (54 / 365)), 2)
```

* **Mechanical failure:** the Delta replacement rate above, `r round(100 * fail.rate[["central"]], 2)`% per year (95% interval `r round(100 * fail.rate[["low"]], 2)`–`r round(100 * fail.rate[["high"]], 2)`%), applied to each quarter's sales from the middle of the quarter. (A chip replaced under warranty is swapped for a new one, so this is an upper bound on the net loss to the fleet.)
* **Economic retirement:** none yet among the chips counted. The oldest generation in the stock is the A100, launched in 2020 and so about six and a half years old at year-end 2026, and no large cloud provider has retired a GPU generation that young. Azure's K80, P100 and P40 families: "These products will be retired on August 31st 2023, and the oldest VMs in this series launched in 2016" (Microsoft 2023); "NVIDIA P100 GPUs on Google Cloud will reach End of Support (EOS) on September 15, 2026" (Google Cloud 2026), ten years after that GPU's launch; Azure retired its V100 family in 2025, about eight years after that GPU's launch (Microsoft 2025).

```{r vintage-loss}
v <- data.frame(vintage = as.integer(format(sal$start, "%Y")), t.sale = as.numeric(format(sal$start, "%Y")) + (as.integer(format(sal$start, "%m")) - 1) / 12 + 0.125,
                h = sal[[Hcol]], units = sal[["Number of Units"]])
v <- v[!is.na(v$h) & !is.na(v$units), ]
v$failed <- 1 - exp(-fail.rate[["central"]] * pmax(0, 2027 - v$t.sale))
by.v <- sapply(split(v, v$vintage), function(d) c("units sold (k)" = sum(d$units) / 1e3, "H100e sold (k)" = sum(d$h) / 1e3,
                                                  "failed by year-end 2026, % of units" = 100 * sum(d$units * d$failed) / sum(d$units), "failed, % of H100e" = 100 * sum(d$h * d$failed) / sum(d$h)))
round(cbind(by.v, all = c(sum(v$units) / 1e3, sum(v$h) / 1e3, 100 * sum(v$units * v$failed) / sum(v$units), 100 * sum(v$h * v$failed) / sum(v$h))), 2)     # 2026 = Epoch's listed rows only, through the partial Q3
```

```{r vintage-loss-model}
#### The same on the WORLD MODEL's flows, which complete 2026 (gap-fill plus the modelled second half); H100e only, since the model has no unit counts.
wm <- data.frame(t.sale = c(as.numeric(substr(rownames(flow), 1, 4)) + (as.numeric(substr(rownames(flow), 7, 7)) - 1) / 4 + 0.125)[rownames(flow) <= "2025 Q4"], h = rowSums(flow)[rownames(flow) <= "2025 Q4"])
wm <- rbind(data.frame(t.sale = a100.pre$t, h = a100.pre$h), wm, data.frame(t.sale = 2026 + c(0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75) + 0.125, h = c(q1f, q2f, world.q$flow[2:3])))   # with the A100s sold before 2022
failed.share <- sapply(fail.rate, function(r) sum(wm$h * (1 - exp(-r * (2027 - wm$t.sale)))) / sum(wm$h))
round(c("world stock, year-end 2026 (M)" = sum(wm$h) / 1e6, "H100e-weighted mean age (years)" = sum(wm$h * (2027 - wm$t.sale)) / sum(wm$h), 100 * failed.share), 2)
round(c("U.S.-located H100e failed by year-end 2026 (k): " = us.frac * fleet.ye2026 * failed.share / 1e3))
```

At the Delta rate, failures run from about 2% of the 2022 vintage to 0.3% of the 2026 vintage; because the stock is young (its H100e-weighted mean age is about one year) they come to about half a percent of the H100e, and nothing has been retired for age. That is a lower bound on what has left service rather than an estimate of it. The Delta rate was measured on chips in their first years at a serviced site, and failure hazards at greater ages are not known: on the Titan supercomputer the original GPUs failed at 12–15% a year after a component defect took hold, while sound replacement boards ran at 0.2–0.3% a year over their first three years (Ostrouchov et al. 2020). Chips that failed and were scrapped are counted here as still in the fleet; since a larger counted fleet means larger breakout exposures, the "no retirements" convention errs on the regime-unfavorable side. For the ledger the relevant number is the last line: the H100e that U.S. owners could *legitimately* report as failed by year-end 2026 is about `r round(us.frac * fleet.ye2026 * failed.share[['central']] / 1e3)`k (`r round(us.frac * fleet.ye2026 * failed.share[['low']] / 1e3)`–`r round(us.frac * fleet.ye2026 * failed.share[['high']] / 1e3)`k over the Delta interval), which is the honest baseline against which any claimed losses would be read (§S.6).

### S.1.2.7 The U.S.-located fleet

Several later sections need the part of the world fleet that sits on U.S. soil, which is what a breakout government could seize (§6.4.2). No dataset measures that directly: Epoch's chip-owners data assigns chips to the buyer's headquarters and says location is out of scope. Two published measurements bear on it.

**Two measurements.**

```{r us-measured}
us.seven <- c("Google", "Microsoft", "Amazon", "Meta", "Oracle", "CoreWeave", "xAI")
gc <- read.csv("data/gpu_clusters.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
gc$h <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(gc[["H100 equivalents"]])); gc$h[is.na(gc$h)] <- 0
gc <- gc[gc$Status == "Existing" & gc[["Include in Standard Analysis"]] %in% c(TRUE, "True", "true"), ]
gc$us <- gc$Country == "United States of America"; gc$cn <- gc$Country == "China"
round(c("OWNED by the seven named U.S. firms, % of the end-2025 world stock (Epoch chip owners)" = 100 * sum(by.owner[us.seven]) / stock.2025,
        "LOCATED in the U.S., % of tracked cluster performance (Epoch GPU clusters, through June 2025)" = 100 * sum(gc$h[gc$us]) / sum(gc$h),
        "  tracked H100e in that dataset, % of the end-2025 stock" = 100 * sum(gc$h) / stock.2025), 1)
```

* **Location.** "The United States contains about three-quarters of global GPU cluster performance, with China in second place with 15%" (Pilz et al. 2025). Recomputed above from Epoch's standard-analysis set. The dataset is now deprecated, stops in June 2025, and tracks only a small part of the stock.
* **Ownership.** Five hyperscalers, CoreWeave and xAI own 78% of the end-2025 world stock (Epoch AI 2026c). This covers the whole stock but is ownership, not location. Two corrections run in opposite directions, and neither is measured: those firms' overseas capacity lowers the located share, and U.S.-located chips owned by everyone else raise it.

Both come out near three quarters. **Adopted: 0.75**, a judgmental input and a round number. It is carried forward to year-end 2026 unchanged; Epoch's data-center timelines have the U.S. share of tracked capacity at 92% at end-2025, 94% now, and 91–92% planned for year-end 2026 and 2027, so the mix of new capacity is not shifting.

```{r us-fleet}
us.fleet.ye2026 <- us.frac * fleet.ye2026
round(c("U.S.-located fleet, year-end 2026 (M H100e)" = us.fleet.ye2026 / 1e6,
        "  share of the world fleet (%)" = 100 * us.frac), 2)
```

**Brackets from data alone.**

```{r us-brackets}
dcs <- read.csv("data/data_centers.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
dcs$h <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(dcs[["Current H100 equivalents"]])); dcs$h[is.na(dcs$h)] <- 0; dcs <- dcs[dcs$h > 0, ]
dcs$us <- dcs$Country %in% c("United States", "United States of America")
round(c("floor: chips Epoch has located at U.S. sites / world stock through Q2 2026 (%)" = 100 * sum(dcs$h[dcs$us]) / stock.q2,
        "all-workload hyperscale capacity, U.S. share (Synergy Research Group 2025) (%)" = 55,
        "largest AI campuses only: U.S. share of tracked data-center capacity (%)" = 100 * sum(dcs$h[dcs$us]) / sum(dcs$h)), 1)
```

Epoch's AI Data Centers hub locates `r round(sum(dcs$h[dcs$us])/1e6, 1)`M H100e at `r sum(dcs$us)` U.S. sites by satellite and permit evidence; that alone is `r round(100 * sum(dcs$h[dcs$us]) / stock.q2)`% of the world stock. The hub's `r round(100 * sum(dcs$h[dcs$us]) / sum(dcs$h))`% U.S. share is not an estimate of the whole: it tracks the very largest campuses, which are nearly all American. Synergy Research's 55% is the U.S. share of hyperscale data-center capacity for all workloads (cloud, search, storage, content delivery), which sit closer to users than AI training does; Synergy notes that "AI-driven expansion has also seen the US share of worldwide hyperscale operational capacity increase" (from 52% three years earlier).

**Judgment calls.**

* **The number itself** is a judgmental input, not a derived quantity; the two measurements inform it and do not determine it.
* **Location, not ownership.** U.S. firms own more than is on U.S. soil (78% by the seven named firms alone). Their overseas capacity is under U.S. corporate control but foreign jurisdiction, and is counted here with the host country.
* **Direction of conservatism.** A larger U.S.-located fleet is the regime-unfavorable side (a larger breakout exposure). 0.75 is not chosen as the unfavorable end: the data alone allow a higher share (§S.5.7). Nothing downstream turns on the difference: between 0.70 and 0.80 the U.S.-located fleet is `r round(0.70 * fleet.ye2026 / 1e6, 1)`–`r round(0.80 * fleet.ye2026 / 1e6, 1)`M H100e.
* The Phase 2 duration (§S.1.2.5) does not depend on the fraction: it scales the fleet and the installable flow alike.

### S.1.2.8 China’s fleet

China's fleet at year-end 2026 is an absolute quantity, not a fraction of the world fleet. It has three layers: the stock Epoch tracks under Chinese ownership at end-2025, the 2026 additions to it, and chips diverted around U.S. export controls (Epoch's term is "smuggled"), which Epoch estimates separately.

**Tracked stock and its 2026 additions.**

```{r china-tracked}
cn25 <- o25[o25$Owner == "China", ]
cn.by <- tapply(cn25[[Hcol]], cn25[["Chip manufacturer"]], sum)
cn.by[["Nvidia"]] <- cn.by[["Nvidia"]] + a100.mix[["China"]] * sum(a100.pre$h)                                  # China's share of the A100s sold before 2022 (section S.1.2.1)
china.official.2025 <- sum(cn.by)
round(c(cn.by, "tracked stock, end-2025" = china.official.2025) / 1e6, 2)
china.add.2026 <- c(Huawei = 4 * huawei.q, Cambricon = 4 * cambricon.q, "Nvidia (licensed H200)" = 0.02e6)     # Huawei, Cambricon: the section S.1.2.3 gap-fill rates; H200: deliveries reported to date
china.official.2026 <- china.official.2025 + sum(china.add.2026)
round(c(china.add.2026, "tracked stock, year-end 2026" = china.official.2026) / 1e6, 2)
```

Source: Epoch AI 2026c. Huawei and Cambricon enter 2026 at exactly the rates already used to gap-fill the world flow in §S.1.2.3, so there is one set of assumptions about Chinese production. The Huawei rate is Somala's (2026) median of 880,000 H100e for the year, an estimate that already allows for the memory bottleneck: only about a fifth of the 1.5M units rely on Chinese-made HBM, half use non-HBM memory, and the rest use the remaining foreign stockpile and HBM obtained around the export controls. Nvidia's sales into China have nearly stopped. Epoch's rows show H20 sales falling from 54k H100e in Q1 2025 to 23k, 3k and then nothing. H200 sales were licensed in January 2026 (up to 75,000 units for each of roughly ten approved buyers), but nothing shipped until August, when "ByteDance and Tencent have each taken delivery of roughly 10,000 H200 processors over recent weeks" (TECHi 2026, relaying the *Financial Times*). Nvidia said these sales were "less than 1 per cent" of its US\$89 billion data-centre revenue for the quarter ending July 26 (South China Morning Post 2026), and its guidance for the following quarter "is not assuming any Data Center compute revenue from China" (NVIDIA 2026e). An H200 is 1.0 H100e in Epoch's data, so the 2026 addition is the 0.02M delivered so far, with nothing assumed for the rest of the year.

**Chips diverted around U.S. export controls.**

Epoch publishes a quarterly cumulative estimate (Juniewicz 2026a), beginning on 1 January 2024. The starting date reflects the evidence: "A late 2023 Center for New American Security (CNAS) analysis suggested that the volume of smuggled chips at the time was relatively low", while reporting in 2024 "found widespread evidence of banned chips being smuggled into China". For year-end 2026 the cumulative series is extrapolated **linearly**: the straight line from zero at the start of 2024 through Epoch's end-2025 median, carried one more year, which is the end-2025 value × 3/2.

```{r china-smuggled}
sm <- own[own$Owner == "China (smuggled)", ]; sm <- sm[order(sm[["End date"]]), ]
smug <- data.frame(t = 2024 + (1:nrow(sm)) / 4, cum = sm[[Hcol]], lo = sm[["H100e (5th percentile)"]], hi = sm[["H100e (95th percentile)"]])
smuggled.2025 <- smug$cum[smug$t == 2026]
smuggled.ye2026 <- smuggled.2025 * 3 / 2
round(c("diverted through 2025, median (M)" = smuggled.2025 / 1e6, "  5th percentile" = smug$lo[smug$t == 2026] / 1e6, "  95th percentile" = smug$hi[smug$t == 2026] / 1e6,
        "share of China's end-2025 fleet (%) ['roughly a third']" = 100 * smuggled.2025 / (smuggled.2025 + china.official.2025),
        "diverted through 2026 = x 3/2 (M)" = smuggled.ye2026 / 1e6), 2)
```

```{r china-smuggled-figure, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 3.8, fig.cap = "Epoch's cumulative estimate of H100e diverted to China around U.S. export controls (points: medians; bars: 5th to 95th percentile), and the linear extrapolation to year-end 2026: a straight line from zero at the start of 2024 through the end-2025 median."}
ggplot(smug, aes(t, cum / 1e6)) +
  geom_linerange(aes(ymin = lo / 1e6, ymax = hi / 1e6), colour = "#C9CBCE", linewidth = 0.8) +
  annotate("segment", x = 2024, y = 0, xend = 2027, yend = smuggled.ye2026 / 1e6, colour = "#8C3B2E", linewidth = 0.7) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  annotate("point", x = 2027, y = smuggled.ye2026 / 1e6, colour = "#8C3B2E", size = 3) +
  year_axis(2024, 2027, limits = c(2024, 2027.05)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.04)),
                     sec.axis = dup_axis(breaks = smuggled.ye2026 / 1e6, labels = sprintf("year-end 2026: %.2fM", smuggled.ye2026 / 1e6), name = NULL)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "M H100e, cumulative", title = "Compute diverted to China around U.S. export controls") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11) + year_theme + theme(panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(), axis.text.y.right = element_text(colour = "#8C3B2E", size = 9.5))
```

The diverted chips are a reallocation inside the world total, not an addition to it: Epoch's cumulative sales equal the sum of the owners' rows without the separate "China (smuggled)" row (§S.1.2.2).

**The fleet.**

```{r china-fleet}
china.fleet.ye2026 <- china.official.2026 + smuggled.ye2026
round(c("China fleet, year-end 2026 (M H100e)" = china.fleet.ye2026 / 1e6,
        "  share of the world fleet (%)" = 100 * china.fleet.ye2026 / fleet.ye2026,
        "  as a multiple of the U.S.-located fleet" = china.fleet.ye2026 / us.fleet.ye2026), 3)
```

**Uncertainty.** The estimate is wide, and most of the width is Epoch's interval on the amount diverted.

```{r china-range}
china.range <- china.official.2026 + 1.5 * c(low = smug$lo[nrow(smug)], median = smuggled.2025, high = smug$hi[nrow(smug)])      # Epoch's 5th / 95th percentile for smuggling, extrapolated the same way
round(rbind("China fleet, year-end 2026 (M H100e)" = china.range / 1e6,
            "  share of the world fleet (%)" = 100 * china.range / fleet.ye2026), 2)
```

The range spans `r round(china.range[["low"]]/1e6, 1)`M to `r round(china.range[["high"]]/1e6, 1)`M, or `r round(100 * china.range[["low"]] / fleet.ye2026, 1)`% to `r round(100 * china.range[["high"]] / fleet.ye2026, 1)`% of the world fleet. It moves no qualitative conclusion anywhere downstream: §S.7.1 shows China’s transitional breakout exposure staying an order of magnitude below the U.S. figure across the whole range.

**Judgment calls.**

* **Chips diverted around U.S. export controls are included**, because they are physically in China and available to a breakout; the median is used, and the extrapolation rule is the simplest one the data allow.
* **Licensed Nvidia sales** are counted at the deliveries reported so far (0.02M). The legal ceiling is far higher (about ten buyers × 75,000), but Beijing has held imports well below it and Nvidia guides to none.
* **Direction of conservatism.** A larger Chinese fleet is the regime-unfavorable side. The diverted part of it is an extrapolation of Epoch's central estimate of 660k H100e through 2025. Nothing downstream turns on it: §S.7.1 shows China's transitional breakout exposure staying an order of magnitude below the U.S. figure across the whole range above.

### S.1.2.9 The leading lab’s fleet

The leading lab's own fleet is estimated from data unrelated to any treaty parameter, which makes it an independent yardstick against which $F_E$ is checked in §S.4.5.

**The data, and the fitted path.**

* **F₀ = 1.7M H100e at end-2025.** You (2026, Epoch AI, 2026-05-20): "OpenAI had the equivalent of around 1.7 million Nvidia H100 GPUs by the end of 2025", from OpenAI's disclosed 1.9 GW of data-center power. Epoch's AI Chip Users hub (Epoch AI 2026f; updated 2026-09-09; `data/ai_chip_users_year_end_by_lab.csv`) now gives the same estimate with an interval:

```{r chip-users}
cu <- read.csv("data/ai_chip_users_year_end_by_lab.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
cu25 <- cu[cu$Year == 2025, c("Lab", "h100e_p5", "h100e_med", "h100e_p95")]
cu25[, -1] <- round(cu25[, -1] / 1e6, 2); cu25[order(-cu25$h100e_med), ]
oa <- cu[cu$Lab == "OpenAI", ]; c("OpenAI growth 2024->2025 (x)" = oa$h100e_med[oa$Year == 2025] / oa$h100e_med[oa$Year == 2024],
                                   "2023->2024 (x)" = oa$h100e_med[oa$Year == 2024] / oa$h100e_med[oa$Year == 2023])
```

**More recent data: OpenAI's fleet through 2026 from Epoch's AI Data Centers hub.** The year-end series stops at December 2025, but the data-centers hub (snapshot 2026-09-11; `data/data_centers.csv` and `data/data_center_timelines.csv`) lists the sites that Epoch tags as used by OpenAI, each with dated construction milestones and the H100e online at each. Epoch attaches a confidence level to each tag (confident, likely or speculative); every tagged site is included here, and a site shared with another user is counted whole. Summing the latest milestone per site gives OpenAI's *tracked* capacity over time. Tracked sites (Stargate, Fairwater, CoreWeave) do not include generic Azure regions or other clouds, so tracked capacity at end-2025 (about 1.2M) is roughly 70% of the Chip Users estimate (1.74M); the first table below scales the tracked series by that ratio.

```{r openai-timeline}
dc <- read.csv("data/data_centers.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
tl <- read.csv("data/data_center_timelines.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
tl$date <- as.Date(tl$Date); tl$h <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(tl[["H100 equivalents"]])); tl$h[is.na(tl$h)] <- 0
oa.sites <- dc$Name[grepl("OpenAI", dc$Users, ignore.case = TRUE) | grepl("OpenAI", dc$Owner, ignore.case = TRUE)]
t.oa <- tl[tl[["Data center"]] %in% oa.sites, ]
snapshot <- as.Date("2026-09-11")
latest.h <- function(site, dt) { x <- t.oa[t.oa[["Data center"]] == site & t.oa$date <= dt, ]; if (nrow(x) == 0) 0 else x$h[which.max(x$date)] }
tracked <- function(dt) sum(sapply(oa.sites, latest.h, dt = dt))
coverage <- oa$h100e_med[oa$Year == 2025] / tracked(as.Date("2025-12-31"))          # Chip Users / tracked at end-2025
key <- as.Date(c("2025-12-31", "2026-03-31", "2026-06-30", "2026-09-11"))                 # realized dates only
data.frame(date = key, tracked.M = round(sapply(key, tracked) / 1e6, 2),
           scaled.by.coverage.M = round(coverage * sapply(key, tracked) / 1e6, 2),
           path.2.5x.M = round(1.74 * 2.5^(as.numeric(key - as.Date("2025-12-31")) / 365.25), 2),
           path.3.5x.M = round(1.74 * 3.5^(as.numeric(key - as.Date("2025-12-31")) / 365.25), 2),
           path.4x.M   = round(1.74 * 4.0^(as.numeric(key - as.Date("2025-12-31")) / 365.25), 2))
```

Reading: scaled tracked capacity reached about 4.0M by the September 2026 snapshot, just under the 3.5×/yr path (4.2M) and above the 2.5× path (3.3M). The realized data through 2026 are consistent with 3.5×/yr.

**Quarterly trend of realized capacity.** Realized points: Epoch's Chip Users year-end estimates for 2023–2025, and for 2026 the tracked capacity at each quarter-end (and at the snapshot) scaled by the end-2025 coverage ratio. A log-linear fit through these points gives OpenAI's fitted path F̂(t), with no intercept forced. It is used only through year-end 2026, the pause date (§S.4.5, §S.4.6). It is not a projection for later years: left to run, it would reach about 400M H100e at year-end 2029, more than half the world stock of §S.1.2.4.

```{r openai-quarterly}
yrs.since <- function(dt) as.numeric(dt - as.Date("2025-12-31")) / 365.25
q.2026 <- as.Date(c("2026-03-31", "2026-06-30", "2026-09-11"))
real <- rbind(data.frame(date = as.Date(sprintf("%d-12-31", 2023:2025)), h = oa$h100e_med[match(2023:2025, oa$Year)], source = "Chip Users year-end"),
              data.frame(date = q.2026, h = coverage * sapply(q.2026, tracked), source = "tracked sites x coverage"))
real$t <- yrs.since(real$date)
fit.oa <- lm(log(h) ~ t, data = real)
g.fit <- exp(coef(fit.oa)[["t"]]); F.fit.2025 <- exp(coef(fit.oa)[["(Intercept)"]])     # fitted growth x/yr and fitted level at end-2025
list(realized = data.frame(real[, c("date", "source")], M.H100e = round(real$h / 1e6, 2)),
     "fitted growth x/yr" = round(g.fit, 2), "fitted level at end-2025 (M)" = round(F.fit.2025 / 1e6, 2),
     "fitted path at year-end 2026 (M)" = round(F.fit.2025 * g.fit / 1e6, 2))
```

* **The fitted growth rate.** You (2026) says OpenAI's compute "grew around 4× annually" through 2025 and reads OpenAI's own 2027 forecast ("low double-digit GW") as 2.5×/yr. The log-linear fit through the six realized points gives `r round(g.fit, 2)`×/yr and `r round(F.fit.2025/1e6, 2)`M at end-2025 (not forced through the Chip Users 1.74M), which puts the lab at `r round(F.fit.2025 * g.fit / 1e6, 1)`M H100e at year-end 2026, `r round(100 * F.fit.2025 * g.fit / fleet.ye2026)`% of the world stock of §S.1.2.4.

### S.1.2.10 The trajectories together

§S.5.7 puts the world, U.S.-located and Chinese stocks on one logarithmic scale, together with the two violator fleet sizes $F_E$ and $F_B$, and discusses how robust each of them is. It sits there rather than here because it needs $F_E$ and $F_B$, which are derived in §S.4 and §S.5; nothing in §S.1 depends on a treaty quantity.

## S.1.3 The dollar value of compute

**Adopted: roughly \$25,000 per H100e for installed accelerators treated as movable property, with a \$15,000–\$35,000 bracket.**

Several arguments in §6.4 and §6.5 are easier to weigh in money than in H100e: how much hardware would have to go missing for a dark-compute scenario to be real, what a state would forgo by hiding rather than operating its fleet, and what a buy-back would cost. Two figures in Epoch's snapshots bracket the conversion, and they differ by a factor of more than two because they measure different things.

```{r chip-dollars}
numd <- function(x) suppressWarnings(as.numeric(gsub("[$,]", "", x)))
sal.c <- sal                                                                     # Epoch's chip-sales timeline, loaded in section S.1.2.2
sal.c$C <- numd(sal.c[["Cost Estimate (USD)"]]); sal.c$Hc <- numd(sal.c[[Hcol]])
sal.c$yr <- as.numeric(format(as.Date(sal.c[["Start date"]]), "%Y"))
cs <- sal.c[!is.na(sal.c$C) & !is.na(sal.c$Hc) & sal.c$C > 0 & sal.c$Hc > 0, ]
cs$nvidia <- cs[["Chip manufacturer"]] == "Nvidia"
per <- function(d) sum(d$C) / sum(d$Hc)
by.yr <- do.call(rbind, lapply(sort(unique(cs$yr)), function(y)
  data.frame(year = y, all.accelerators = per(cs[cs$yr == y, ]), nvidia.only = per(cs[cs$yr == y & cs$nvidia, ]))))
print(format(by.yr, digits = 4, big.mark = ","), row.names = FALSE)
c("2025-26 shipments, Nvidia only ($ per H100e)" = per(cs[cs$yr >= 2025 & cs$nvidia, ]),
  "2025-26 shipments, all designers ($ per H100e)" = per(cs[cs$yr >= 2025, ]),
  "annual decline 2022 -> 2025, Nvidia only (x per year)" =
    (per(cs[cs$yr == 2022 & cs$nvidia, ]) / per(cs[cs$yr == 2025 & cs$nvidia, ]))^(1 / 3))
```

**The chip.** Epoch's chip-sales timeline carries a cost estimate for every shipment row. Over 2025–26 shipments those estimates work out at about \$17k per H100e for Nvidia data-center GPUs (\$43k for a B300, \$37k for a B200) and about \$15k across all designers. The all-designer figure is lower because captive silicon is costed internally rather than sold: TPU v6e is about \$4k a chip and TPU v7 about \$12k. For hardware that someone has to buy, or that a thief has to fence, the Nvidia figure is the relevant one.

**The installed site.** Epoch's data-center directory carries a total capital cost for each tracked site, which includes the building, the power and cooling plant, and the networking as well as the accelerators.

```{r site-dollars}
dcc <- read.csv("data/data_centers.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
dcc$Hc <- numd(dcc[["Current H100 equivalents"]]); dcc$K <- numd(dcc[["Current total capital cost (2025 USD billions)"]]) * 1e9
dcc <- dcc[!is.na(dcc$Hc) & !is.na(dcc$K) & dcc$Hc > 0 & dcc$K > 0, ]
c("sites with both figures" = nrow(dcc), "H100e covered (M)" = sum(dcc$Hc) / 1e6, "capital covered ($B)" = sum(dcc$K) / 1e9,
  "all-in capital, aggregate ($ per H100e)" = sum(dcc$K) / sum(dcc$Hc),
  "  median site" = median(dcc$K / dcc$Hc), "  lower quartile" = quantile(dcc$K / dcc$Hc, 0.25),
  "  upper quartile" = quantile(dcc$K / dcc$Hc, 0.75))
usd <- function(x) format(signif(x, 2), big.mark = ",", scientific = FALSE)               # 36,000, not 3.6e+04
```

The `r nrow(dcc)` sites that carry both figures hold `r round(sum(dcc$Hc)/1e6, 1)`M H100e against \$`r round(sum(dcc$K)/1e9)`B of capital, or about \$`r usd(sum(dcc$K)/sum(dcc$Hc))` per H100e; the median site is \$`r usd(median(dcc$K/dcc$Hc))` and the interquartile range is \$`r usd(quantile(dcc$K/dcc$Hc, .25))`–\$`r usd(quantile(dcc$K/dcc$Hc, .75))`. That is `r round((sum(dcc$K)/sum(dcc$Hc)) / per(cs[cs$yr >= 2025 & cs$nvidia, ]), 1)` times the bare silicon.

**The value adopted.** Hardware that goes missing is neither of these. A building does not walk out of a data center, but a server does, and a server is more than its accelerators: CPUs, memory, the interconnect fabric and the chassis. The figure used here is **\$25k per H100e**, between the two measured ends and closer to the chip; it is an interpolation, not itself a measurement, and the \$15k–\$35k bracket is what the two Epoch figures support.

```{r dollar-scenarios}
usd.per.h100e <- 25e3                                                     # judgmental input, between chip (~$17k) and all-in site (~$36k)
q <- c("10k H100e" = 10e3, "100k H100e" = 100e3, "300k H100e" = 300e3, "1M H100e" = 1e6)
round(q * usd.per.h100e / 1e9, 2)                                         # $ billions
```

So ten thousand H100e unaccounted for is about \$0.25B of hardware and a million is \$25B; §S.6.6 prices the dark-compute scenarios themselves. The fleets are larger still: the U.S.-located fleet of §S.1.2.7 is about \$`r round(us.frac * fleet.ye2026 * 25e3 / 1e9)`B and China's about \$`r round(3.09e6 * 25e3 / 1e9)`B at the same rate.

**Judgment calls.**

* *Which price.* Replacement cost, resale value and book value differ, and for hardware under export control they can differ by a lot in either direction. The figure here is a replacement-cost reading: what a state would have to spend to reconstitute what went missing. A resale reading would be lower for older generations and, on reported grey-market behaviour, higher for controlled parts in controlled destinations; this notebook does not attempt either.
* *Which rating.* Epoch's cost estimates are paired with Epoch's H100e, which takes a Blackwell chip at 2.53 H100e (§S.0). At the lower of NVIDIA's two ratings, 2.28, the same chip counts for about 10% fewer H100e and the dollar figure per H100e would be about 10% higher. Both readings sit inside the bracket.
* *Direction of travel.* The price per H100e fell about 1.3× a year from 2022 to 2025 and was flat from 2025 to 2026. If the decline resumes, a fixed count of H100e becomes cheaper to assemble over time, which makes a dark fleet easier to build and cuts against durability; a fixed sum of money buys correspondingly more. Under a pause the direction could reverse, since new training-capable production would stop while demand for the installed base continued.
* *Direction of conservatism.* A lower dollar figure makes hiding hardware look cheaper and the regime's task harder. \$25k is a central choice, not a conservative one; \$15k is the regime-unfavorable end of the bracket.

# S.2 Compute ceiling C_T and parameter ceiling N_T (Table 3.1; §3.2.2, fn 21; §6.2.4)

**Adopted: the treaty compute ceiling $C_T = 2\times10^{24}$ FLOP and the parameter ceiling $N_T = 13$B parameters.**

## S.2.1 C_T = β_T · C_F

$C_T$ is indexed to the frontier: $C_T = \beta_T \cdot C_F$ with $\beta_T = 10^{-3}$, "three orders of magnitude below $C_F$" (§6.2.4). $\beta_T$ is a judgmental input. Two considerations favour a higher ceiling: enforceability (a higher $C_T$ leaves fewer legitimate runs near the threshold to police) and room for useful sub-frontier training. Two favour a lower one, and they are the purposes of the ceiling: preventing the frontier from advancing, and limiting the large-scale experimentation that drives training efficiency gains.

```{r ct}
beta.T <- 1e-3
C.T <- beta.T * C.F
c(C_T = C.T)
```

$C_T = 2\times10^{24}$ is the training compute of the 2022–2023 frontier (PaLM-540B, GPT-3.5, Claude 2), but a model trained at that budget today is far more capable than those were. Many recent models were trained within a factor of two of $C_T$. The frontier subset used in §S.1.1 contains none of them, so the table below reads Epoch's complete AI Models database (`data/all_ai_models.csv`, Epoch AI 2026j, retrieved 2026-09-18): it counts the models released since the start of 2025 whose estimated training compute lies between $C_T$ / 2 and 2 · $C_T$, and lists a named selection of the widely known ones with their parameter counts.

```{r ct-recent}
allm <- read.csv("data/all_ai_models.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
allm$C <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(allm[["Training compute (FLOP)"]])); allm$N <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(allm$Parameters))
allm$date <- as.Date(allm[["Publication date"]])
near <- allm[!is.na(allm$C) & !is.na(allm$date) & allm$C >= C.T / 2 & allm$C <= 2 * C.T & allm$date >= as.Date("2025-01-01"), ]
N.T <- 13e9                                                                                     # derived in section S.2.2 below
c("models since 2025 within a factor of 2 of C_T" = nrow(near), "  of which with at most N_T = 13B parameters" = sum(near$N <= N.T, na.rm = TRUE),
  "  parameter count not recorded" = sum(is.na(near$N)))
pick <- c("DeepSeek-R1", "DeepSeek-V3 (Mar 2025)", "Gemma 3 27B", "Llama 4 Maverick", "Qwen3-8B", "Kimi K2", "NVIDIA-Nemotron-Nano-12B-v2", "DeepSeek-V4-Flash")
sel <- near[match(pick, near$Model), c("Model", "Organization", "date", "C", "N")]
data.frame(model = sel$Model, organization = sel$Organization, released = sel$date, compute.FLOP = signif(sel$C, 2), parameters.B = round(sel$N / 1e9), under.N_T = sel$N <= N.T, row.names = NULL)
```

Most of these models exceed $N_T$ = 13B parameters (§S.2.2); the models under both ceilings are heavily overtrained small ones such as Qwen3-8B and Nemotron Nano. Since $C_T$ is indexed to $C_F$ it moves with that input: at $C_F = 1\times10^{27}$ it would be $1\times10^{24}$. The neighbouring choices are $\beta_T = 10^{-2}$ ($C_T = 2\times10^{25}$) and $10^{-4}$ ($2\times10^{23}$); the same database shows what has recently been trained at those budgets:

```{r ct-neighbours}
band <- function(centre) { x <- allm[!is.na(allm$C) & !is.na(allm$date) & allm$C >= centre / 2 & allm$C <= 2 * centre & allm$date >= as.Date("2025-01-01"), ]; x[order(x$date), ] }
