hi <- band(10 * C.T); lo <- band(C.T / 10)
list("beta_T = 1e-2, C_T = 2e25: models since 2025 within a factor of 2" = nrow(hi),
     "  examples" = data.frame(model = c("Claude 3.7 Sonnet", "Qwen3-Max", "Kimi K3"), released = hi$date[match(c("Claude 3.7 Sonnet", "Qwen3-Max", "Kimi K3"), hi$Model)], compute.FLOP = signif(hi$C[match(c("Claude 3.7 Sonnet", "Qwen3-Max", "Kimi K3"), hi$Model)], 2)),
     "beta_T = 1e-4, C_T = 2e23: models since 2025 within a factor of 2" = nrow(lo),
     "  examples" = data.frame(model = c("Qwen3-1.7B", "Phi-4-Multimodal", "Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B"), released = lo$date[match(c("Qwen3-1.7B", "Phi-4-Multimodal", "Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B"), lo$Model)], compute.FLOP = signif(lo$C[match(c("Qwen3-1.7B", "Phi-4-Multimodal", "Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B"), lo$Model)], 2)))
```

At $\beta_T = 10^{-2}$ the ceiling would sit among near-frontier commercial models of 2025–2026 (Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Qwen3-Max, Kimi K3); at $10^{-4}$ it would sit among small models of a few billion parameters (Qwen3-1.7B, Phi-4-Multimodal) and sparse mixtures with a few billion active parameters (Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B). The private-evasion fleet $F_P$ (§6.2.4) scales with $C_T$.

## S.2.2 N_T from C_T via an overtraining assumption (fn 21)

Chinchilla-optimal training uses D = 20·N tokens, so C = 6·N·D = 120·N². Small commercial models are trained on far more tokens per parameter for cheaper inference: Llama-3-8B on 15T tokens versus a Chinchilla-optimal 160B, about 94×. Footnote 21 rounds this to 100× overtraining, C = 12,000·N², and $N_T$ is the parameter count whose 100×-overtrained run costs exactly $C_T$.

```{r nt}
N.chinchilla <- function(C, overtrain = 1) sqrt(C / (120 * overtrain))
data.frame(overtraining = c(1, 10, 30, 100),
           N.at.C_T.B = round(N.chinchilla(C.T, c(1, 10, 30, 100)) / 1e9, 1),
           tokens.T = round(20 * c(1, 10, 30, 100) * N.chinchilla(C.T, c(1, 10, 30, 100)) / 1e12, 1),
           example = c("dense Chinchilla-optimal model (130B)", "Llama-3-70B (15T tokens / 1.4T optimal)",
                       "", "Llama-3-8B (15T / 0.16T) -> N_T"))
```

**Judgment calls.**

* *Which mapping.* $N_T$ is set on the overtrained (100×) mapping, the strict end of the 13B–130B range that 100×–1× overtraining would give. The two ceilings bind jointly: a model is a beyond-threshold model if *either* C > $C_T$ or N > $N_T$, so a dense Chinchilla-optimal model trained at exactly $C_T$ (about 130B parameters) is above $N_T$. (For a mixture-of-experts model the Chinchilla mapping counts active parameters, so its total count would be higher still.)
* *How strict.* The purpose of the parameter ceiling is to forbid plausibly commercially competitive models, and an overtrained small model can be one, so the strict end is intended. A lower $N_T$ is also easier to enforce after the fact (parameter counts are observable at deployment) and makes $C_T$ the binding constraint only for extremely overtrained small models; it forbids parameter counts common in today's open-weight models (Llama-3-70B, Qwen-72B), whose *compute* would in any case exceed $C_T$.
* *Mixture-of-experts.* $N_T$ counts **total** parameters, not active ones, so that a mixture-of-experts design with many experts cannot route around it (DeepSeek-V3 has 671B total / 37B active). The compute mapping C = 6·N·D uses *active* parameters; the two conventions serve different purposes and both are stated.

**Adopted: the parameter ceiling $N_T = 13$B, set on the 100× overtraining mapping and counting total parameters.**

**Direction of conservatism.** A lower $N_T$ and lower $\beta_T$ are stricter on private actors (regime-favorable for enforcement, costlier for commercial sub-frontier use); neither affects the state-level ledgers in §6.4.

# S.3 Covert evasion threshold C_E = β_E · C_F (Table 3.1; §6.2.2, fn 65)

**Adopted: the covert evasion multiple $\beta_E = 10$, and with it the covert evasion threshold $C_E = \beta_E C_F = 2\times10^{28}$ FLOP, the training compute a covert model would need to be strategically relevant against the frozen frontier.**

## S.3.1 The argument

An illicit model is served on scarce dark compute, while whitelisted models are served fast and abundantly on inference-only hardware (§6.2.2). To be *strategically relevant* the illicit model must beat the frozen frontier per token by enough to overcome that inference-time handicap. Ord (2025) summarizes the inference-scaling literature as a performance-equivalence along log(training FLOP) + $\eta$·log(inference compute), $\eta \approx 0.7$: a k-fold inference advantage for the defender is worth k^$\eta$ in training compute for the attacker. So $\beta_E$ ≈ k^$\eta$ and $C_E = \beta_E \cdot C_F$.

The defender's advantage that is used for k is **serial inference speed**: hardwired MSICs serve Llama-3.1-8B at 17,000 tokens/s against 353 tokens/s on a B200 (Taalas n.d.), k ≈ 48. Footnote 65 gives 50^0.7 ≈ 15 and rounds *down* to $\beta_E = 10$ as the conservative choice.

```{r beta-e}
T.E <- 5                                               # derived in section S.4 below; needed here for F_E
F.E.of <- function(beta.E, rF = rho.F, T = T.E, U = U.F, dl = delta) h100e(rho.E.of(beta.E, rF, dl) * beta.E * C.F / (T * secs.per.yr * U))   # rho_E depends on beta_E through the blind steps
k.speed <- 17000 / 353
tab <- data.frame(eta = c(0.5, 0.7, 1.0))
tab$beta.E <- round(k.speed^tab$eta, 1)
tab$F.E.M  <- round(F.E.of(tab$beta.E) / 1e6, 2)
list(k = round(k.speed, 1), k.to.the.eta = tab)
```

```{r beta-e-chosen}
beta.E <- 10
C.E <- beta.E * C.F
rho.E <- rho.E.of(beta.E)                              # research overhead at beta_E (section S.4.2)
frontier.growth <- trend$growth.per.yr[1]              # 4.45x/yr from section S.1.1
c(C_E = C.E, "years of frontier progress that 10x represents" = round(log(beta.E) / log(frontier.growth), 2))
```

## S.3.2 Why this is a floor, and the cross-checks

* **$\eta$.** Villalobos and Atkinson (2023) find 0.5–1 across tasks; Snell et al. (2024) find ≈ 1 on easy and medium problems and ≈ 0 on the hardest; Ord's 0.7 is a rule of thumb. At $\eta = 0.5$ the speed advantage is worth 7×, at $\eta = 1$ it is worth 48×. $\beta_E = 10$ sits inside that range, below the central 15.
* **The attacker is compute-poor after training.** Whatever inference the frozen frontier can spend per task, the evader must serve its model on what is left of the same dark stock that trained it, with no legal way to replenish it. So the evader cannot spend to the point where inference scaling saturates; the per-token comparison is the right one, and it favors the defender by more than the raw chip-speed ratio.
* **Covert operating overhead.** Using an illicit model strategically means operating it without leaving tracks: restricted or laundered internet access, no public API or user base, concealment of the data center's power and network signature, and a small circle of people who can be told the model exists. Each of these lowers the effective capability the evader can extract per token, which is a further argument that the *training* advantage needed for strategic relevance is at least the one implied by the speed ratio alone.
* **One meaningful generation (cross-check).** 10× in training compute is about `r round(log(10)/log(trend$growth.per.yr[1]), 1)` years of frontier progress at the fitted 4.45×/yr, roughly one model generation. A strategically relevant covert model being "one generation ahead" of the frozen frontier is a natural reading of the threshold, independent of the exchange-rate argument.

**Direction of conservatism.** A smaller $\beta_E$ gives a smaller $C_E$ and so a smaller $F_E$, the regime-unfavorable side. Taking 10 rather than the central 15 is conservative, and so is ignoring the covert-operating overhead.

# S.4 Covert evasion fleet F_E: U_F, ρ_E, T_E (Table 3.1; §6.2.1–6.2.2, fn 67)

**Adopted: the frontier utilization $U_F = `r round(U.F, 2)`$; the research overhead $\rho_E = `r round(rho.E, 1)`$, which is the frontier research overhead $\rho_F = `r round(rho.F, 1)`$ times the cost of reaching $\beta_E = 10$ in blind leaps of at most $\delta = 1/3$ of an order of magnitude; and the time horizon $T_E = 5$ years; giving a covert evasion fleet $F_E = `r signif(F.E.of(beta.E) / 1e6, 2)`$M H100e.**

The covert evasion fleet $F_E$ is the number of H100e that, running at frontier-lab utilization $U_F$, completes a research program of $\rho_E$ final-run-equivalents of the covert evasion threshold $C_E$ within the time horizon $T_E$:

$$F_E = \frac{\rho_E \, C_E}{T_E \, U_F},$$

converted from FLOP per second to H100e at the peak rate of §S.0. This section takes the three inputs in turn.

## S.4.1 Utilization U_F

The utilization $U_F$ is the fraction of peak throughput a frontier lab achieves over a whole training run. It is derived in §S.1.1.4 as the FLOP-weighted blend of a pretraining utilization of 0.40 and an RL utilization of 0.125 at a 40% post-training share, which gives `r round(U.F, 3)`. Each of the two is the mid-range of a published band:

* **Pretraining, 30–50%.** "Typical utilization rates for large distributed training runs are around 30-50%" (Epoch AI n.d., the AI-models estimation documentation). The calculator on that page carries a **30% default**; **the 0.40 midpoint adopted here is therefore the conservative end**, since a higher $U_F$ means smaller required fleets and so larger ledger ratios (at 0.30 the blend would be `r round(U.blend(0.4, 0.3, 0.125), 3)`, with $F_E$ = `r round(F.E.of(10, U = U.blend(0.4, 0.3, 0.125))/1e6, 2)`M). Meta's reported 38–43% for Llama-3-405B sits inside that band and corroborates the 40% midpoint. Denain and Wu (2026) use a lower 0.15–0.35 for pretraining and supervised fine-tuning, **but that is a chip-specific discount, not a competing estimate of frontier utilization**: their footnote says they use a smaller utilization than the default in Epoch's AI models database because H800s have the same peak FLOP/s as H100s but worse memory and interconnect bandwidth. So the 30–50% adopted here is not in conflict with them. At their midpoint of 0.25 the blend would be `r round(U.blend(0.4, 0.25, 0.125), 3)` and $F_E$ would be `r round(F.E.of(10, U = U.blend(0.4, 0.25, 0.125))/1e6, 1)`M.
* **RL post-training, 5–20%.** For reinforcement learning (RL) we use Denain and Wu's (2026) estimate, 5–20% of peak throughput, at its midpoint of 0.125. Their reason is that RL is inference-heavy, and inference runs at a lower utilization than training.
* **Post-training share, 0.40.** The share of a frontier run's FLOP that goes to RL post-training is taken at 0.40, Epoch's estimate for GPT-5 (§S.1.1.4). This is a conservative value. There is evidence that RL post-training has been taking up a growing part of training since then (§S.1.1.4), and a larger share would lower $U_F$ and raise every fleet threshold.

A higher $U_F$ gives a smaller $F_E$ and so larger ledger ratios, which is the regime-unfavorable direction. The 0.40 pretraining utilization (against the 30% default of Epoch's calculator) and the 0.40 post-training share both err in that direction.

## S.4.2 Research overhead ρ_E

Before a final run can begin, the research program needs training-capable hardware for exploratory experimentation, synthetic-data generation and test runs; $\rho > 1$ is the ratio of the program's R&D compute to the final run. Denain and Wu (2026) estimate the final-run share of R&D compute from company spending data (OpenAI's investor documents; Z.ai's and MiniMax's IPO filings):

```{r rho-e}
share.final <- c("OpenAI 2024" = 0.096, "Z.ai" = 0.123, "MiniMax (excl. Hailuo, median)" = 0.122, "MiniMax (all)" = 0.226)
rho.of.share <- g.F^(-lag.rd) / share.final                                 # one lag's worth of frontier growth removed
data.frame(final.run.share = share.final, rho = round(rho.of.share, 1),
           rho.E.with.blind.steps = round(rho.E.of(beta.E, rF = rho.of.share), 1),
           F.E.M = round(F.E.of(beta.E, rF = rho.of.share) / 1e6, 2))
rho.P <- rho.of.share[["Z.ai"]]                                             # trailing overhead, used for F_P in section S.8
```

**The frontier overhead $\rho_F$.** OpenAI's 9.6% final-run share is a ratio between two things estimated for the *same* calendar year, but the R&D compute a program spends in a given year supports a final run that happens some months later, by which time the frontier has moved. Dividing the R&D by the *contemporaneous* final runs therefore overstates the overhead of a single program by roughly one lag's worth of frontier growth. Taking that lag as four months and the growth rate as the historical $g = `r g.F`$ (§S.1.1.1) gives the frontier research overhead
$$\rho_F = \frac{g^{-4/12}}{0.096} = `r round(rho.F, 2)`,$$
an estimate carried at full precision, and OpenAI is the only frontier-pushing lab in the sample. The same construction on Z.ai's 12.3% share gives a **trailing overhead** $\rho_P = g^{-4/12}/0.123 = `r round(rho.P, 2)`$ for a program that stays *below* the frozen frontier; it is used for the private evasion fleet in §S.8. The four-month lag and the round $g = `r g.F`$ are judgmental inputs; the lag lowers both overheads and so lowers every required fleet, the regime-unfavorable direction. Z.ai (Zhipu, GLM) and MiniMax are fast followers producing near-frontier open-weight models, and MiniMax's headline figure is inflated by its Hailuo video product, which is why Denain & Wu also report the 12.2% (90% CI 6.4–23.5%) excluding it. So the sample reads as: frontier lab `r round(rho.F, 1)`, fast follower `r round(rho.P, 1)` (video is a different kind of data and does not belong in the comparison).

**Blind leaps.** A research program aiming at $\beta \cdot C_F$ for a large multiple $\beta$ must either attempt a far larger blind leap than frontier companies make now, or bridge the gap from $C_F$ in several steps. The blind-leap increment $\delta$ is the largest step, in orders of magnitude, that one program can take beyond the best model it has already trained. Reaching $\beta$ then takes $n = \log_{10} \beta / \delta$ steps of $\beta^{1/n}$ each; $n$ is not rounded, and it is a whole number at the adopted values. If each step is a program with the frontier overhead $\rho_F$, the total compute is
$$\sum_{i=1}^{n} \rho_F\, \beta^{i/n}\, C_F = \rho_F\, \beta\, C_F \cdot \frac{1 - \beta^{-1}}{1 - \beta^{-1/n}}, \qquad\text{so}\qquad \rho_E = \rho_F \cdot \frac{1 - \beta_E^{-1}}{1 - \beta_E^{-1/n}}.$$
The adopted $\delta = 1/3$ is a judgmental input: each step is at most about 2.15×, roughly `r round(12 * (1 / 3) / log10(trend$growth.per.yr[1]))` months of frontier growth at the fitted `r round(trend$growth.per.yr[1], 2)`×/yr. For $\beta_E = 10$ that is three programs, at $10^{1/3}$, $10^{2/3}$ and $10$ times $C_F$, and a factor of `r round(blind.factor(beta.E), 2)`.

```{r blind-leaps}
dl <- c("one leap (delta = Inf)" = Inf, "delta = 1" = 1, "delta = 1/2" = 1 / 2, "delta = 1/3 (adopted)" = 1 / 3, "delta = 1/4" = 1 / 4)
data.frame(increment = names(dl), steps = blind.steps(beta.E, dl), factor = round(blind.factor(beta.E, dl), 3),
           rho.E = round(rho.E.of(beta.E, dl = dl), 1), F.E.M = round(F.E.of(beta.E, dl = dl) / 1e6, 2), row.names = NULL)
```

**Judgment calls** ($\rho_F$ is a published estimate adjusted for a lag; $\delta$ is a judgmental input; §6.2.2 gives the argument in full).

* *Why the frontier value and not the follower value.* The covert program aims *above* the frozen frontier ($C_E = 10 \cdot C_F$), so it either attempts a far larger blind leap than a frontier lab makes in any one run or bridges the gap in several steps; either way it is frontier-pushing work, and $\rho_F$ is the right basis for each step. The follower figures describe a leaner program that follows the frontier; with the same blind steps they would give $F_E$ = `r round(F.E.of(beta.E, rF = rho.P)/1e6, 1)`M at $\rho_P = `r round(rho.P, 1)`$.
* *Why $\rho_E$ is above $\rho_F$.* The blind steps are the part of the argument that can be put in numbers. The rest points the same way but cannot be quantified credibly: a covert program lacks much of what a frontier lab has (the pull of riches and status on the most ambitious researchers, a steady inflow of people carrying insights from competing firms, and several concurrent research programs over which to amortize effort), and it must control its AI agents far more reliably, since a leak ends the program. In the other direction, AI agents' engineering skills may offset some of this, and legally served frontier-model inference could take on tasks such as grading RL rollouts, at some added risk of discovery.
* *Possible overlap.* $\rho_F$ is estimated for a frontier lab whose R&D compute already includes its own intermediate and experimental models. Charging each blind step a full frontier overhead on top may overstate $\rho_E$ somewhat, the regime-favorable direction.
* *Direction of conservatism.* A lower $\rho_E$ means a smaller $F_E$ and less to police. $\rho_F$ is the estimated frontier value, not a conservative choice, and $\delta = 1/3$ is a central judgment, not the conservative end: one leap ($\delta = \infty$) gives $\rho_E = \rho_F$ and $F_E$ = `r round(F.E.of(beta.E, dl = Inf)/1e6, 1)`M, the regime-unfavorable bound, and $\delta = 1/2$ gives `r round(F.E.of(beta.E, dl = 1/2)/1e6, 1)`M. The adopted program is $\rho_E \cdot C_E / U_F$ = `r round(rho.E * h100e.years(C.E / U.F) / 1e6)`M H100e-years.

## S.4.3 Time horizon T_E

The time horizon $T_E$ is the number of years the covert program is given to complete its research program. It is a judgmental input, set at five years, and it rests on two considerations.

* **Time discounting.** A capability delivered many years out is worth much less to the state pursuing it than one delivered soon; a program that needs ten years to reach $C_E$ is a different proposition from one that needs five.
* **Concealment.** Five years is already a long time to keep a large government program hidden, and every further year is another year of exposure through power, procurement and personnel.

Hardware lifetime is a supporting consideration, not the basis of the choice. The paper mentions it (§6.2.2, on maintaining a fleet past its intended retirement age without vendor service, with cloud providers' retirement ages in fn 67), so the evidence is recorded here, and the failure rate it yields is reused in §S.1.2.6 and §S.6.3. The only published count of physical GPU replacements we have found is from the Delta supercomputer: four A100s replaced in 895 days on 448 A100s and two H100s in 146 days on 608 H100s (Cui et al. 2025), six replacements in about 1,340 GPU-years, roughly half a percent a year. Meta's Llama-3-405B run logged 148 faulty-GPU and 72 HBM3 interruptions in 54 days on 16,384 H100s (Llama Team 2024), about 9% of GPUs a year; that is an interruption rate, not a loss rate, since "only three incidents required significant manual intervention; the rest were managed by automation."

```{r t-e}
attrition <- fail.rate[["central"]]                                                           # measured in section S.1.2.6
data.frame(T.E = c(3, 5, 7, 10), F.E.M = round(F.E.of(beta.E, T = c(3, 5, 7, 10)) / 1e6, 2),
           fleet.lost.pct.low = round(100 * (1 - exp(-fail.rate[["low"]] * c(3, 5, 7, 10))), 1), fleet.lost.pct = round(100 * (1 - exp(-attrition * c(3, 5, 7, 10))), 1),
           fleet.lost.pct.high = round(100 * (1 - exp(-fail.rate[["high"]] * c(3, 5, 7, 10))), 1))
```

The Delta rate is measured on young chips at one well-supported site, and it says little about a fleet run for years without vendor service. The one long-run record we have found points the other way: on the Titan supercomputer, both the original 2014 GPUs and the replacement boards installed in 2016–2019 showed failure hazards that rose with age over their first several years (the authors' analysis of the data released with Ostrouchov et al. 2020). The original boards, whose failures were driven by a component defect, reached 12–15% a year; the sound replacement boards started near the Delta rate, at 0.2–0.3% a year, and their hazard rose by roughly 1.6× per year of age, though much of that rise traces to a single lot. Cloud providers retire GPU generations about seven to ten years after launch (§S.1.2.6), and no published data describe failure rates at those ages. So early-life failures alone would not stop a patient evader (at the Delta rate an unreplenished fleet loses about `r round(100 * (1 - exp(-5 * attrition)))`% of its chips in five years and `r round(100 * (1 - exp(-10 * attrition)))`% in ten), while the aging behaviour that might is unmeasured. Lifetime therefore does one job here. Since a longer $T_E$ always gives a smaller $F_E$, a critic could otherwise push the horizon out to fifteen or twenty years and shrink $F_E$ toward nothing; a fleet whose chips are retired at seven to ten years cannot support such a program, so the horizon has an upper limit even though it is discounting and concealment that put it at five.

**Direction of conservatism.** A longer $T_E$ gives a smaller $F_E$: seven years would give `r round(F.E.of(beta.E, T = 7) / 1e6, 1)`M and ten `r round(F.E.of(beta.E, T = 10) / 1e6, 1)`M, against `r round(F.E.of(beta.E, T = 3) / 1e6, 1)`M at three. Five is the regime-unfavorable choice relative to three or four, and a judgment rather than a bound relative to longer horizons.

## S.4.4 F_E assembled

```{r fe}
F.E <- F.E.of(beta.E)                                   # rho_E = rho_F x blind-leap factor, T_E = 5, U_F = 0.21, beta_E = 10, C_F = 2e27
c("C_E / U_F (FLOP)" = C.E / U.F,
  "C_E / U_F (H100e-years)" = h100e.years(C.E / U.F),
  "x rho_E (H100e-years)" = rho.E * h100e.years(C.E / U.F),
  "F_E (H100e)" = F.E)
```

$F_E$ = `r big(F.E)` H100e at the adopted inputs ($\beta_E = 10$, $\rho_E = `r round(rho.E, 1)`$, $T_E = 5$, $U_F = `r round(U.F, 2)`$), printed as `r signif(F.E / 1e6, 2)`M.

§6.2.2 compares this with OpenAI's projected fleet at the end of 2026, 6.4M H100e. That figure is the log-linear fit of §S.1.2.9, through Epoch's year-end estimates and the sites it tags as OpenAI's, so the comparison is internal to this notebook: a covert program would need a fleet about `r round(F.E / 6.4e6, 1)` times what the leading lab is expected to have at the moment of the freeze.

## S.4.5 Cross-check: F_E against the leading lab’s fleet at the freeze

```{r crosscheck-fe}
oa.ye2026 <- F.fit.2025 * g.fit                                             # the fitted path of section S.1.2.9 at year-end 2026
c("leading lab's fleet at year-end 2026, on the fitted path (H100e)" = oa.ye2026, "F_E (H100e)" = F.E, "F_E / that fleet" = F.E / oa.ye2026,
  "world fleet at year-end 2026 (H100e)" = fleet.ye2026, "F_E / world fleet" = F.E / fleet.ye2026)
```

The covert evasion fleet is `r sprintf("%.2f", F.E / oa.ye2026)` times the fleet the leading lab holds at the freeze on its fitted path, and `r round(100 * F.E / fleet.ye2026, 1)`% of the whole world fleet: a covert evader would need to assemble and hide roughly what OpenAI operates in the open at year-end 2026, and about twice China's entire national fleet (§S.1.2.8). Nothing about the leading lab's fleet enters $F_E$, which is built from $C_F$, $\beta_E$, $\rho_E$, $T_E$ and $U_F$ alone, so the near-equality is not a construction. It is, though, the right order of magnitude for a threshold meant to mark a strategically relevant program: a covert evader must field a frontier lab, not a research group.

## S.4.6 Cross-check: the construction run backwards

The second check runs the $F_E$ construction backwards over a period where the answer is known. Substituting $C_F$ for $C_E$ asks what a frontier lab would have spent to climb one order of magnitude to *today's* frontier — that is, the 18 months of frontier progress ending at the freeze, since $\beta_E = 10$ is about `r round(log(10)/log(g.F) * 12)` months on the historical trajectory. The answer can be compared with what the leading lab actually spent over the same 18 months, which is the integral of the fitted path.

```{r crosscheck-backcast}
backcast <- h100e.years(rho.E * C.F / U.F)                                   # rho_E C_F / U_F, the program for one order of magnitude
win  <- c(-0.5, 1)                                                           # t in years from end-2025: mid-2025 to end-2026
oa.18mo <- F.fit.2025 * (g.fit^win[2] - g.fit^win[1]) / log(g.fit)           # integral of the fitted path over that window
c("back-cast program (H100e-years)" = backcast, "leading lab's compute over the same 18 months (H100e-years)" = oa.18mo,
  "back-cast as a share of it" = backcast / oa.18mo)
```

The back-cast comes to `r round(backcast / 1e6, 1)`M H100e-years, about `r round(100 * backcast / oa.18mo)`% of the `r sprintf("%.1f", oa.18mo / 1e6)`M H100e-years the fitted path puts into the leading lab over the same period. So the covert construction, applied to a leap the industry has just made, comes out at the scale of one frontier lab's compute over the same period. This is a sanity check on the order of magnitude of $\rho_E$ and $U_F$ taken together, and nothing more.

# S.5 Overt breakout fleet F_B (Table 3.1; §6.2.3)

**Adopted: the overt breakout threshold $C_B = 2\times10^{29}$ FLOP — two orders of magnitude, six blind steps, above the frozen frontier — which at the frozen frontier implies the multiple $\beta_B = C_B / C_F = 100$; the research overhead $\rho_B = `r round(rho.E.of(100), 1)`$; and the breakout horizon $T_B = 2$ years; giving an overt breakout fleet $F_B = `r signif(h100e(rho.E.of(100) * 100 * C.F / (2 * secs.per.yr * U.F)) / 1e6, 2)`$M H100e.**

## S.5.1 The construction

The overt breakout fleet is built by the same two formulas as the covert evasion fleet of §S.4, but the two thresholds are *fixed differently*, and the difference matters later.

$C_E$ is a **relative** quantity. A covert evader needs an advantage over the frozen frontier large enough to be strategically useful against it, so §S.3 fixes the multiple $\beta_E$ and $C_E = \beta_E C_F$ follows. If the pause began a year later, $C_E$ would be higher by a year of frontier progress: the target moves with the frontier because it is defined against it.

$C_B$ is an **absolute** capability level. A strategically decisive model is decisive whenever it arrives; nothing about it is defined relative to what came before. So $C_B$ is the fixed quantity, and

$$\beta_B = \frac{C_B}{C_F}, \qquad F_B = \frac{\rho_B \, C_B}{T_B \, U_F}.$$

The derived $\beta_B$ still earns its keep: within a pause it is what the regime holds fixed, so that $C_B(t) = \beta_B C_F(t)$ tracks training efficiency gains like every other threshold (§6.2.3). But *across* possible pause dates it is an output, not an input — the same $C_B$ names a smaller multiple the later the pause begins. That is the whole of the window-of-opportunity mechanism, and it is worked in §S.5.5.

The three inputs are taken in turn below. Only $C_B$ is new: $\rho_B$ uses the blind-leap construction of §S.4.2 at the implied multiple, and $T_B$ is a judgmental input in the same sense as $T_E$.

## S.5.2 The breakout threshold C_B

$C_B$ is not an estimate of the compute a strategically decisive model would actually take. Nobody can estimate that: such a model is, almost by definition, beyond present experience. What the treaty regime has to bound is what a *bullish would-be defector would believe*, since the states most likely to attempt a breakout are the ones most optimistic about AI progress.

It is specified here as a distance above the frozen frontier, in the same units the rest of the analysis already uses: **whole blind steps of $\delta = 1/3$ of an order of magnitude**. The adopted value is six steps, two orders of magnitude, $\beta_B = 100$ and $C_B = 2\times10^{29}$ FLOP. Specifying it this way keeps the breakout program divisible into equal steps of exactly $\delta$, so $\rho_B$ is the closed form of §S.4.2 rather than a rounded-up approximation to it.

```{r beta-b}
n.B    <- 6                                                       # judgmental input: blind steps above the frozen frontier
beta.B <- 10^(n.B * delta)                                        # = 100 exactly at delta = 1/3
C.B    <- beta.B * C.F                                            # the absolute capability level it names
k.of   <- function(beta, g = g.F) log(beta) / log(g)              # years of baseline progress a multiple represents
c("blind steps" = n.B, "orders of magnitude" = n.B * delta, "beta_B" = beta.B, "C_B (FLOP)" = C.B,
  "months of trajectory per blind step" = 12 * delta / log10(g.F), "years of trajectory to C_B" = k.of(beta.B))
```

**The arrival date is a gloss, not the input.** On the race trajectory that prevailed before the pause, one blind step is `r round(12 * delta / log10(g.F), 1)` months, so six steps is about `r round(k.of(beta.B), 1)` years and the adopted $C_B$ can be described as roughly what a leader expecting a decisive model at the **end of 2029** would be aiming at. That is a way of making the number intelligible, not a forecast, and the paper says as much: the trend is used only as a translation device between a date and a compute level, and the value ultimately describes the psychology of national leaders rather than a physical quantity, so it would be negotiated rather than estimated. §S.5.5 shows what other distances imply, and what happens to the same $C_B$ if the pause starts later.

## S.5.3 The research overhead ρ_B

$\rho_B$ uses the blind-leap construction of §S.4.2 unchanged, at $\beta_B$ instead of $\beta_E$. Reaching a multiple of 100 in steps of at most $\delta = 1/3$ of an order of magnitude takes $n_B = \log_{10} \beta_B / \delta$ programs, each carrying the frontier overhead $\rho_F$:

$$\rho_B = \frac{1 - \beta_B^{-1}}{1 - 10^{-\delta}} \cdot \rho_F.$$

```{r rho-b}
rho.B <- rho.E.of(beta.B)                                          # rho_F x blind-leap factor at beta_B
c("blind steps n_B" = blind.steps(beta.B), "blind-leap factor" = blind.factor(beta.B), "rho_B" = rho.B, "for comparison, rho_E" = rho.E)
```

The factor is close to its limit: as $\beta$ grows the sum is dominated by its last term, so the factor approaches $1/(1 - 10^{-\delta}) = `r round(1 / (1 - 10^(-1/3)), 2)`$ and $\rho_B$ approaches `r round(rho.F / (1 - 10^(-1/3)), 1)`. A breakout program is therefore charged only about `r round(100 * (rho.B / rho.E - 1))`% more overhead than the covert program, even though it aims ten times higher.

## S.5.4 The breakout horizon T_B

The breakout horizon is a judgmental input, set at two years. A breakout is overt: detection is immediate, so what protects the other states is not concealment but time. The defector must reach its target before the rest of the world can organize a response — sanctions, sabotage, or a resumption of racing with a more complete supply chain and, eventually, a larger fleet. Two years is a central judgment about how long that would take, not a conservative one; one year and three years bracket it in §S.5.5.

A longer $T_B$ gives a smaller $F_B$, and a smaller $F_B$ is the regime-unfavorable side, since $F_B$ is the ceiling a state's overt ledger must stay under.

## S.5.5 F_B assembled, and its sensitivity to the arrival date and the horizon

```{r fb-backbone}
T.B <- 2
F.B <- h100e(rho.B * C.B / (T.B * secs.per.yr * U.F))
c("F_B at T_B = 2 (adopted)" = F.B, "F_B at T_B = 1" = F.B * 2, "F_B at T_B = 3" = F.B * 2 / 3,
  "F_B / F_E" = F.B / F.E, "F_B / world fleet at year-end 2026" = F.B / fleet.ye2026)
```

$F_B$ = `r big(F.B)` H100e at the adopted inputs, printed as `r signif(F.B / 1e6, 2)`M. It is `r round(F.B / F.E, 1)` times the covert evasion fleet and `r round(F.B / fleet.ye2026, 1)` times the whole world accelerator fleet at year-end 2026 (§S.1.2.4), so on this construction no state's year-end 2026 holdings come close to a breakout fleet: the U.S.-located fleet of §S.1.2.7 is `r round(100 * us.frac * fleet.ye2026 / F.B)`% of it.

**Moving the target.** The ladder is in whole blind steps, with the arrival date carried alongside as the gloss it is.

```{r fb-arrival}
ar <- data.frame(n.B = 3:8)
ar$oom      <- ar$n.B * delta
ar$beta.B   <- 10^ar$oom
ar$C.B      <- signif(ar$beta.B * C.F, 2)
ar$rho.B    <- rho.E.of(ar$beta.B)
for (tb in 1:3) ar[[sprintf("F.B.M.T%d", tb)]] <- h100e(ar$rho.B * ar$beta.B * C.F / (tb * secs.per.yr * U.F)) / 1e6
gloss <- function(k) { w <- k %% 1                                        # k years after a year-end 2026 pause
  sprintf("~%s %d", ifelse(w < 0.25 | w >= 0.75, "end", "mid"), 2026 + floor(k) + (w >= 0.25)) }
ar$arrival  <- gloss(k.of(ar$beta.B))
print(format(ar, digits = 3), row.names = FALSE)
```

Each step multiplies $C_B$, and so very nearly $F_B$, by $10^{\delta} = `r round(10^delta, 2)`$, since $\rho_B$ barely moves once the program is more than a step or two long. The adopted six steps give `r signif(F.B/1e6, 2)`M at $T_B = 2$ and `r signif(2*F.B/1e6, 2)`M at $T_B = 1$. A more bullish leader at **four steps** — $4/3$ of an order of magnitude, $\beta_B = `r round(10^(4*delta), 1)`$, printing `r signif(10^(4*delta), 2)`, $C_B = `r signif(10^(4*delta) * C.F, 2)`$ FLOP, roughly an end-2028 arrival — gives **$F_B = `r signif(ar$F.B.M.T2[ar$n.B == 4], 2)`$M** at $T_B = 2$ and **`r signif(ar$F.B.M.T1[ar$n.B == 4], 2)`M** at $T_B = 1$.

That four-step figure is where the breakout allowance starts to bite. A quarter of it (the allowance $\alpha_B$ of §S.7.5) is `r round(0.25 * ar$F.B.M.T2[ar$n.B == 4], 1)`M against a U.S.-located fleet of `r round(us.frac * fleet.ye2026 / 1e6)`M, so the transitional exposure of §6.4.2 breaches the allowance there; at the adopted `r signif(F.B/1e6, 2)`M the same quarter is `r round(0.25 * F.B / 1e6)`M and it does not.

**A later pause: the same $C_B$, a smaller $\beta_B$.** Because $C_B$ is absolute it does not move if the pause begins later — but the frozen frontier does, so the multiple shrinks. One blind step is `r round(12 * delta / log10(g.F), 1)` months of trajectory, so **roughly every half-year of delay removes one blind step from the breakout program**: a target six steps above a year-end 2026 frontier is about five steps above a mid-2027 frontier and about four above a year-end 2027 one. Step counts are not rounded: the last step may be partial.

```{r fb-delay}
delay <- c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2)                                            # years by which the pause starts later than year-end 2026
dl <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c("four steps" = 4, "six steps (adopted)" = 6), function(n) {
  cb <- 10^(n * delta) * C.F                                             # C_B fixed: an absolute capability level
  data.frame(target = sprintf("%d steps", n), delay.yr = delay, C.F.at.pause = signif(C.F * g.F^delay, 2),
             beta.B = cb / (C.F * g.F^delay), oom = log10(cb / (C.F * g.F^delay)),
             F.B.M = h100e(rho.E.of(cb / (C.F * g.F^delay)) * cb / (T.B * secs.per.yr * U.F)) / 1e6) }))
print(format(dl, digits = 3), row.names = FALSE)
```

At a mid-2027 pause the four-step target is `r round(log10(10^(4*delta) / g.F^0.5), 2)` orders of magnitude above the frontier — about three steps — and the adopted six-step target is `r round(log10(10^(6*delta) / g.F^0.5), 2)`, about five steps. $F_B$ itself declines only gently, because $C_B$ is fixed and $\rho_B$ falls slowly as the steps shrink in number; what moves is everything it is compared against. The installed fleet grows at the world-flow rate of §S.1.2.4, roughly `r round(g.flow, 1)`× a year, so the breakout exposure as a share of $F_B$ **worsens with delay at close to the rate the fleet grows**. The covert side goes the other way: $C_E$ is relative, so $F_E$ grows with the frontier and the covert ratios improve. That asymmetry — delay eases covert verification and tightens breakout deterrence — is the quantitative core of a window-of-opportunity argument, and it follows directly from $C_E$ being relative and $C_B$ absolute.

The last row is the starker point. By a year-end 2028 pause the four-step target sits $`r round(log10(10^(4*delta) / g.F^2), 2)`$ orders of magnitude above the frozen frontier — it has been all but overtaken. The model our bullish leader expected to be decisive is by then roughly the frontier itself, and a regime freezing there would be freezing at a capability level that leader already considered transformative. Nothing in the ledger arithmetic registers that; it is the reason a window-of-opportunity argument has to rest on more than these ratios.

## S.5.6 Judgment calls

* **$\beta_B$ is a belief, not a measurement**, and it is the input every ledger percentage in §6.4–6.5 is divided by. A smaller $\beta_B$ gives a smaller $F_B$, the regime-unfavorable side, so the end-2029 default is conservative relative to later arrival dates and optimistic relative to earlier ones. The paper says explicitly that this value would be negotiated.
* **The trend extrapolation.** $g^k$ translates a date into a multiple using a rate fitted to 2020–2025 data. Three years past the freeze is a long way to carry it, and a pause would itself bend the trajectory by design. The translation is offered for intuition, as §6.2.3 and its footnote say, not as a forecast.
* **$\rho_B$ inherits every judgment behind $\rho_E$** (§S.4.2): the estimated $\rho_F$, the four-month lag, the blind-leap increment $\delta$, and the possibility that a frontier lab's R&D compute already contains its own intermediate-scale staircase, which would make multiplying by the blind-leap factor a double count in the regime-favorable direction.
* **Direction of conservatism, overall.** The regime-unfavorable choice here is the end-2029 arrival date (rather than a later one). $T_B = 2$ is a central judgment; one year and three years are shown beside it in §S.5.5.

## S.5.7 Reference magnitudes: the installed stocks against $F_E$ and $F_B$

This is the reference figure for the opening of §6.2: the hardware that exists, on one scale, against the two violator fleet sizes the rest of §6.2 derives and §6.4 compares every ledger line with. It sits here in the supplement, rather than with the fleet trajectories in §S.1.2, because the chunk needs $F_E$ and $F_B$ to draw them; both quantities are in the paper's Table 3.1.

The figure below puts the world stock, the U.S.-located stock and China's stock on one logarithmic scale, with the shaded bands showing how far each could move under the alternatives considered above. The chips diverted to China around U.S. export controls are counted inside China's line and are not drawn as a series of their own; they are what gives China's band its width. What the bands do *not* show is that the three series are known to very different degrees, so the reading below the figure matters as much as the figure.

```{r q-trajectories, fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4.1, fig.cap = "Filled circles mark values a source reports; open circles mark values derived here from contemporaneous data (the world stock in the first two quarters of 2026, gap-filled against partial 2026 records); everything else after end-2025 is an extrapolation and is drawn as a line only, through year-end 2027. Lines are solid where Epoch's quarterly owner data run, to end-2025, and modelled thereafter: the world flow gap-filled through Q2 2026, then grown at 2.41x per year. The United States is drawn as a band rather than a line because no dataset measures it: it is an uncertain fraction of a well-determined world total, and the series starts only at the first measurement of that fraction (Epoch's GPU-clusters set, through June 2025). The band spans what the data alone permit, from Synergy's 55% all-workload hyperscale share to the hub's 94% share of tracked capacity; the thin line inside it is the adopted 0.75. The two grey curves, labelled on the right, are the violator fleet sizes $F_E$ (§S.4.4) and $F_B$ (§S.5.5) as functions of the pause date, for pause dates from 1 October 2026: read at any date, each is the initial value a pause beginning then would face. $F_E$ rises with the frontier (4.5x per year), because the covert evasion threshold is relative to it; $F_B$ drifts slightly down, because the breakout threshold $C_B$ is fixed and a later pause leaves fewer blind steps to it. Once a pause begins, both fall with training efficiency gains, which the curves do not show. Shaded bands: for the world, flow growth of 1.75x to 2.56x per year; for China, whose line includes the chips diverted around U.S. export controls, Epoch's 5th and 95th percentiles on that diverted stock."}
qe     <- function(d) as.Date(d)
ow     <- own[own[["End date"]] <= "2025-12-31", ]                                  # complete quarters only
agg    <- function(d, col = Hcol) tapply(d[[col]], d[["End date"]], sum)
w.obs  <- agg(ow[ow$Owner != "China (smuggled)", ]) + sum(a100.pre$h); cn.obs <- agg(ow[ow$Owner == "China", ]) + a100.mix[["China"]] * sum(a100.pre$h)   # with the A100s sold before 2022
sm.obs <- agg(ow[ow$Owner == "China (smuggled)", ])
sm.lo  <- agg(ow[ow$Owner == "China (smuggled)", ], "H100e (5th percentile)")
sm.hi  <- agg(ow[ow$Owner == "China (smuggled)", ], "H100e (95th percentile)")
yr     <- function(d) as.numeric(qe(d) - qe("2025-12-31")) / 365.25                 # the world model's clock, years from end-2025
t.mod  <- seq(0, 2, by = 1 / 24)                                                  # through year-end 2027
W.lo   <- make.W(make.world(1.75)); W.hi <- make.W(make.world(2.56))                # flow-growth alternatives, section S.1.2.5
sm.mod <- function(t, base = smuggled.2025) base * (1 + t / 2)
cn.mod <- function(t) china.official.2025 + t * sum(china.add.2026) + sm.mod(t)
cn.lo  <- function(t) china.official.2025 + t * sum(china.add.2026) + sm.mod(t, smug$lo[nrow(smug)])
cn.hi  <- function(t) china.official.2025 + t * sum(china.add.2026) + sm.mod(t, smug$hi[nrow(smug)])
us.frac.lo <- 0.55; us.frac.hi <- sum(dcs$h[dcs$us]) / sum(dcs$h)                   # what the data alone permit (section S.1.2.7)
us.start   <- "2025-06-30"                                                          # the first measurement of the U.S. FRACTION; nothing earlier measures it
gcl <- read.csv("data/gpu_clusters.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)   # that measurement: the only direct read on LOCATION
gcl$h <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(gcl[["H100 equivalents"]])); gcl$h[is.na(gcl$h)] <- 0
gcl <- gcl[gcl$Status == "Existing" & gcl[["Include in Standard Analysis"]] %in% c(TRUE, "True", "true"), ]
us.clusters.share <- sum(gcl$h[gcl$Country == "United States of America"]) / sum(gcl$h)   # 0.76 (Pilz et al. 2025), through June 2025
us.located <- sum(dcs$h[dcs$us])                                                    # H100e physically located at U.S. sites: a floor, not plotted

cn.tot <- as.numeric(cn.obs) + ifelse(is.na(sm.obs[names(cn.obs)]), 0, sm.obs[names(cn.obs)])
## W.of() extrapolates flat before t = 0 (approx rule = 2), so it cannot be used to carry the U.S. band
## back into 2025.  W.any() uses the observed quarters before end-2025 and the model after it.
W.any  <- function(t) { kn <- rbind(data.frame(t = yr(names(w.obs)), y = as.numeric(w.obs)),
                                    data.frame(t = t.mod[t.mod > 0], y = W.of(t.mod[t.mod > 0])))
  kn <- kn[order(kn$t), ]; exp(approx(kn$t, log(kn$y), xout = t, rule = 2)$y) }
t.us   <- seq(yr(us.start), 2, by = 1 / 24)
ser <- rbind(
  data.frame(t = yr(names(w.obs)), y = as.numeric(w.obs), lo = NA, hi = NA, k = "World"),
  data.frame(t = t.mod, y = W.of(t.mod), lo = W.lo(t.mod), hi = W.hi(t.mod), k = "World"),
  data.frame(t = t.us, y = us.frac * W.any(t.us), lo = us.frac.lo * W.any(t.us), hi = us.frac.hi * W.any(t.us), k = "United States"),
  data.frame(t = yr(names(cn.obs)), y = cn.tot,
             lo = as.numeric(cn.obs) + ifelse(is.na(sm.lo[names(cn.obs)]), 0, sm.lo[names(cn.obs)]),
             hi = as.numeric(cn.obs) + ifelse(is.na(sm.hi[names(cn.obs)]), 0, sm.hi[names(cn.obs)]), k = "China"),
  data.frame(t = t.mod, y = cn.mod(t.mod), lo = cn.lo(t.mod), hi = cn.hi(t.mod), k = "China"))   # the diverted chips are inside China's line and band, not a series of their own
lev <- c("World", "United States", "China")
labs <- c("World", "United States", "China")
ser$k <- factor(ser$k, levels = lev); ser$date <- qe("2025-12-31") + round(365.25 * ser$t)

## Anchors: filled circles where a source reports the number, diamonds where we derive it here.
pts <- rbind(
  data.frame(date = qe(names(w.obs)),  y = as.numeric(w.obs),  k = "World",           kind = "reported"),
  data.frame(date = qe(names(cn.obs)), y = cn.tot,             k = "China",           kind = "reported"),
  ## open circles only where a derivation rests on contemporaneous data (the gap-filled 2026 quarters); extrapolations are lines only
  data.frame(date = qe(c("2026-03-31", "2026-06-30")), y = W.of(c(0.25, 0.5)), k = "World", kind = "derived"))
pts$k <- factor(pts$k, levels = lev); pts$kind <- factor(pts$kind, levels = c("reported", "derived"))
cols <- setNames(c("#1A1A1A", "#2E5F8C", "#8C3B2E"), lev)
tp  <- seq(yr("2026-10-01"), 2, by = 1 / 48)                                       # pause dates from 2026-10-01, on the world model's clock (t = 1 is year-end 2026)
F.E.at <- function(t) F.E * g.F^(t - 1)
F.B.at <- function(t) { cf <- C.F * g.F^(t - 1); h100e(rho.F * blind.factor(C.B / cf) * C.B / (T.B * secs.per.yr * U.F)) }
fx  <- rbind(data.frame(t = tp, y = F.E.at(tp), k = "F_E(0)"), data.frame(t = tp, y = sapply(tp, F.B.at), k = "F_B(0)"))
fx$date <- qe("2025-12-31") + round(365.25 * fx$t)

ggplot(ser, aes(date, y / 1e6, colour = k, fill = k, linetype = k)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = lo / 1e6, ymax = hi / 1e6), colour = NA, alpha = 0.18, na.rm = TRUE) +
  ## F_E and F_B as functions of the PAUSE DATE: F_E scales with the frontier C_F; F_B holds C_B fixed (unrounded blind steps)
  geom_line(data = fx, aes(date, y / 1e6, group = k), inherit.aes = FALSE, colour = "#5A6470", linewidth = 0.6) +
  geom_line(aes(linewidth = k), na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_point(data = pts[pts$kind == "reported", ], aes(date, y / 1e6, fill = k), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             shape = 21, colour = "white", stroke = 0.35, size = 2.4, na.rm = TRUE) +
  geom_point(data = pts[pts$kind == "derived", ],  aes(date, y / 1e6, colour = k), inherit.aes = FALSE,
             shape = 21, fill = "white", stroke = 0.9, size = 2.4, na.rm = TRUE) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = cols, labels = labs, name = NULL) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = cols, labels = labs, name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "solid", "solid"), labels = labs, name = NULL) +
  scale_linewidth_manual(values = c(0.85, 0.6, 0.85), labels = labs, name = NULL, guide = "none") +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(order = 1, override.aes = list(linewidth = 0.9, alpha = 1, shape = NA, fill = NA, linetype = "solid")),
         linetype = "none", fill = "none") +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.1, 1, 10, 100), labels = c("0.1", "1", "10", "100"), limits = c(0.07, 700),
                sec.axis = dup_axis(breaks = c(F.E.at(2), F.B.at(2)) / 1e6, labels = c(expression(F[E](0)), expression(F[B](0))), name = NULL)) +
  year_axis(2024, 2027, date = TRUE, limits = qe(c("2024-01-01", "2028-01-01")), expand = c(0, 0)) +
  labs(x = "Pause date", y = "M H100e",
       title = "Initial fleet thresholds vs installed accelerator stocks (projected)") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) + year_theme +
  theme(panel.grid.minor.y = element_blank(), plot.title = element_text(size = 11.5),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 10), axis.title.y = element_text(size = 10.5), axis.title.x = element_text(size = 10.5, margin = margin(t = 2)), axis.text.y.right = element_text(size = 11, colour = "#5A6470"),
        legend.position = "bottom", legend.box = "horizontal", legend.text = element_text(size = 10, colour = "grey25"),
        legend.key.size = unit(0.9, "lines"), legend.key.width = unit(2.2, "lines"), legend.margin = margin(0, 2, 0, 2), legend.box.spacing = unit(4, "pt"),
        plot.margin = margin(4, 14, 2, 2)) +
  ## the reported/derived key, bottom right, on an opaque (but borderless) panel so the rules and
  ## gridlines behind it are hidden rather than showing through the text
  annotate("rect", xmin = qe("2026-10-20"), xmax = qe("2028-01-01"), ymin = 0.071, ymax = 0.19,
           fill = "white", colour = NA) +
  annotate("point", x = qe(c("2026-12-05", "2026-12-05")), y = c(0.141, 0.0886), shape = 21, size = 2.4,
           fill = c("#5A6470", "white"), colour = c("white", "#5A6470"), stroke = c(0.35, 0.9)) +
  annotate("text", x = qe(c("2027-02-15", "2027-02-15")), y = c(0.141, 0.0886), hjust = 0, size = 3.55, colour = "grey25",
           label = c("reported", "derived"))
```

**Reading, in order of how well each is known.**

* **The world stock is the firmest.** Epoch's quarterly owner data run to end-2025 (`r round(stock.2025/1e6, 1)`M), the first half of 2026 is gap-filled by us, and only the second half is modelled. At $t_0$ the flow-growth alternatives of §S.1.2.5 span `r round(make.W(make.world(1.75))(1)/1e6, 1)`–`r round(make.W(make.world(2.56))(1)/1e6, 1)`M around the adopted `r round(fleet.ye2026/1e6, 1)`M, a spread of about `r round(100*(make.W(make.world(2.56))(1)/make.W(make.world(1.75))(1)-1))`%, and an alternative gap-fill moves it by about 0.2M. That is the sense in which "47M" is robust: `r round(100 * stock.q2 / fleet.ye2026)`% of it is sales recorded or gap-filled through mid-2026. It loosens quickly afterwards — by mid-2027 the same alternatives span `r round(make.W(make.world(1.75))(1.5)/1e6)`–`r round(make.W(make.world(2.56))(1.5)/1e6)`M — which is why §S.5.5's delay analysis is more uncertain than anything evaluated at $t_0$.

* **The U.S.-located stock is not a measurement, and the figure is drawn to say so.** No dataset carries a U.S. time series, so there is no U.S. *trajectory* to plot: there is a well-determined world total and an uncertain fraction of it. It is therefore drawn as a band, not a line, and it begins only where the fraction is first measured — Epoch's GPU-clusters set through June 2025, which puts `r round(100*us.clusters.share)`% of tracked cluster performance in the United States (Pilz et al. 2025). Even that covers only about `r round(100*sum(gcl$h)/stock.2025)`% of the stock. The band spans what the data alone permit, `r round(100*us.frac.lo)`% (Synergy's all-workload hyperscale share) to `r round(100*us.frac.hi)`% (the hub's share of *tracked* capacity), or `r round(us.frac.lo*fleet.ye2026/1e6, 1)`–`r round(us.frac.hi*fleet.ye2026/1e6, 1)`M at year-end 2026; the thin line inside it is the adopted 0.75, whose own bracket of 0.70–0.80 (`r round(0.70*fleet.ye2026/1e6, 1)`–`r round(0.80*fleet.ye2026/1e6, 1)`M) is narrower than the band by a factor of three. It is the judgment, not the evidence, that makes $Q_{US}$ look well determined. For what it is worth as a floor, Epoch has physically located `r round(us.located/1e6)`M H100e at U.S. sites by satellite and permit evidence — about `r round(100*us.located/(us.frac*W.of(0.5)))`% of what the adopted share claims was there in mid-2026. It is not plotted, because a single point on that scale reads as an estimate of the series rather than as a bound on it.

* **China's stock is the weakest of the three totals**, and almost all of its weakness is in one component. Its range at $t_0$ is `r round(china.range[["low"]]/1e6, 1)`–`r round(china.range[["high"]]/1e6, 1)`M around `r round(china.fleet.ye2026/1e6, 2)`M, a factor of `r round(china.range[["high"]]/china.range[["low"]], 1)` from end to end.

* **The diverted stock is the least robust component of any series on the plot and the reason the China band is wide.** It is part of China's line and is not drawn separately. Epoch's own 5th–95th interval on the diverted stock is a factor of `r round(smug$hi[nrow(smug)]/smug$lo[nrow(smug)], 1)`, and our extrapolation to $t_0$ (a straight line from zero at the start of 2024, §S.1.2.8) adds a further choice that could plausibly run from 0.33M to 0.66M of 2026 additions alone. Centrally it is `r round(100*smuggled.ye2026/china.fleet.ye2026)`% of China's fleet; at the two ends of Epoch's interval it is `r round(100 * 1.5 * smug$lo[nrow(smug)] / china.range[["low"]])`% or `r round(100 * 1.5 * smug$hi[nrow(smug)] / china.range[["high"]])`% of it.

Two structural points the figure makes better than a table. The world and U.S. curves are **parallel by construction**, so any argument that turns on the U.S. share is a judgment about one number and not about a trend. And China's fleet is about `r round(100*china.fleet.ye2026/fleet.ye2026, 1)`% of the world's, with the U.S.-located fleet roughly `r round(0.75*fleet.ye2026/china.fleet.ye2026)`× China's — a gap that has been roughly stable on this log scale since 2022, and which is what makes the two states' ledgers look so different in §S.7.

# S.6 Dark compute (§3.3.2, §5.4–§5.5, §6.4.3, §6.5)

## S.6.1 The U.S. stock outside the seven firms

This section estimates the U.S.-located stock held outside the seven large firms, the paper's non-hyperscale stock. §S.6.4 splits it into **named owners**, whose holdings are individually documented, and the **unnamed residual**, the long tail; the paper describes the U.S. stock in those three parts. In the code below, `us.residual` is the whole non-hyperscale stock. It is the U.S.-located stock held by owners other than the seven large firms whose inventories are presumed to be well accounted for (Google, Microsoft, Amazon, Meta, Oracle, CoreWeave, xAI): neoclouds, the federal government, firms such as Tesla and Apple, universities, and a long tail. The estimate uses one measured share and one judgmental input:

```{r us-residual}
other.share  <- (by.owner[["Other"]] - smuggled.2025) / stock.2025   # owners other than the seven U.S. firms and China, end-2025 (Epoch chip owners), less the chips diverted to China, which sit in this row
other.us.loc <- 0.45                                     # share of that stock located in the U.S.: judgmental input, bracketed below
us.residual  <- other.share * other.us.loc * fleet.ye2026
round(c("'Other' owners, share of the end-2025 world stock (%)" = 100 * by.owner[["Other"]] / stock.2025,
        "  less chips diverted to China around U.S. export controls (%)" = 100 * other.share,
        "evidence: U.S. share of non-China clusters under 10k H100e (Epoch GPU clusters, %)" = 100 * sum(gc$h[gc$us & gc$h < 1e4]) / sum(gc$h[!gc$cn & gc$h < 1e4]),
        "U.S. residual, year-end 2026 (M H100e)" = us.residual / 1e6, "  as % of the U.S.-located fleet" = 100 * us.residual / us.fleet.ye2026,
        "  so the seven firms hold (%)" = 100 * (1 - us.residual / us.fleet.ye2026), "China's fleet / U.S. residual" = china.fleet.ye2026 / us.residual), 1)
```

* **`r round(100 * other.share, 1)`%** is measured (Epoch AI 2026c) and carried from end-2025 to year-end 2026, on the assumption that a similar composition holds. Epoch's "Other" row holds `r round(100 * by.owner[["Other"]] / stock.2025, 1)`% of the end-2025 stock, but that includes the chips diverted to China around U.S. export controls (`r round(100 * (by.owner[["Other"]] / stock.2025 - other.share), 1)`%). Epoch's owner rows add up to its sales totals without the "China (smuggled)" row (§S.1.2.1), so the diverted chips are already counted in one of them. The seven firms are named buyers and the "China" row is official sales, which leaves "Other"; the diverted chips are 22% of its NVIDIA part. They are located in China, so they are taken out before the location share is applied. The diverted stock is projected separately (§S.1.2.8).
* **About 45%** is a judgmental input. The holders in this bucket resemble the owners of small clusters, and in Epoch's clusters data the U.S. hosts 41–46% of non-Chinese cluster capacity below 10k H100e (against 100% of the largest clusters). Those data do not include diverted chips, so the share applies to the rest of the bucket. Nothing measures it directly.

**Uncertainty.**

```{r us-residual-range}
res.range <- other.share * c(low = 0.30, central = 0.45, high = 0.60) * fleet.ye2026
round(rbind("U.S. residual (M H100e)" = res.range / 1e6, "  as % of the U.S.-located fleet" = 100 * res.range / us.fleet.ye2026), 1)
```

A location share of 0.30–0.60 gives roughly `r round(res.range[["low"]] / 1e6, 1)`–`r round(res.range[["high"]] / 1e6, 1)`M; Epoch's own 90% interval on the "Other" bucket is a further −34% / +42%.

The range moves no qualitative conclusion. The residual enters the ledger only through the census of §S.6.5, where about 0.3% of the stock that is not publicly identifiable goes missing, so the whole range moves $K_M$ by a few thousand H100e. It also supports the observation that the U.S. residual and China's fleet (`r round(china.fleet.ye2026/1e6, 1)`M, range `r round(china.range[["low"]]/1e6, 1)`–`r round(china.range[["high"]]/1e6, 1)`M) are of the same order.

## S.6.2 Non-deniable concealment and the one-million example

```{r dark-scenarios}
scen <- c("high cooperation", "low cooperation", "non-deniable concealment")
dark.nd <- c("U.S." = 300e3, "China" = 1e6)                                      # non-deniable concealment: K_0 per state before discounting, set by the authors (§6.4.3)
round(rbind("K_0 (k H100e)" = dark.nd / 1e3, "  % of F_E" = 100 * dark.nd / F.E, "  % of F_B" = 100 * dark.nd / F.B), 3)
```

Two of the paper's three dark-compute scenarios, high and low cooperation, are derived from a model of the census (§S.6.4–§S.6.6). The third, **non-deniable concealment**, is not an estimate. Its sizes are the authors' definitions of a stock that could not be explained as loss and would require deliberate under-declaration by a large holder: 1M H100e for China, roughly its pre-pause diverted stock (§S.1.2.8), and 300k for the United States, where a large stock would be harder to keep secret. Those are `r signif(100 * dark.nd[["U.S."]] / F.E, 2)`% and `r round(100 * dark.nd[["China"]] / F.E)`% of $F_E$, and `r signif(100 * dark.nd[["U.S."]] / F.B, 2)`% and `r signif(100 * dark.nd[["China"]] / F.B, 2)`% of $F_B$. The example that opens §6.4.3, a million missing H100e, is the same `r round(100 * 1e6 / F.E)`% of $F_E$.

## S.6.3 What runs out of records

A working definition of dark compute for a cooperative regime: follow the legitimate records for every chip (the vendor's sales ledger, distributors' and server makers' customer records, owners' inventories, warranty returns, recyclers' destruction certificates) until the chain ends in a shell company, a fraud, or a chip destroyed without a confirmed record; what cannot be followed to a chip or to a confirmed disposal is dark. Every accelerator must be held by a licensed operator, so an unregistered chip is contraband whatever its owner's size. Chips already diverted around export controls by the time the agreement takes effect are counted separately (§S.1.2.8). Large owners, in China as in the United States, are assumed to keep ordinary asset records and to recycle retired hardware through documented channels; a state could not plausibly claim otherwise.

The one line that can be computed is failed hardware:

```{r records-failed}
failed.by.age <- function(h, t.sale, rate, at = 2027, w = 3) { age <- at - t.sale                             # w: warranty in years
  c(all = sum(h * (1 - exp(-rate * age))), out.of.warranty = sum((h * (exp(-rate * w) - exp(-rate * age)))[age > w])) }   # failures after the warranty ran out
us.failed <- sapply(fail.rate, function(r) us.frac * failed.by.age(wm$h, wm$t.sale, r))
oq <- read.csv("data/ai_chip_owners_quarters_by_chip_type.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE); oq <- oq[oq$Owner == "China", ]
oq$t <- as.numeric(substr(oq[["Start date"]], 1, 4)) + (as.numeric(substr(oq[["Start date"]], 6, 7)) - 1) %/% 3 / 4 + 0.125
cn <- aggregate(list(h = oq[[Hcol]]), list(t = oq$t), sum, na.rm = TRUE); cn <- cn[cn$t < 2026, ]
cn <- rbind(data.frame(t = a100.pre$t, h = a100.mix[["China"]] * a100.pre$h), cn)                              # China's share of the A100s sold before 2022
cn <- rbind(cn, data.frame(t = 2026 + (0:3) / 4 + 0.125, h = sum(china.add.2026) / 4))                     # China's stock excluding diverted chips: Epoch's quarterly rows, then the 2026 additions of S.1.2.8 spread over the year
cn.failed <- sapply(fail.rate, function(r) failed.by.age(cn$h, cn$t, r))
## the census (S.6.5) takes a rate that rises with age, to be conservative: the measured rate to year three, then haz.rise more per year each year
haz.rise <- 0.03
Hz <- function(a, r = fail.rate[["central"]]) r * a + 0.5 * haz.rise * pmax(a - 3, 0)^2          # cumulative hazard at age a
late.rising <- function(h, t.sale, at = 2027, w = 3) { age <- at - t.sale; sum((h * (exp(-Hz(w)) - exp(-Hz(age))))[age > w]) }
failed.rising <- c("U.S." = us.frac * late.rising(wm$h, wm$t.sale), "China" = late.rising(cn$h, cn$t))
round(rbind("U.S.: H100e failed by year-end 2026 (k)" = us.failed["all", ], "  of which after the three-year warranty ran out (k)" = us.failed["out.of.warranty", ],
            "China, excluding diverted chips: H100e failed by year-end 2026 (k)" = cn.failed["all", ], "  of which after the three-year warranty ran out (k)" = cn.failed["out.of.warranty", ]) / 1e3, 1)
round(c("failed after the warranty if the rate rises by three points a year after year three (k): U.S." = failed.rising[["U.S."]] / 1e3, "  China, excluding diverted chips" = failed.rising[["China"]] / 1e3,
        "the rate in years four to seven on that assumption (% a year, mid-year)" = 100 * (fail.rate[["central"]] + haz.rise * (0.5 + 0:3))), 1)
```

* **Failed chips.** A chip that fails under warranty goes back to the vendor, which keeps the return under its serial number, so it rarely goes missing (the census of §S.6.5 takes 1% of these failures to leave no record). Accelerators are sold in servers that typically remain under warranty for three years (NVIDIA 2026c; Dell Technologies 2026; Hewlett Packard Enterprise 2026); the terms large operators negotiate with their manufacturers are not public. A failure after the warranty has run out could be scrapped with no record outside the owner's own, and few chips are old enough for that: about `r sprintf("%.1f", us.failed["out.of.warranty", "central"] / 1e3)`k H100e in the U.S. (`r sprintf("%.1f", us.failed["out.of.warranty", "low"] / 1e3)`–`r sprintf("%.1f", us.failed["out.of.warranty", "high"] / 1e3)`k) and about `r sprintf("%.1f", cn.failed["out.of.warranty", "central"] / 1e3)`k in China. That is an upper bound, since large owners scrap through certified recyclers. Those figures hold the measured rate at every age. The rate was measured on chips under three years old, and nothing measures these chips later in life, so the census of §S.6.5 takes a less favorable assumption: the measured rate to year three, then **three percentage points more per year for each further year of age** (about `r round(100 * (fail.rate[["central"]] + haz.rise * 0.5))`% in year four and `r round(100 * (fail.rate[["central"]] + haz.rise * 3.5))`% in year seven). That is a judgmental input with no source, chosen to err on the regime-unfavorable side. On it the failures after warranty are about `r signif(failed.rising[["U.S."]] / 1e3, 2)`k H100e in the U.S. and `r signif(failed.rising[["China"]] / 1e3, 2)`k in China. Chips diverted around U.S. export controls are a separate case: they carry no warranty, so none of their failures has a vendor record (§S.6.5).
* **Retired chips.** None yet (§S.1.2.6). After the agreement, licensed operators destroy retired chips verifiably, so retirement does not become a channel for losing them.
* **No data found** for two further lines. (i) *Customers of record that no longer exist, and undocumented resale:* a secondary market exists (a marketplace for used H100s and A100s opened in July 2026 reporting requests "from hundreds to tens of thousands of GPUs"; used H100s trade at roughly \$18–22k), but no source gives its volume, and chips this young and supply-constrained have mostly stayed with their first owners. (ii) *Diverters' unshipped inventory:* chips held by shell companies on the day the agreement takes effect; at the §S.1.2.8 diversion flow of about 0.3–0.5M H100e a year and a dwell time of one to three months (a guess), 30–120k worldwide, mostly in third countries.

**Reading.** On this definition the one line that can be computed is failures after the warranty, about `r signif(failed.rising[["U.S."]] / 1e3, 2)`k H100e in the U.S. and `r signif(failed.rising[["China"]] / 1e3, 2)`k in China on the rising rate, of which the census takes a tenth to leave no record (§S.6.5). What a census would miss beyond that lies in the lines that cannot, above all chips in the long tail of owners that are neither declared nor traced through records; §S.6.4 and §S.6.5 estimate that by holding type. Most of the genuinely dark stock is the diverted stock, counted separately. Two independent checks bound what a state could conceal by under-declaring *production* rather than holdings: lithography-tool usage records held by the tool and laser vendors, and above all high-bandwidth-memory shipments, which go almost entirely into accelerators at a fixed number of stacks per package (Patel, AJ, and Xie 2025: "13 million stacks of HBM" reached China before the December 2024 controls, enough for "1.6M Ascend 910C packages"; Chinese-made memory from 2026 on is outside foreign ledgers, and about half of Huawei's 2026 units are 950PRs built on "non-HBM DRAM" for the prefill stage of inference (Somala 2026), which the memory check does not see at all).

## S.6.4 Who holds the stock: named owners, the unnamed residual, and China's true tail

A census does two jobs (§3.3.2): it gets most chips declared, and it classifies and quantifies what is not. Both depend on who holds the chips. Owners with a sourced, individually documented holding (company filings and releases, government budgets, press reports of specific clusters, and Epoch's data-center hub, Epoch AI 2026g) are called **named owners**. Like the seven large U.S. firms, they are presumed accounted for: audited books or public budgets, known sites, and chips that report their identity when running. The two lists are in `data/large_owners_us.csv` (`r nrow(read.csv("data/large_owners_us.csv"))` rows) and `data/large_owners_cn.csv` (`r nrow(read.csv("data/large_owners_cn.csv"))` rows); each row carries its source and the basis of its number, and the census counts the rows marked `in_tally` = `y`. Every link in the two lists was opened and compared with its row on October 9, 2026. Rows that this check could not confirm, and that the authors did not then review themselves, are not counted and are left out of the published lists. Holdings are in Epoch's H100e. A holding counts from the date of its evidence, so the end-2025 figures are floors.

```{r census-named}
own.c <- read.csv("data/ai_chip_owners_cumulative_by_designer.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
a100.n <- sum(a100.pre$h)                                                                                     # A100s sold before 2022 (section S.1.2.1)
nd.c <- function(e) { x <- own.c[own.c[["End date"]] == e, ]; sum(x[x$Owner == "Other", Hcol]) - sum(x[x$Owner == "China (smuggled)", Hcol]) + a100.mix[["Other"]] * a100.n }   # 'Other' less diverted
wd.c <- function(e) { x <- own.c[own.c[["End date"]] == e, ]; sum(x[x$Owner != "China (smuggled)", Hcol]) + a100.n }                                         # world, no diverted row
lo.us <- read.csv("data/large_owners_us.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE); lo.us <- lo.us[lo.us$in_tally == "y", ]
lo.cn <- read.csv("data/large_owners_cn.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE); lo.cn <- lo.cn[lo.cn$in_tally == "y", ]
held.at <- function(r, q) {       # a holding at quarter-end q: its dated milestones, or its end-2025 value from its install date
  pts <- if (nzchar(r$ms)) do.call(rbind, lapply(strsplit(strsplit(r$ms, ";")[[1]], ":"), function(z) data.frame(t = as.numeric(z[1]), v = as.numeric(z[2]))))
         else data.frame(t = numeric(0), v = numeric(0))
  if (!nzchar(r$ms)) { if (r$e25 > 0) pts <- rbind(pts, data.frame(t = ifelse(is.na(suppressWarnings(as.numeric(r$t0))), 2026, as.numeric(r$t0)), v = r$e25))
                       if (r$firm > max(c(0, pts$v))) pts <- rbind(pts, data.frame(t = 2026.75, v = r$firm)) }
  z <- pts[pts$t <= q + 1e-9, ]; if (nrow(z)) z$v[which.max(z$t)] else 0 }
named.us <- sapply(c(2024, 2025, 2026), function(q) sum(sapply(seq_len(nrow(lo.us)), function(i) held.at(lo.us[i, ], q))))
ends  <- c("2023-12-31", "2024-12-31", "2025-12-31")
tw    <- sapply(ends, nd.c) - named.us; ww <- sapply(ends, wd.c)
s.add <- mean(diff(tw) / diff(ww))                               # the unnamed tail's share of world additions, 2024 and 2025
tail25.us <- other.us.loc * nd.c("2025-12-31") - named.us[3]      # unnamed U.S. residual, end-2025
g.u   <- 1 + s.add * (fleet.ye2026 - ww[3]) / tw[3]              # 2026 growth: it keeps its share of world additions
N.us  <- unname(tail25.us * g.u)
## China: official stock (diverted chips excluded) = named + unnamed large buyers + true tail
ct.c <- read.csv("data/ai_chip_owners_cumulative_by_chip_type.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
ct.c <- ct.c[ct.c$Owner == "China" & ct.c[["End date"]] == "2025-12-31", ]; stk.cn <- setNames(ct.c[[Hcol]], ct.c[["Chip type"]])
stk.cn[["A100"]] <- stk.cn[["A100"]] + a100.mix[["China"]] * a100.n
cn.official <- china.fleet.ye2026 - smuggled.ye2026
large.share <- c(H20 = 0.80, A800 = 0.83, H800 = 0.53, A100 = 0.53, `Instinct MI308X` = 0)
big.cn <- max(0, sum(large.share * stk.cn[names(large.share)]) - sum(lo.cn$sched[grepl("A100|A800|H800|Hopper|H20 assumed|6,500 GPUs", lo.cn$basis)])) +
          max(0, 0.79 * (stk.cn[["Siyuan 590"]] + 4 * 0.01e6) - sum(lo.cn$sched[grepl("Siyuan 590", lo.cn$basis)]))
tail.cn <- cn.official - sum(lo.cn$sched) - big.cn
cbind(value = round(c("U.S.: named owners' holdings, end-2023 (k)" = named.us[1] / 1e3, "  end-2024 (k)" = named.us[2] / 1e3, "  end-2025 (k)" = named.us[3] / 1e3,
    "  year-end 2026, including deliveries due in 2026 (M)" = sum(lo.us$sched) / 1e6,
    "U.S.: the unnamed tail's share of world additions, 2024 (%)" = 100 * unname(diff(tw) / diff(ww))[1], "  2025 (%)" = 100 * unname(diff(tw) / diff(ww))[2],
    "U.S.: unnamed residual, end-2025 (M)" = tail25.us / 1e6, "  2026 growth factor" = unname(g.u), "  year-end 2026 (M)" = unname(N.us) / 1e6,
    "China: official stock, end-2025 (M)" = sum(stk.cn) / 1e6, "  year-end 2026 (M)" = cn.official / 1e6,
    "China: named owners, end-2025 (M)" = sum(lo.cn$e25) / 1e6, "  year-end 2026 (M)" = sum(lo.cn$sched) / 1e6,
    "China: unnamed large buyers, year-end 2026 (M)" = big.cn / 1e6, "China: true tail, year-end 2026 (M)" = tail.cn / 1e6), 3))
```

* **The U.S.** Named owners outside the seven firms hold `r signif(named.us[3] / 1e6, 2)`M H100e dated to end-2025 and `r sprintf("%.1f", sum(lo.us$sched) / 1e6)`M at year-end 2026 if the deliveries they announce for 2026 arrive: Tesla, the Department of Energy's laboratories, neoclouds (Nscale, Lightning AI, Lambda), universities. The **unnamed residual** is what is left of the non-hyperscale stock of §S.6.1 once they are subtracted: `r signif(tail25.us / 1e6, 2)`M at end-2025. It grows in 2026 by keeping the share of world additions that the stock outside the seven firms, China and the named owners took in 2024 and 2025 (`r round(100 * s.add)`%), a factor of `r signif(g.u, 2)`, to **`r sprintf("%.1f", N.us / 1e6)`M** at year-end 2026. Two alternatives bracket it: no 2026 purchases (`r signif(tail25.us / 1e6, 2)`M) and the 2025 growth factor carried forward (about 2.3M), which would outgrow the world stock.
* **China.** Epoch does not name Chinese owners, so the list was built from filings, tenders and press reports: the telecom operators' owned capacity (China Mobile's self-built 33 EFLOPS, China Telecom's 71 EFLOPS, China Unicom's 45 EFLOPS of unstated precision, counted at half), Huawei's Horinger campus and a VNET campus in Ulanqab (estimates from Epoch's data-center hub; Epoch AI 2026g), ByteDance (third-party estimates of its purchases), Alibaba's Zhangbei site, city and national computing centres, and AI labs. Named holdings are `r signif(sum(lo.cn$e25) / 1e6, 2)`M at end-2025 (`r round(100 * sum(lo.cn$e25) / sum(stk.cn))`% of the official stock) and `r signif(sum(lo.cn$sched) / 1e6, 2)`M at year-end 2026. Capacity stated in FP16 converts at 1 H100e per PFLOPS; capacity of unstated precision at 0.5 (the regime-unfavorable reading, since fewer named chips leave a larger tail).
* **Unnamed large buyers.** NVIDIA's China-specific chips went mostly to a few buyers: ByteDance, Alibaba, Tencent and Baidu took more than 80% of 2024 H20 demand (a Bernstein estimate, as reported by Sina Finance 2025); four firms ordered about 100,000 A800s for 2023 delivery, 83% of Epoch's total (Reuters 2023); ByteDance alone had about 100,000 A100 and H800 delivered or on order in mid-2023, 53% of those two chips (IT Home 2023, citing LatePost). Cambricon's largest customer took 79% of its 2024 revenue (Cambricon Technologies 2025). Those shares, less the named holdings of the same chips, give `r signif(big.cn / 1e6, 2)`M. **Ascend (about three quarters of the year-end 2026 official stock) has no buyer data,** so its unnamed part is all counted as tail: the **true tail** is **`r signif(tail.cn / 1e6, 2)`M**. That is the regime-unfavorable reading.

## S.6.5 What a census would miss, by holding type (§5.5)

The **missing stock** $K_M(s)$ in state $s$ is what a census conducted in good faith fails to find. Each state's stock is sorted into four **holding types** $h$, with $Q(h, s)$ the stock of type $h$. Failed chips are taken out of each type first, and a share of them is missing because no record shows that they failed. A **missing fraction** $\mu(h)$ then applies to the functional chips that remain:

$$K_M(s) \;=\; \sum_h \Big[\,D(h, s) \;+\; \mu(h)\,\big(Q(h, s) - \text{failed chips}(h, s)\big)\Big],$$

where $D(h, s)$ is the number of failed chips that go missing, the paper's symbol.

The four holding types, in decreasing order of visibility:

* **Publicly identifiable holdings:** the seven large U.S. firms, the named owners of §S.6.4 and, in China, the named owners and the unnamed large buyers.
* **On-books business and institutional holdings:** firms, laboratories and smaller clouds that hold chips on their books and appear in the chain of sales records, but are not individually documented here. In the U.S. this is the unnamed residual less its informal part; in China, the true tail less its informal part, plus the diverted chips whose holders have some state record, such as a customs entry or a tax invoice.
* **Off-books business and institutional holdings:** chips bought without paperwork and run by an operating business or institution. Only China's diverted stock has these.
* **Informal holdings:** individuals, and the shell companies and traders engaged in diversion, with their stock in transit.

Every rate below is a judgment or an analogy from another domain, chosen for its structure, with the direction of its bias stated.

```{r census-missing}
d.F <- 0.94; p.T <- 0.80                                     # on-books holdings: declaration, tracing
d.IS <- 0.80; p.IS <- 0.50                                   # off-books and informal holdings: declaration, recovery (judgmental inputs)
v.off <- 0.01                                                # share of the stock not publicly identifiable that is held informally, in both states
out.dc <- 0.10; miss.dc <- 0.06                                # business-held chips outside a data center; chips in a data center that its operator's declaration and an inspection both miss
f.site <- out.dc + miss.dc                                     # share of business-held chips not found at a site
srv <- rbind("2023" = c(small = 8.5, hyperscale = 30.0), "2025" = c(small = 6.4, hyperscale = 34.8))   # % of U.S. servers, measured from Figure 4.1 of Shehabi et al. (2024)
venue <- c(enterprise.dc = 45, colocation = 16, closet.edge = 14) / 75      # for comparison: operators' own IT by venue (Uptime Institute 2025, Figure 13)
mu <- c(0, (1 - d.F) * (1 - p.T) * f.site, (1 - d.IS) * (1 - p.IS) * f.site, (1 - d.IS) * (1 - p.IS))   # missing fraction of functional chips, by holding type
w.in <- 0.01; w.out <- 0.10; w.off <- 0.50                     # failed chips with no record made at the time: under warranty, after it, at off-books holdings (all at informal holdings)
## failed chips as a share of each group's year-end 2026 stock: at any age, and after the three-year warranty
oq.o <- read.csv("data/ai_chip_owners_quarters_by_chip_type.csv", check.names = FALSE, stringsAsFactors = FALSE); oq.o <- oq.o[oq.o[["Start date"]] <= "2025-12-31", ]
oq.o$t <- as.numeric(substr(oq.o[["Start date"]], 1, 4)) + (as.numeric(substr(oq.o[["Start date"]], 6, 7)) - 1) %/% 3 / 4 + 0.125
oq.o$h <- suppressWarnings(as.numeric(oq.o[[Hcol]])); oq.o <- oq.o[!is.na(oq.o$h), c("Owner", "t", "h")]
oq.o <- rbind(oq.o, do.call(rbind, lapply(names(a100.mix), function(o) data.frame(Owner = o, t = a100.pre$t, h = a100.mix[[o]] * a100.pre$h))))   # with the A100s sold before 2022
oow.c <- function(x, w = 3) { a <- 2027 - x$t; sum((x$h * (exp(-Hz(w)) - exp(-Hz(a))))[a > w]) }          # Hz: the rate rises after year three (S.6.3)
x7 <- oq.o[oq.o$Owner %in% us.seven, ]; xo <- oq.o[oq.o$Owner == "Other", ]; xc <- oq.o[oq.o$Owner == "China", ]
## the 2026 vintage: Epoch's owner data end in 2025, so each group's 2026 additions (its year-end 2026 stock less its end-2025 stock) are added,
## spread over the four quarters in proportion to the world model's quarterly flow
wq26 <- c(stock.q2 - q2f - ww[[3]], world.q$flow[1:3]); wq26 <- wq26 / sum(wq26); t26 <- 2026 + c(0.125, 0.375, 0.625, 0.875)
add26 <- function(x, tot) rbind(x[, c("t", "h")], data.frame(t = t26, h = max(tot, 0) * wq26))
s7 <- sum(x7$h)                                                                                               # the seven firms' end-2025 stock
x7 <- add26(x7, s7 * (fleet.ye2026 / ww[[3]] - 1)); xo <- add26(xo, other.share * (fleet.ye2026 - ww[[3]])); xc <- add26(xc, cn.official - sum(xc$h))
dv <- data.frame(t = 2024 + (0:11) / 4 + 0.125, h = smuggled.ye2026 / 12)          # diverted chips: the straight line from zero at the start of 2024
fail <- rbind(seven    = c(all = oow.c(x7, 0), late = oow.c(x7)) / (s7 * fleet.ye2026 / ww[[3]]),     # the seven keep their share of the world stock in 2026
              other    = c(all = oow.c(xo, 0), late = oow.c(xo)) / (other.share * fleet.ye2026),
              china    = c(all = oow.c(xc, 0), late = oow.c(xc)) / cn.official,
              diverted = c(all = oow.c(dv, 0), late = oow.c(dv, 0)) / smuggled.ye2026)                        # no warranty: every failure counts as after it
off.div <- 0.10; transit <- smuggled.2025 / 2 / 12             # a tenth of the diverted stock off the books; one month of diverted flow at Epoch's central rate for 2024-25, in transit
named.us26 <- sum(lo.us$sched); N7 <- us.fleet.ye2026 - N.us - named.us26; named.cn <- sum(lo.cn$sched) + big.cn
cell <- function(Q, g, win, wout, nowarranty = FALSE) { all <- Q * fail[[g, "all"]]; late <- if (nowarranty) all else Q * fail[[g, "late"]]
  c(Q = Q, failed = all, miss.failed = win * (all - late) + wout * late) }
hl <- c("publicly identifiable holdings", "on-books holdings", "off-books holdings", "informal holdings")
fin <- function(m) { dimnames(m) <- list(hl, c("Q", "failed", "miss.failed")); fun <- m[, "Q"] - m[, "failed"]
