  cbind(m, functional = fun, mu = mu, miss.fun = mu * fun, missing = m[, "miss.failed"] + mu * fun) }
hold.us <- fin(rbind(cell(N7, "seven", w.in, w.out) + cell(named.us26, "other", w.in, w.out),
                     cell((1 - v.off) * N.us, "other", w.in, w.out), c(0, 0, 0),
                     cell(v.off * N.us, "other", 1, 1) + c(transit / 2, 0, 0)))                               # stock in transit has not failed
hold.cn <- fin(rbind(cell(named.cn, "china", w.in, w.out),
                     cell((1 - v.off) * tail.cn, "china", w.in, w.out) + cell((1 - off.div - v.off) * smuggled.ye2026, "diverted", w.out, w.out, TRUE),
                     cell(off.div * smuggled.ye2026, "diverted", w.off, w.off, TRUE),
                     cell(v.off * tail.cn, "china", 1, 1) + cell(v.off * smuggled.ye2026, "diverted", 1, 1, TRUE) + c(transit / 2, 0, 0)))
K.miss.us <- sum(hold.us[, "missing"]); K.miss.cn <- sum(hold.cn[, "missing"])
div.miss <- function(off = off.div, D = smuggled.ye2026) { fd <- fail[["diverted", "all"]]                    # what the diverted stock adds to China's missing stock
  D * ((1 - off - v.off) * (w.out * fd + mu[2] * (1 - fd)) + off * (w.off * fd + mu[3] * (1 - fd)) + v.off * (fd + mu[4] * (1 - fd))) }
signif(100 * fail, 3)        # failed, % of the year-end 2026 stock: all failures, and those after the warranty
tab <- function(m) cbind("Q (k H100e)" = round(m[, "Q"] / 1e3), "failed (k)" = round(m[, "failed"] / 1e3, 2), "failed chips missing (k)" = round(m[, "miss.failed"] / 1e3, 2),
                         "functional (k)" = round(m[, "functional"] / 1e3), "mu (%)" = signif(100 * m[, "mu"], 2), "functional missing (k)" = round(m[, "miss.fun"] / 1e3, 2),
                         "total missing (k)" = round(m[, "missing"] / 1e3, 2))
tab(hold.us); tab(hold.cn)
round(c("K_M, U.S. (k)" = K.miss.us / 1e3, "  missing failed chips" = sum(hold.us[, "miss.failed"]) / 1e3, "  functional chips missing" = sum(hold.us[, "miss.fun"]) / 1e3,
        "K_M, China (k)" = K.miss.cn / 1e3, "  missing failed chips" = sum(hold.cn[, "miss.failed"]) / 1e3, "  functional chips missing" = sum(hold.cn[, "miss.fun"]) / 1e3,
        "  of China's K_M, from the diverted stock" = div.miss() / 1e3), 1)
```

**The formula as the paper states it.** The paper states the formula with $\mu(h)$ applied to the whole stock $Q(h, s)$ and notes (its footnote 53) that this makes no difference; the table above, like the paper's Table 5.1, applies it to the functional chips. Failed chips are at most `r signif(100 * max(c(hold.us[, "failed"] / hold.us[, "Q"], hold.cn[, "failed"] / hold.cn[, "Q"]), na.rm = TRUE), 2)`% of any group, and applying $\mu(h)$ to the whole stock would add `r round(sum(hold.us[, "miss.fun"] / pmax(hold.us[, "Q"] - hold.us[, "failed"], 1) * hold.us[, "failed"]))` H100e to the U.S. total and `r round(sum(hold.cn[, "miss.fun"] / pmax(hold.cn[, "Q"] - hold.cn[, "failed"], 1) * hold.cn[, "failed"]))` to China's.

**Failed chips, and how many of them are missing**

* **How many have failed.** By year-end 2026, `r signif(100 * fail[["seven", "all"]], 2)`% of the seven firms' stock has failed at some age, `r signif(100 * fail[["other", "all"]], 2)`% of other U.S. holders', `r signif(100 * fail[["china", "all"]], 2)`% of China's non-diverted stock and `r signif(100 * fail[["diverted", "all"]], 2)`% of the diverted stock, which has a mean age of 1.5 years. The rate is the measured one to year three and rises by three percentage points a year after it (§S.6.3), which is on the regime-unfavorable side. Purchases are dated by quarter: through 2025 from Epoch's owner data, and for 2026, which Epoch's owner data do not yet cover, from each group's additions in the world model, spread over the year's quarters in proportion to the world flow. In all, `r signif(sum(hold.us[, "failed"]) / 1e3, 2)`k H100e of the U.S. stock and `r signif(sum(hold.cn[, "failed"]) / 1e3, 2)`k of China's have failed.
* **Under warranty: 1% missing.** A chip that fails within its three-year warranty goes back to the vendor, which records the return (§S.6.3). At publicly identifiable and on-books holdings, 1% of these failures are taken to leave no record, the vendor's or any other made at the time. That is a judgment.
* **After the warranty: 10% missing.** Only chips bought before 2024 can have failed after year three: `r signif(100 * fail[["seven", "late"]], 2)`% of the seven firms' year-end 2026 stock, `r signif(100 * fail[["other", "late"]], 2)`% of other U.S. holders' and `r signif(100 * fail[["china", "late"]], 2)`% of China's non-diverted stock. Any record made at the time that the chip failed and was taken out of service counts: a maintenance ticket or monitoring log, an entry in the holder's inventory, a write-off in its books, or a recycler's disposal record (China's rules on waste electrical and electronic products require licensed disposal enterprises to keep data on what they process for three years; State Council of the People's Republic of China 2009). A disposal certificate is not required. **A tenth** of these failures are taken to leave no record of any of these kinds. That is a judgment: no rule requires a record when an accelerator fails, and nothing measures how often one is kept. An operator that monitors its machines learns of a failure from its own logs, which is where the measured failure rate itself comes from (Cui et al. 2025), so a tenth is probably on the high side for data-center operators and less certain for a small business with a few machines.
* **Diverted chips have no warranty** (NVIDIA provides no support or repairs for restricted products; Olcott 2026a), so every failure of a diverted chip held on the books is counted at the after-warranty share, a tenth.
* **Off-books holdings: half missing. Informal holdings: all.** Both are judgments. A business running chips bought without paperwork still keeps operating records, taken to show half of its failures. An informal holder has nothing to show, so all of its failures count, inside the warranty period or after it.
* **In all,** the missing failed chips are `r signif(sum(hold.us[, "miss.failed"]) / 1e3, 2)`k H100e in the U.S. and `r signif(sum(hold.cn[, "miss.failed"]) / 1e3, 2)`k in China. The U.S. figure is the larger because of the size of its publicly identifiable holdings, which account for `r signif(hold.us[1, "miss.failed"] / 1e3, 2)`k of it.

**Functional chips: the missing fraction**

A functional chip goes missing only if three things happen in turn: it is not found at a site; of the chips not found there, its holder does not declare it; and of those not found and not declared, the census cannot trace it from the seller's records. The rates below are conditional in that order, as the paper states them (§5.5.2).

* **Publicly identifiable holdings: none.** Their functional chips are presumed accounted for: public filings, vendor records, known sites, chips that report their identity when running. The failed chips above are this type's whole contribution. Chips these holders have resold are not counted: the stock counts purchases, and nothing public measures the secondary market.
* **The site: `r round(100 * f.site)`% not found.** A chip that escapes the paper trail but sits at an operating business is still found if it is in a data center: a colocation operator declares its tenants and their power by cage, and an enterprise data center is a known site from utility and permit records that the census can inspect. Two inputs set the share that is not found. **A tenth** of business-held chips are taken to sit outside any data center, in closets, server rooms, edge sites and small businesses' own premises. Counted by racks, `r srv[["2023", "small"]]`% of U.S. servers sat in such places in 2023 and `r srv[["2025", "small"]]`% in 2025; of the servers outside hyperscale facilities, the closer comparison for holders that are not named, `r round(100 * srv[["2023", "small"]] / (100 - srv[["2023", "hyperscale"]]))`% and `r round(100 * srv[["2025", "small"]] / (100 - srv[["2025", "hyperscale"]]))`% (Shehabi et al. 2024, Figure 4.1, measured from the chart). That is all servers, not AI servers, whose power density keeps most of them out of closets; the same report's model places every AI-accelerated server in a hyperscale or large colocation facility. So a tenth is on the regime-unfavorable side. A survey of data-center operators gives a higher figure, `r round(100 * venue[["closet.edge"]])`% of the IT on their own hardware (Uptime Institute 2025, Figure 13), but it averages over the operators who answered, not over hardware. **A further `r round(100 * miss.dc)`%** are taken to be in a data center and still missed, by its operator's declaration and by its owner's; the figure borrows the IRS rate below. The two are added, giving `r round(100 * f.site)`%; applying the `r round(100 * miss.dc)`% only to the nine tenths inside a data center would give `r signif(100 * (out.dc + (1 - out.dc) * miss.dc), 3)`%. Informal holdings have no site to inspect.
* **Undeclared, on the books: 6%.** A business that bought a chip is the end of a chain of sales records. The IRS measures that 6% of income subject to substantial third-party information reporting goes unreported (category II; Internal Revenue Service 2024, p. 16), which is used for $d_F$ = 0.94. The analogy overstates non-declaration: the IRS measures misreporting where it saves tax, whereas a chip is a capital asset already in the holder's books and on its tax return, and under the regime declaring earns licensed use or a buyback while an undeclared chip is contraband. A business has little reason not to declare; the 6% stands for the declaration channel failing, through error or a defunct holder, and is the regime-unfavorable reading.
* **Untraced, on the books: 20%.** An ATF trace follows a gun's serial forward from the manufacturer through wholesaler and dealer to the first retail buyer; it reached the buyer in 77% of traces over 2017–21 and 80% in 2021 (Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives 2023), which is used for the tracing rate $p_T$ = 0.80. Crime guns are older and more often resold than these chips, so this analogy too is on the regime-unfavorable side.
* **Off the books and informal: 20% undeclared, half of those not recovered.** Both are judgmental inputs; no measurement applies to a holder whose purchase is off the books. Such a holder can keep a chip for the black market more easily than one whose purchase is in the tax record, so more go undeclared. With no sales record to trace from, recovery rests on other records (power, employees, customers) and on tips, taken to find half.
* **So the missing fraction** of functional chips is `r signif(100 * mu[2], 2)`% for on-books holdings (`r round(100 * f.site)`% × 6% × 20%), `r signif(100 * mu[3], 2)`% for off-books holdings (`r round(100 * f.site)`% × 20% × 50%) and `r signif(100 * mu[4], 2)`% for informal holdings (20% × 50%).

**How each state's stock is sorted**

* **The U.S.** The seven firms and the named owners are publicly identifiable holdings, `r signif(hold.us[1, "Q"] / 1e6, 2)`M H100e. Of the unnamed residual (`r sprintf("%.1f", N.us / 1e6)`M), `r round(100 * v.off)`% is taken to be held informally, a judgment that nothing measures; no evidence was found of individuals holding data-center GPUs in quantity. The rest is on the books.
* **China's non-diverted stock.** Named owners and unnamed large buyers are publicly identifiable holdings, `r signif(hold.cn[1, "Q"] / 1e3, 2)`k; the true tail is split as the U.S. residual is.
* **China's diverted stock** (`r signif(smuggled.ye2026 / 1e6, 2)`M: Epoch's central estimate through 2025, carried a third year, §S.1.2.8; the same stock as everywhere else in this supplement). **A tenth** is taken to be off the books, `r signif(off.div * smuggled.ye2026 / 1e3, 2)`k, and `r round(100 * v.off)`% informal, as for any stock that is not publicly identifiable. The remaining `r round(100 * (1 - off.div - v.off))`% is on the books (a customs entry, a tax invoice, a tender, a financing filing). The tenth is a judgment, meant to err on the high side, since a firm has to hold the invoice to claim the tax credit; the evidence behind it follows.
* **Stock in transit.** One month of diverted flow at Epoch's central rate for 2024–25 (`r signif(smuggled.2025 / 1e6, 2)`M over two years, the rate at which the stock is carried through 2026, so `r signif(transit / 1e3, 2)`k H100e a month) is taken to be with shell companies and traders on the pause date. Half of it is added to each state's informal holdings. It is new stock, so none of it has failed.

**Why only a tenth of the diverted stock is taken to be off Chinese records**

No source measures the share. Four kinds of evidence bear on it.

```{r customs-record}
cl <- read.csv("data/customs_server_lanes.csv", stringsAsFactors = FALSE); hk.c <- read.csv("data/hk_server_imports_by_consignment.csv")
cv <- function(rep, flow, code, partner, from, to, col = "value_usd")
  sum(cl[[col]][cl$reporter == rep & cl$flow == flow & cl$code_hs6 == code & cl$partner == partner & cl$period >= from & cl$period <= to])
## China's own import record, servers (HS 847150) at AI-server prices: Malaysia (Epoch's corridor), Singapore and Mexico (the other origins Epoch flags)
cust.cn <- c(Malaysia = cv("china", "M", 847150, "Malaysia", "2024-04", "2025-06"), Singapore = cv("china", "M", 847150, "Singapore", "2024-04", "2025-12"),
             Mexico = cv("china", "M", 847150, "Mexico", "2024-10", "2025-09"))
cust.trays <- cv("china", "M", 847180, "Mexico", "2025-03", "2025-07")                   # Mexican-origin "other units of computers"
trays.n <- cv("china", "M", 847180, "Mexico", "2025-03", "2025-07", "qty_units"); trays.kg <- cv("china", "M", 847180, "Mexico", "2025-03", "2025-07", "weight_kg")
## Thailand's own export record: to China above the 2022-23 monthly mean (24 months less 24 at that mean); to Hong Kong (nil before 2024)
cust.th.cn <- cv("thailand", "X", 847150, "China", "2024-01", "2025-12") - cv("thailand", "X", 847150, "China", "2022-01", "2023-12")
cust.th.hk <- cv("thailand", "X", 847150, "Hong Kong", "2024-01", "2025-12")
## Hong Kong's import record by sending place: monthly lines of at least $20M averaging $50,000 a unit or more, from Taiwan and Indonesia, to end-2025.
## Lines sent from Thailand are in cust.th.hk; lines sent from Malaysia are left out, since they may re-enter China as Malaysian origin (cust.cn).
dear <- function(usd, units) ifelse(usd >= 20e6 & units > 0 & usd / units >= 50e3 & hk.c$period <= "2025-12", usd, 0)
cust.hk <- sum(dear(hk.c$M_consigned_TW_usd, hk.c$M_consigned_TW_units)) + sum(dear(hk.c$M_consigned_ID_usd, hk.c$M_consigned_ID_units))
cust <- c("China's record: Malaysian, Singaporean, Mexican servers" = sum(cust.cn), "China's record: Mexican-origin other computer units" = cust.trays,
          "Thailand's record: to China" = cust.th.cn, "Thailand's record: to Hong Kong" = cust.th.hk, "Hong Kong's record: from Taiwan and Indonesia" = cust.hk)
cust.total <- sum(cust); usd.per.h100e <- 25e3                                           # Epoch's conversion for its Malaysian corridor
round(cust / 1e9, 2)                                                                     # US$ billion, to end-2025
c("total ($bn)" = round(cust.total / 1e9, 1), "H100e at $25,000 (k)" = round(cust.total / usd.per.h100e / 1e3), "share of the end-2025 diverted stock (%)" = round(100 * cust.total / usd.per.h100e / smuggled.2025),
  "China's own entries alone (%)" = round(100 * (sum(cust.cn) + cust.trays) / usd.per.h100e / smuggled.2025))
```

* **The law and the buyer's interest.** Receiving and selling these chips was legal in China provided border taxes were paid (Wu and Olcott 2025). A business needs a special VAT invoice to credit the 13% input tax and an invoice to deduct the purchase against income tax (Standing Committee of the National People's Congress 2024; State Taxation Administration 2018): to a profitable firm, `r round(100 * 0.13 / 1.13, 1)`% and `r round(100 * 0.25 / 1.13, 1)`% of the tax-inclusive price. A firm that sells computing must also invoice its own customers, which puts the revenue, and the servers that earn it, on its books. The buyers reported are data-center operators that rent out computing, and other companies (Wu and Olcott 2025).
* **The customs record.** Importers record the country of origin and exporters the destination, so both ends of a shipment are published. By the end of 2025:
  * China's own import statistics record `r signif(sum(cust.cn) / 1e9, 2)`bn dollars of servers of Malaysian, Singaporean and Mexican origin in the months they arrived at AI-server prices. The Malaysian part, `r signif(cust.cn[["Malaysia"]] / 1e9, 3)`bn at about \$106,000 a machine against \$600 before, is Epoch's finding; the importers "were breaking no Chinese law, so had less reason to lie to their own customs" (Juniewicz 2026c). China also records `r signif(cust.trays / 1e9, 2)`bn of Mexican-origin "other units of computers" in March–July 2025, `r format(round(trays.n, -2), big.mark = ",")` units at about \$`r format(round(cust.trays / trays.n, -3), big.mark = ",")` and `r round(trays.kg / trays.n)` kg each.
  * Thailand records `r signif(cust.th.cn / 1e9, 2)`bn of server exports to China above its 2022–23 level, most of it in March–May 2025, and `r signif(cust.th.hk / 1e9, 2)`bn to Hong Kong. The timing coincides with the largest case charged so far: according to the U.S. Department of Justice, a buyer in Southeast Asia took about \$2.5bn of servers, and at least about \$510M of them are alleged to have gone on to China between late April and mid-May 2025 (Department of Justice 2026). That this lane is the route in that case is our inference from the timing; the customs record does not show it.
  * Hong Kong records `r signif(cust.hk / 1e9, 2)`bn arriving from Taiwan and Indonesia in consignments averaging \$50,000 a unit or more (Census and Statistics Department 2026).
  * Together `r signif(cust.total / 1e9, 2)`bn dollars. At Epoch's \$25,000 per H100e that is `r signif(cust.total / usd.per.h100e / 1e3, 2)`k H100e, **`r round(100 * cust.total / usd.per.h100e / smuggled.2025)`% of the end-2025 diverted stock**; China's own entries alone are `r round(100 * (sum(cust.cn) + cust.trays) / usd.per.h100e / smuggled.2025)`%. The conversion is rough: the values are for whole machines, and newer chips carry more H100e per dollar.
* **How the hardware is sold.** On a public brokers' board in August–October 2026 (Jujianbao 2026), the offers that state tax terms mostly price the goods tax-inclusive or with an invoice, and many cite contracts, bank guarantees or letters of credit. These are offers, not completed sales, and the posters are not verified. On concealing restricted chips inside permitted imports, a trader told the *Financial Times*: "You can go against the American rules, but not the Chinese" (Olcott 2026a).
* **What is not measured.** Small lots: single cards carried by hand or sent under false labels (Huang 2024; Swanson and Fu 2024). They are where a sale without paper is most plausible, and no source sizes them. A record also need not name the chip: invoices often say only "servers", and the holder of record can be a lessor or a trading company, not the user.

A tenth is left for small lots and for sales without paper; that is a judgment. At a quarter instead, $K_M(\text{China})$ would be `r signif((K.miss.cn - div.miss() + div.miss(off = 0.25)) / 1e3, 2)`k.

**Result:** $K_M(s)$ = **`r signif(K.miss.us / 1e3, 2)`k H100e for the U.S.** and **`r signif(K.miss.cn / 1e3, 2)`k for China**. Missing failed chips are `r signif(sum(hold.us[, "miss.failed"]) / 1e3, 2)`k and `r signif(sum(hold.cn[, "miss.failed"]) / 1e3, 2)`k of that, and functional chips `r signif(sum(hold.us[, "miss.fun"]) / 1e3, 2)`k and `r signif(sum(hold.cn[, "miss.fun"]) / 1e3, 2)`k. The diverted stock accounts for `r signif(div.miss() / 1e3, 2)`k of China's figure.

## S.6.6 From the missing stock to the ledger: the scenarios

A state acting in good faith cannot marshal chips its own census failed to find. A state that is **hiding** chips does so inside that noise, in the mass balance of shipped, declared and removed chips, where hidden chips look like chips the census missed. So the raw dark stock is $K_0 = (1 + \gamma)\,K_M(s)$, with $\gamma$ the hidden stock as a multiple of the missing stock, and the ledger counts $K_E = \pi_E K_0$, $K_B = \pi_B K_0$. Here $\pi$ is a rival's conservative, one-significant-figure estimate of the share of the dark stock the state controls: it cannot tell hidden chips from missing ones, so it rounds the hidden share up. $\tau_E = \tau_B = 1$: at the pause date the dark stock is young (most of the U.S. residual was bought in 2025–26); aging belongs in a technical discount that declines over a long pause.

```{r dark-census}
hid <- rbind("U.S." = c(0.20, 4), "China" = c(0.20, 9))                        # gamma = hidden stock / K_M: high, low cooperation
K.miss <- c("U.S." = K.miss.us, "China" = K.miss.cn)
dark <- cbind((1 + hid) * K.miss, dark.nd)     # K_0 per state; non-deniable concealment is set politically, as in the paper
colnames(dark) <- scen
pi.dark <- rbind("U.S." = c(0.5, 1, 1), "China" = c(0.5, 1, 1)); dimnames(pi.dark) <- dimnames(dark)   # pi_E = pi_B, tau = 1
K.E.dark <- pi.dark * dark
round(rbind("U.S. K_0 (k)" = dark["U.S.", ] / 1e3, "  pi" = pi.dark["U.S.", ], "  K_E (k)" = K.E.dark["U.S.", ] / 1e3, "  K_E / F_E (%)" = 100 * K.E.dark["U.S.", ] / F.E,
            "  K_B / F_B (%)" = 100 * K.E.dark["U.S.", ] / F.B, "  dark alone: headroom to alpha_E F_E (OOM)" = log10(0.25 * F.E / K.E.dark["U.S.", ]),
            "China K_0 (k)" = dark["China", ] / 1e3, "  pi" = pi.dark["China", ], "  K_E (k)" = K.E.dark["China", ] / 1e3, "  K_E / F_E (%)" = 100 * K.E.dark["China", ] / F.E,
            "  K_B / F_B (%)" = 100 * K.E.dark["China", ] / F.B, "  dark alone: headroom to alpha_E F_E (OOM)" = log10(0.25 * F.E / K.E.dark["China", ])), 3)
```

* **Values.** High cooperation, the same for both states: a state stashes at most a fifth of its missing stock ($\gamma$ = 0.2, so $K_0 = 1.2\,K_M(s)$), and a rival, to whom the cooperation is evident, counts at most half of the missing compute as in the state's hands ($\pi$ = 0.5), so the ledger carries $0.6\,K_M(s)$. Low cooperation: politically sensitive records are refused and each state holds back what it deniably can, taken as ten times the missing stock for China ($\gamma$ = 9) and five times for the U.S. ($\gamma$ = 4), where a large stock would be harder to keep secret; undiscounted ($\pi$ = 1). These multiples are judgmental inputs. Non-deniable concealment is not a multiple of the missing stock; it keeps the paper's political sizes, 300k and 1M. At the \$25,000 per H100e of §S.1.3 the raw dark stock $K_0$ is worth about \$`r signif(dark[["U.S.", 1]] * usd.per.h100e / 1e9, 2)`B in each state under high cooperation, \$`r signif(dark[["U.S.", 2]] * usd.per.h100e / 1e9, 2)`B (U.S.) and \$`r signif(dark[["China", 2]] * usd.per.h100e / 1e9, 2)`B (China) under low cooperation, and \$`r signif(dark[["U.S.", 3]] * usd.per.h100e / 1e9, 2)`B and \$`r signif(dark[["China", 3]] * usd.per.h100e / 1e9, 2)`B under non-deniable concealment.
* **High cooperation:** $K_0$ is `r signif(dark["U.S.", 1] / 1e3, 2)`k (U.S.) and `r signif(dark["China", 1] / 1e3, 2)`k (China); the ledger counts `r signif(K.E.dark["U.S.", 1] / 1e3, 2)`k and `r signif(K.E.dark["China", 1] / 1e3, 2)`k, `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * K.E.dark["U.S.", 1] / F.E)`% and `r sprintf("%.2f", 100 * K.E.dark["China", 1] / F.E)`% of $F_E$. **Low cooperation:** `r signif(dark["U.S.", 2] / 1e3, 2)`k and `r signif(dark["China", 2] / 1e3, 2)`k, `r signif(100 * dark["U.S.", 2] / F.E, 2)`% and `r signif(100 * dark["China", 2] / F.E, 2)`% of $F_E$ and `r signif(100 * dark["U.S.", 2] / F.B, 2)`% and `r signif(100 * dark["China", 2] / F.B, 2)`% of $F_B$.

## S.6.7 Judgment calls

* **Direction of conservatism.** A larger residual is the regime-unfavorable side. `r round(us.residual / 1e6, 1)`M is central. Leaving the diverted chips in the "Other" share before applying the location share would give 3.5M, the regime-unfavorable reading, but it would place chips that are in China in the United States.
* The seven firms' inventories are *presumed* accounted for; that presumption, not the residual's size, carries the argument.
* **Census inputs (§S.6.4–§S.6.6), with the direction of each.** Judgments: the location share (0.45), the 2026 growth of the unnamed residual (it keeps its share of world additions), $v$ = 0.01, the tenth of business-held chips outside a data center and the further 6% missed inside one, the off-books share of diverted chips (a tenth; §S.6.5 gives the evidence), the declaration and recovery rates for off-books and informal holdings (20% undeclared, half recovered), one month of diverted stock in transit split between the two states, the shares of failed chips that leave no record (1% under warranty and a tenth after it at publicly identifiable and on-books holdings, half at off-books holdings, all at informal holdings), the rise of three percentage points a year in the failure rate after year three, and the hidden multiples and discounts ($\gamma$, $\pi$). Analogies, each on the regime-unfavorable side: declaration at the IRS category II rate, tracing at the ATF rate, the share outside a data center for all servers rather than AI servers, and Ascend's unnamed part counted as tail. Capacity statements of unstated precision count at half.

# S.7 The ledger lines (§6.4.2, §6.4.4–§6.4.7)

## S.7.1 Transitional training-capable inference service (§6.4.2)

The largest single line on either ledger, early in the regime, is the legacy training-capable fleet left in commercial service through Phases 1 and 2. Its raw size is the fleet measurement of §S.1.2.7 and §S.1.2.8; what this section adds is the discounting.

Under an overt breakout the host state could seize that hardware in industry-grade data centers and run it at full rate, so $\pi_B = \tau_B = 1$ and the breakout capacity is the fleet itself. Under covert evasion the verification measures of §3.3.3 bite: the U.S. figure assumes pessimistically that 10% of hardware operators evade while diverting 1% of their computing power, which is $\pi_E = 0.001$; the Chinese figure assumes the state can suborn every operator into diverting 1%, which is $\pi_E = 0.01$.

```{r transitional-exposure}
pi.E.us <- 0.10 * 0.01; pi.E.cn <- 0.01                                   # 10% of operators x 1% diverted; all operators x 1%
K.trans <- rbind("U.S."  = c(K_0 = us.fleet.ye2026,    K_B = us.fleet.ye2026,    K_E = pi.E.us * us.fleet.ye2026),
                 "China" = c(K_0 = china.fleet.ye2026, K_B = china.fleet.ye2026, K_E = pi.E.cn * china.fleet.ye2026))
round(cbind(K.trans / 1e6, "K_B % of F_B" = 100 * K.trans[, "K_B"] / F.B, "K_E % of F_E" = 100 * K.trans[, "K_E"] / F.E), 3)
```

At the adopted $F_B$ the U.S. transitional fleet is `r round(100 * us.fleet.ye2026 / F.B)`% of the breakout fleet and China's is `r round(100 * china.fleet.ye2026 / F.B, 1)`%, so both sit inside the allowance $\alpha_B = 0.25$ of §S.7.5 from entry into force. §S.5.5 shows the conclusion reversing if the breakout target is set on an end-2028 arrival rather than end-2029. On the covert side the discounting does the work: `r round(100 * pi.E.us * us.fleet.ye2026 / F.E, 2)`% of $F_E$ for the United States and `r round(100 * pi.E.cn * china.fleet.ye2026 / F.E, 2)`% for China.

```{r transitional-china-range}
round(rbind("China fleet (M H100e)" = china.range / 1e6, "K_B % of F_B" = 100 * china.range / F.B,
            "K_E % of F_E" = 100 * pi.E.cn * china.range / F.E), 3)
```

Across the full range for China's fleet (§S.1.2.8) the breakout share stays between `r round(100 * china.range[["low"]] / F.B, 1)`% and `r round(100 * china.range[["high"]] / F.B, 1)`% and the covert share under 1% of $F_E$, an order of magnitude below the U.S. breakout figure throughout. The range moves no qualitative conclusion.

## S.7.2 Inference-only accelerators (§6.4.4)

```{r inference-only}
inference.fleet <- 2 / 3 * fleet.ye2026                                  # Deloitte (Crossan et al. 2025): two thirds of AI compute on inference in 2026
pi.E.infonly <- 0.001                                                    # §6.4.4: "as assumed above", the transitional-fleet value
## phi = peak training throughput (H100e) / licensed inference rating (inference-H100e): 1 for a legacy chip, 0 for the idealized inference-only machine
phi.adopted <- 1e-4                                                      # the adopted illustrative residual training factor
phi.cases <- c("phi = 0.01" = 0.01, "phi = 0.001" = 0.001, "phi = 1e-4 (adopted)" = phi.adopted, "phi = 3e-5 (an optimistic case)" = 3e-5)
inf <- sapply(phi.cases, function(f) c("1M of breakout ledger serves (M H100e of demand)" = 1e6 / f / 1e6, "K_B: world inference replicated 100x (k H100e)" = 100 * inference.fleet * f / 1e3,
                                       "  ... as % of F_B" = 100 * 100 * inference.fleet * f / F.B, "K_E = pi_E x K_B (k H100e)" = pi.E.infonly * 100 * inference.fleet * f / 1e3,
                                       "  ... as % of F_E" = 100 * pi.E.infonly * 100 * inference.fleet * f / F.E))
signif(inf, 3)
round(c("inference fleet = 2/3 x world fleet (M)" = inference.fleet / 1e6,
        "adopted phi = 1e-4 in TFLOP/s per inference-H100e" = phi.adopted * h100e.peak / 1e12,
        "phi = 0.001 in TFLOP/s per inference-H100e"    = 0.001 * h100e.peak / 1e12), 3)
```

* **The residual training factor $\varphi$ is a hardware system's peak arithmetic throughput for training operations, in H100e, divided by its licensed inference rating, in inference-H100e.** A legacy training-capable chip has $\varphi = 1$ and the idealized inference-only machine has $\varphi = 0$; a system hobbled by four orders of magnitude has $\varphi = 10^{-4}$. The inference rating is known and the residual training throughput is what an inspector bounds from above, so a certified bound on a system is an upper bound on its $\varphi$.
* **A fleet's $\varphi$ is its total training throughput divided by its total inference rating,** which is the mean of its units' $\varphi$ weighted by inference-H100e. The fleet's training capacity is then the inference it serves times $\varphi$, which is what the ledger uses, and a ceiling on every unit's $\varphi$ is a ceiling on the fleet's.

* **The adopted residual training factor is $\varphi = 10^{-4}$**, an illustrative design target as in the paper (§6.4.4): one order of magnitude below $10^{-3}$ and well above the optimistic case of $3\times10^{-5}$ shown below. **The value is illustrative, and the conclusions do not rest on it.** The inference-only line is the inference served times $\varphi$, so the regime sets the size of the line through the amount of inference-only service it licenses: if certified hardware reached only $\varphi = 10^{-3}$, licensing a tenth as much inference-only service would leave the line where it is. The first row of the table gives the inference demand that one million H100e of breakout ledger serves at each $\varphi$. (With a hundred times today's inference served at $10^{-3}$, the line alone would be `r signif(100 * 100 * inference.fleet * 0.001 / F.B, 2)`% of $F_B$.)
* **$\pi_E = 0.001$** (§6.4.4: "as assumed above owing to the difficulty of evading discovery by the recomputation server", i.e. the transitional-fleet value of §6.4.2). At the adopted $\varphi$, $K_E$ = `r round(pi.E.infonly * 100 * inference.fleet * phi.adopted, 0)` H100e = `r sprintf("%.4f", 100 * pi.E.infonly * 100 * inference.fleet * phi.adopted / F.E)`% of $F_E$.
* **The optimistic case.** At $\varphi = 3\times10^{-5}$, replicating the world's inference a hundred times over costs about `r round(100 * inference.fleet * 3e-5 / 1e3)`k H100e of breakout ledger, `r round(100 * 100 * inference.fleet * 3e-5 / F.B, 2)`% of $F_B$.
* **The two-thirds inference share is market-wide.** It need not match a frontier lab's own split: the SemiAnalysis model cited in §S.1.1.4 has inference at 36–38% of the combined capacity of OpenAI and Anthropic (Xie et al. 2026). The two differ because they describe different populations.
* The inference fleet is `r round(inference.fleet / 1e6)`M on the world model (§6.4.4); $K_B$ at the adopted $\varphi$ is `r round(100 * inference.fleet * phi.adopted / 1e3)`k H100e, `r signif(100 * 100 * inference.fleet * phi.adopted / F.B, 2)`% of $F_B$ (at $\varphi = 10^{-3}$ it would be `r round(100 * inference.fleet * 0.001 / 1e6, 1)`M and `r signif(100 * 100 * inference.fleet * 0.001 / F.B, 2)`%).

## S.7.3 Consumer GPUs (§6.4.5, fn 72–73)

```{r consumer}
K0.consumer <- h100e(100e6 * 30e12); tau.consumer <- 0.10; pi.B.consumer <- 0.25
round(c("fn 72: Q2 2026 desktop add-in boards, JPR (M)" = 12.5, "fn 72: laptop residual = 20M - 12.5M (M)" = 20 - 12.5, "K_0 = 100M cards x 30 TFLOP/s (M H100e)" = K0.consumer / 1e6,
        "K_E = 0.01 x tau x K_0 (k)" = 0.01 * tau.consumer * K0.consumer / 1e3, "  ... % of F_E" = 100 * 0.01 * tau.consumer * K0.consumer / F.E,
        "K_B = 0.25 x tau x K_0 (k)" = pi.B.consumer * tau.consumer * K0.consumer / 1e3, "  ... % of F_B" = 100 * pi.B.consumer * tau.consumer * K0.consumer / F.B), 3)
```

The overt political discount is $\pi_B = 0.25$: a state marshalling hobbyist and gaming cards for an overt program would recover at most a quarter of them. The covert discount is $\pi_E = 0.01$. The 12.5M in the paper's footnote 72 is the reported shipment figure for the second quarter of 2026 (Jon Peddie Research 2026); nothing downstream depends on it, since $K_0$ rests on the rounded bound of 100M cards. The technical discount is $\tau_E = \tau_B = 0.10$, twice the usefulness factor of about 0.05 that the AI 2040 compute supplement assigns to gaming GPUs (memory bandwidth near 1.0 TB/s against the H100's 3.35, and 64 Gb/s networking against a 400 Gb/s threshold; Dean 2026a). Doubling it is the regime-unfavorable margin. fn 73 cites NVIDIA (2021) for GeForce cards halving FP16 throughput with FP32 accumulation.

## S.7.4 El Capitan and the remaining carve-outs (§6.4.6–6.4.7)

```{r elcap}
K0.elcap <- h100e(46e3 * 980.6e12)
round(c("K_0 = 46k APUs x 980.6 TFLOP/s (k H100e)" = K0.elcap / 1e3, "K_B = K_0 (tau = pi_B = 1), % of F_B" = 100 * K0.elcap / F.B,
        "K_E = 0.2 x K_0 (k H100e)" = 0.2 * K0.elcap / 1e3, "  ... % of F_E" = 100 * 0.2 * K0.elcap / F.E, "HPL-MxP utilization 37% relative to U_F (tau, capped at 1)" = min(1, 0.37 / U.F)), 2)
```

$K_B$ = `r signif(K0.elcap / 1e3, 2)`k is `r signif(100 * K0.elcap / F.B, 2)`% of $F_B$ and $K_E$ = `r signif(0.2 * K0.elcap / 1e3, 2)`k is `r signif(100 * 0.2 * K0.elcap / F.E, 2)`% of $F_E$. §6.4.7 prints no numbers.

## S.7.5 The allowances α_E, α_B and each line's headroom (§6.4.1, §6.5)

```{r allowances}
alpha.E <- 0.25; alpha.B <- 0.25                                               # §6.5: allowances of 25% on both ledgers
K.E <- c("transitional, U.S." = 0.001 * us.fleet.ye2026, "transitional, China" = 0.01 * china.fleet.ye2026, "inference-only" = pi.E.infonly * 100 * inference.fleet * phi.adopted,
         "consumer" = 0.01 * tau.consumer * K0.consumer, "El Capitan" = 0.2 * K0.elcap)
K.B <- c("transitional, U.S." = us.fleet.ye2026, "transitional, China" = china.fleet.ye2026, "inference-only" = 100 * inference.fleet * phi.adopted,
         "consumer" = pi.B.consumer * tau.consumer * K0.consumer, "El Capitan" = K0.elcap)
round(c("alpha_E F_E (M)" = alpha.E * F.E / 1e6, "alpha_B F_B (M)" = alpha.B * F.B / 1e6), 3)
## each line on its own: its share of the fleet threshold, and its headroom, the orders of magnitude of erosion before that line alone reaches the allowance
line.tab <- function(K, F, a) cbind("k H100e" = K / 1e3, "% of F" = 100 * K / F, "headroom (OOM)" = log10(a * F / K))
signif(line.tab(K.E, F.E, alpha.E), 3)                                         # covert lines against F_E
signif(line.tab(K.B, F.B, alpha.B), 3)                                         # overt lines against F_B
```

* **$\alpha_B \cdot F_B$.** 0.25 × $F_B$ at full precision is `r round(alpha.B * F.B / 1e6, 2)`M, which prints as `r signif(alpha.B * F.B / 1e6, 2)`M; $\alpha_E \cdot F_E$ = `r round(alpha.E * F.E / 1e6, 2)`M prints as `r signif(alpha.E * F.E / 1e6, 2)`M.
* **The lines are not added up.** The ledger values are not meant as constants over the decade of a pause: verification is assumed to get better. Nor are they estimates for the same date. The transitional fleets are largest at the pause date and are retired by the end of Phase 2. The inference-only line is an illustrative fleet serving a hundred times today's inference demand. The consumer line rests on a forecast of the installed base at the end of 2028. And by the time dark compute becomes the binding term, the political discounts on the other sources would be much steeper than the opening values used here: the paper's example for El Capitan is a further factor of five on each of $\pi_E$ and $\tau_E$, which takes its covert line to `r sprintf("%.4f", 100 * K.E[["El Capitan"]] / 25 / F.E)`% of $F_E$. So each line is compared with its allowance separately. Its **headroom** (§6.4.1) is the number of orders of magnitude of training efficiency gains before that line alone reaches $\alpha F$.
* **Line by line.** Apart from the transitional fleets, the largest overt line is the illustrative inference-only fleet at the adopted $\varphi = 10^{-4}$: `r round(K.B[["inference-only"]] / 1e3)`k H100e, `r signif(100 * K.B[["inference-only"]] / F.B, 2)`% of $F_B$, with `r round(log10(alpha.B * F.B / K.B[["inference-only"]]), 2)` orders of magnitude of headroom; consumer GPUs have `r round(log10(alpha.B * F.B / K.B[["consumer"]]), 2)` and El Capitan `r round(log10(alpha.B * F.B / K.B[["El Capitan"]]), 2)`. On the covert side the largest is El Capitan at $\pi_E = 0.2$, `r signif(100 * K.E[["El Capitan"]] / F.E, 2)`% of $F_E$ with `r round(log10(alpha.E * F.E / K.E[["El Capitan"]]), 2)` orders; consumer GPUs have `r round(log10(alpha.E * F.E / K.E[["consumer"]]), 2)` and the inference-only fleet `r round(log10(alpha.E * F.E / K.E[["inference-only"]]), 2)`. Every line other than transitional service and dark compute therefore has at least two orders of magnitude of headroom. The transitional lines are in §S.7.1 and dark compute, scenario by scenario, in §S.6.6.
* **Lines with no entry.** The paper gives no figure for scientific preserves or sealed strategic reserves (§6.4.7): preserves are taken to contribute negligibly to either ledger, and sealed reserves nothing to the covert ledger, though they would count in full on the overt side. It gives China no sovereign-fleet line.

## S.7.6 A mid-2027 pause, tentatively (§6.1)

§6.1 also assesses a pause taking effect half a year later, in mid-2027. The numbers in this section are more tentative than the near-term ones, for a plain reason: every judgmental input is held at the value chosen for a year-end 2026 pause, and several of those choices would be made differently with half a year more information. What moves is only what the method itself moves: the frozen frontier $C_F$ and with it the covert evasion fleet size $F_E$; the breakout multiple $\beta_B = C_B / C_F$, because the breakout threshold $C_B = 2\times10^{29}$ is an absolute capability level and stays put; and the fleets, read off the same world model six months further on. Held fixed: the U.S. share of the world fleet (0.75), China's domestic production rate, the dark-compute scenarios, and every political and technical discount, the residual training factor $\varphi$ and the allowances $\alpha_E = \alpha_B = 0.25$. Holding the dark-compute scenarios fixed is **not** the conservative choice, since a later pause leaves more time to divert hardware.

```{r mid-range}
t.mid  <- 1.5                                                      # mid-2027, on the world model's clock (years from end-2025)
C.F.m  <- C.F * g.F^0.5; F.E.m <- F.E * g.F^0.5                    # the frontier moves half a year along its trend
beta.B.m <- C.B / C.F.m                                             # 5.02 blind steps (not rounded)
F.B.m  <- h100e(rho.F * blind.factor(beta.B.m) * C.B / (T.B * secs.per.yr * U.F))
Q.m <- W.of(t.mid); Q.us.m <- us.frac * Q.m; Q.cn.m <- cn.mod(t.mid)
K.B.inf.m <- 100 * (2 / 3) * Q.m * phi.adopted
signif(c("C_F (1e27 FLOP)" = C.F.m / 1e27, "F_E (M)" = F.E.m / 1e6, "beta_B" = beta.B.m, "blind steps" = blind.steps(beta.B.m),
         "F_B (M)" = F.B.m / 1e6, "alpha_E F_E (M)" = alpha.E * F.E.m / 1e6, "alpha_B F_B (M)" = alpha.B * F.B.m / 1e6,
         "world stock (M)" = Q.m / 1e6, "U.S. stock (M)" = Q.us.m / 1e6, "China stock (M)" = Q.cn.m / 1e6), 3)
signif(100 * c("K_B(Transitional, U.S.) / F_B" = Q.us.m / F.B.m,
               "K_B(Transitional, China) / F_B" = Q.cn.m / F.B.m, "K_E(Transitional, U.S.) / F_E" = 0.001 * Q.us.m / F.E.m,
               "K_E(Transitional, China) / F_E" = 0.01 * Q.cn.m / F.E.m), 3)
round(100 * K.E.dark / F.E.m, 2)                                     # dark compute as the covert ledger counts it (pi_E K_0), % of F_E at mid-2027
signif(c("inference-only line, % of F_B" = 100 * K.B.inf.m / F.B.m, "  ... headroom (OOM)" = log10(alpha.B * F.B.m / K.B.inf.m)), 3)
```

* **The breakout fleet barely moves.** At mid-2027 the frontier is $4.2\times10^{27}$ FLOP, so $\beta_B$ = `r round(beta.B.m)` and $C_B$ sits `r round(log10(beta.B.m) / delta, 2)` blind steps above it; the step count is not rounded, so the program takes five full steps of $\delta$ and a sliver of a sixth. That gives $F_B \approx$ `r signif(F.B.m, 2) / 1e6`M, against `r signif(F.B, 2) / 1e6`M for a year-end 2026 pause.
* **The covert fleet doubles.** $F_E$ tracks the frontier, so it is about `r signif(F.E.m, 2) / 1e6`M, and every covert ratio roughly halves: China's dark compute under non-deniable concealment is about `r signif(100 * dark["China", 3] / F.E.m, 2)`% of $F_E$ rather than `r signif(100 * dark["China", 3] / F.E, 2)`%.
* **The other ledger lines.** The chunk gives each as a share of its fleet threshold. China's transitional fleet is about `r signif(100 * Q.cn.m / F.B.m, 2)`% of $F_B$. The inference-only line grows with the world's inference fleet: it is about `r signif(100 * K.B.inf.m / F.B.m, 2)`% of $F_B$, with `r sprintf("%.2f", log10(alpha.B * F.B.m / K.B.inf.m))` orders of magnitude of headroom against `r sprintf("%.2f", log10(alpha.B * F.B / K.B[["inference-only"]]))` at year-end 2026; §6.4.4 treats the size of that fleet as adjustable to the headroom available.

## S.7.7 An informal pause, then a treaty with a descending allowance schedule (§6.1, §6.5)

The ledger comparisons above are made at the pause date. This section follows them forward under one account of how a pause could begin: the U.S. and China stop frontier training at once under an informal bilateral arrangement, joined soon afterwards by the states that supply the chip supply chain and then by the other major chip-owning states; a treaty is signed two to three years later, with an allowance schedule that starts high and descends to $\alpha = 0.25$ over the time the census of pre-pause accelerators and the development of inference-only hardware will take. The clock here is **training efficiency since the pause date**, counted in doublings and in orders of magnitude (OOM) rather than years, since each doubling halves both $F_E$ and $F_B$ whatever its date. One doubling is $\log_{10} 2 \approx 0.30$ OOM, so one OOM is about 3.3 doublings and two OOM about 6.6. Signing is assumed to come before two doublings (0.6 OOM). Transitional fleets are counted in full throughout that window, which overstates them once the Phase 2 drawdown has begun in month 26 (§4.4).

```{r schedule}
## each line as a share of its own fleet threshold at the pause date; dark compute as the ledger counts it (pi K_0, §S.6.6); nothing is added across lines
sh <- c("U.S. transitional, overt" = K.B[["transitional, U.S."]] / F.B, "China transitional, overt" = K.B[["transitional, China"]] / F.B,
        "U.S. transitional, covert" = K.E[["transitional, U.S."]] / F.E, "China transitional, covert" = K.E[["transitional, China"]] / F.E)
dk <- K.E.dark / F.E                                                           # the dark-compute line, covert, by state and scenario
round(100 * outer(sh, c("at the pause" = 1, "1 doubling" = 2, "2 doublings" = 4)), 1)          # % of its fleet threshold, transitional fleets in service
round(100 * rbind("U.S. dark compute, at the pause" = dk["U.S.", ], "  ... after 2 doublings" = 4 * dk["U.S.", ],
                  "China dark compute, at the pause" = dk["China", ], "  ... after 2 doublings" = 4 * dk["China", ]), 2)
round(c("doublings until the U.S. transitional fleet exceeds alpha_B F_B" = log2(alpha.B * F.B / K.B[["transitional, U.S."]]),
        "doublings until it exceeds F_B itself" = log2(F.B / K.B[["transitional, U.S."]])), 2)
round(log2(alpha.E / dk), 2)                                                   # headroom of the dark-compute line alone at an allowance of 0.25, in doublings from the pause date
bind.lc <- which.max(dk[, "low cooperation"])                                  # the state whose dark compute is the larger share of F_E under low cooperation
round(c("rest-of-world stock (M)" = (fleet.ye2026 - us.fleet.ye2026 - china.fleet.ye2026) / 1e6,
        "  ... as a multiple of F_E" = (fleet.ye2026 - us.fleet.ye2026 - china.fleet.ye2026) / F.E), 2)
```

* **Stopping at once is safe on the overt side for about two doublings.** The whole U.S. fleet in transitional service is `r round(100 * K.B[["transitional, U.S."]] / F.B)`% of $F_B$ at the pause, and it stays below $F_B$ itself for `r round(log2(F.B / K.B[["transitional, U.S."]]), 1)` doublings. It passes a 25% allowance after only `r round(log2(alpha.B * F.B / K.B[["transitional, U.S."]]), 1)` of a doubling, so a treaty signed within two doublings needs an overt allowance that starts at about `r round(4 * sh[["U.S. transitional, overt"]], 1)` and falls to 0.25 as the transitional fleet is retired. That is the one line the schedule exists for; China's transitional fleet is about `r round(100 * 4 * sh[["China transitional, overt"]])`% of $F_B$ after two doublings.
* **On this clock the allowance schedule is a drawdown requirement.** For the U.S. transitional line to sit under an allowance $\alpha$ after $d$ doublings, the share of that fleet still in service can be at most $\alpha \cdot 2^{-d} F_B / K_B$. At 0.25 that is `r round(100 * min(1, 0.25 * F.B / 2 / K.B[["transitional, U.S."]]))`% after one doubling, `r round(100 * 0.25 * F.B / 4 / K.B[["transitional, U.S."]])`% after two and `r round(100 * 0.25 * F.B / 10 / K.B[["transitional, U.S."]])`% at one OOM; merely staying below $F_B$ itself requires `r round(100 * F.B / 10 / K.B[["transitional, U.S."]])`% or less at one OOM. For scale: at the 18-month Moore's Law rate the transition of §4.4 (Phase 1 of 26 months plus Phase 2 of `r round(phase2.months)`) ends at `r sprintf("%.2f", (26 + phase2.months) / 12 * log10(1.587))` OOM, which is where $F_B$ falls to the size of the whole U.S. fleet (`r sprintf("%.2f", log10(F.B / K.B[["transitional, U.S."]]))` OOM). That is not a breach, because the drawdown runs through Phase 2.
* **The covert side needs no schedule unless hardware is concealed.** Under low cooperation dark compute reaches about `r round(100 * 4 * dk[["U.S.", "low cooperation"]], 1)`% (U.S.) and `r round(100 * 4 * dk[["China", "low cooperation"]], 1)`% (China) of $F_E$ after two doublings, under 25%. Under non-deniable concealment China's reaches about `r round(100 * 4 * dk[["China", "non-deniable concealment"]])`%, and a census cannot remove hardware that is hidden deliberately.
* **Once the schedule reaches 0.25, the binding line is dark compute.** Counted from the pause date, the dark-compute line alone has `r round(min(log2(alpha.E / dk[, "high cooperation"])), 1)` doublings of headroom under high cooperation (two orders of magnitude is 6.64 doublings), `r round(min(log2(alpha.E / dk[, "low cooperation"])), 1)` under low cooperation (`r c("the U.S.", "China")[bind.lc]` binds, with `r signif(dark[bind.lc, "low cooperation"] / 1e3, 2)`k of dark compute), and `r round(log2(alpha.E / dk[["China", "non-deniable concealment"]]), 1)` for China under non-deniable concealment, which is used up before a treaty would be signed. The other lines are not carried forward on this clock at their opening values, for the reason given in §S.7.5: by the time dark compute binds, their political discounts would be much steeper.
* **Why supplier and chip-owner states matter early.** Outside the U.S. and China the world holds `r round((fleet.ye2026 - us.fleet.ye2026 - china.fleet.ye2026) / 1e6, 1)`M H100e, `r signif((fleet.ye2026 - us.fleet.ye2026 - china.fleet.ye2026) / F.E, 3)` times $F_E$, all of it outside an informal bilateral pause until its owners join.

```{r schedule-figure, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4.4, fig.cap = paste0("Three ledger lines, each as a fraction of its own fleet threshold, against doublings of training efficiency since the pause date; each doubling halves $F_E$ and $F_B$, so every line rises by a factor of two per doubling. The lines are separate estimates and are not added together. Shaded: the informal phase, before a treaty is signed (assumed within two doublings). Blue: the U.S. transitional inference fleet against $F_B$, while it is all in service. Red: China's dark compute against $F_E$, under low cooperation (", signif(dark[["China", "low cooperation"]] / 1e3, 2), "k) and under non-deniable concealment (1M). The allowance schedule has to sit above the blue line at signing and reach 0.25 once transitional service is retired; the right-hand axis marks the 0.25 allowance and the fleet threshold itself, the top axis gives the same clock in orders of magnitude (one doubling is 0.30 OOM), and the dotted vertical line marks two orders of magnitude (6.64 doublings).")}
dd <- seq(0, 7, by = 0.05)
ln <- rbind(
  data.frame(d = dd, y = sh[["U.S. transitional, overt"]] * 2^dd, k = "U.S. transitional fleet (overt)"),
  data.frame(d = dd, y = dk[["China", "low cooperation"]] * 2^dd, k = "China's dark compute, low cooperation (covert)"),
  data.frame(d = dd, y = dk[["China", "non-deniable concealment"]] * 2^dd, k = "China's dark compute, non-deniable concealment (covert)"))
ln$k <- factor(ln$k, levels = unique(ln$k))
ggplot(ln, aes(d, y, colour = k, linetype = k)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = 0, xmax = 2, ymin = 1e-4, ymax = 100, fill = "#D9DCE0", alpha = 0.4, colour = NA) +
  annotate("text", x = 1, y = 0.0013, label = "informal phase", size = 3.55, colour = "#5A6470") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = c(0.25, 1), colour = "#1A1A1A", linetype = c("solid", "13"), linewidth = 0.45) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.85) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("#2E5F8C", "#8C3B2E", "#8C3B2E"), name = NULL) +
  scale_linetype_manual(values = c("solid", "solid", "42"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:7, expand = c(0, 0), sec.axis = dup_axis(breaks = log2(10^c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.5, 2)), labels = c("0", "0.5", "1", "1.5", "2"),
                                                                     name = "Orders of magnitude since the pause date")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = log2(100), colour = "#5A6470", linetype = "13", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_y_log10(breaks = c(0.001, 0.01, 0.1, 1), labels = c("0.1%", "1%", "10%", "100%"),
                sec.axis = dup_axis(breaks = c(0.25, 1), labels = c("allowance 0.25", "fleet threshold F"), name = NULL)) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(0.001, 1.6)) +
  guides(colour = guide_legend(ncol = 1), linetype = guide_legend(ncol = 1)) +
  labs(x = "Doublings of training efficiency since the pause date", y = "Share of its fleet threshold",
       title = "What the allowance schedule has to cover") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 12) +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank(), plot.title = element_text(size = 11.5),
        axis.text = element_text(size = 10), axis.title = element_text(size = 10.5),
        axis.text.y.right = element_text(size = 10, colour = "#1A1A1A"), axis.text.x.top = element_text(size = 10), axis.title.x.top = element_text(size = 10.5),
        legend.position = "bottom", legend.text = element_text(size = 9.5, colour = "grey25"),
        legend.key.width = unit(2.2, "lines"), legend.margin = margin(0, 2, 0, 2), plot.margin = margin(4, 6, 2, 2))
```

# S.8 Short items elsewhere in Sections 4–6

```{r short-items}
L.ctx <- 1e9; r.tok <- 1e6; oracle.rate <- (2 / 3) * sqrt(L.ctx / 3) * r.tok
F.P <- h100e(rho.P * 100 * C.T / (secs.per.yr * U.F))    # private runs stay below the frozen frontier: TRAILING overhead, no blind steps
signif(c("fn 52: P(at least one hit in six months) = 1 - (1 - 0.01 x 0.25)^1200" = 1 - (1 - 0.01 * 0.25)^1200, "fn 52: Poisson(3) approximation, 1 - exp(-3)" = 1 - exp(-3),
         "fn 39: idealized machine, (2/3) sqrt(L/3) r, GFLOP/s" = oracle.rate / 1e9, "4.1: such machines per H100" = h100e.peak / oracle.rate,
         "6.2.4: F_P = rho_P x 100 C_T / (1 yr x U_F), k H100e" = F.P / 1e3), 3)
```

* **fn 52 (§5.3.2):** sampling 2,400 chips per line per year is 1,200 in six months; with 1% of output diverted and a one-in-four chance of recognizing a diverted die, the chance of at least one hit is 1 − (1 − 0.0025)^1200 ≈ 95%, the same as the Poisson(3) approximation.
* **fn 39 (§4.1):** an idealized inference-only machine with a $10^{9}$-token context serving $10^{6}$ tokens per second can launder at most (2/3)·√(L/3)·r ≈ 12 GFLOP/s of general matrix multiplication, so matching one H100 takes about 81,000 of them ("more than 80,000").
* **$F_P$ (§6.2.4):** $V(x) = 100/x$ undetected violations a year above $x \cdot C_T$ means 100·$C_T = 2\times10^{26}$ FLOP a year of private training. A private evader trains *below* the frozen frontier rather than above it, so it takes no blind steps and it is doing the work of a fast follower, not of a frontier lab: the right overhead is the trailing $\rho_P = `r round(rho.P, 1)`$ of §S.4.2, not the frontier $\rho_F$. At that overhead and the frontier utilization $U_F$, the private evasion fleet is $F_P = `r round(F.P / 1e3)`$k H100e, printed as `r signif(F.P / 1e3, 2)`k. At the frontier overhead $\rho_F$ instead it would be `r round(h100e(rho.F * 100 * C.T / (secs.per.yr * U.F)) / 1e3)`k; a larger $F_P$ is the regime-favorable direction, so $\rho_P$ is the conservative choice.

  **What that fleet is worth.** At the \$25k per H100e adopted in §S.1.3, the private evasion fleet is a standing stock of hardware costing

```{r fp-dollars}
c("F_P (H100e)" = F.P, "F_P at $25k per H100e ($B)" = F.P * usd.per.h100e / 1e9,
  "  at the $15k-$35k bracket ($B)" = c(low = F.P * 15e3 / 1e9, high = F.P * 35e3 / 1e9),
  "per violator, if the rate is 100 actors a year ($M)" = F.P / 100 * usd.per.h100e / 1e6,
  "if evaders sustain only half of frontier utilization ($B)" = F.P / 0.5 * usd.per.h100e / 1e9,
  "F_P as a share of the world fleet (%)" = 100 * F.P / fleet.ye2026)
```

  — about \$`r round(F.P * usd.per.h100e / 1e9, 1)`B, or \$`r round(F.P * 15e3 / 1e9, 1)`–\$`r round(F.P * 35e3 / 1e9, 1)`B across the bracket. Three readings of that figure. It is a *stock that must exist continuously*, not a one-off purchase: the violation rate V(a) is per year, so the fleet has to be replenished as hardware fails and ages, without detection, in a world where training-capable production has stopped. Spread over the worked example's 100 violators a year it is about \$`r round(F.P / 100 * usd.per.h100e / 1e6)`M of concealed accelerators each, which is a data center, not a basement. And it is an underestimate twice over: the calculation counts only training and not the inference an illicit model would have to serve, and it charges evaders full frontier utilization — at half of it the fleet doubles, to \$`r round(F.P / 0.5 * usd.per.h100e / 1e9, 1)`B. For scale, $F_E$ at the same rate is \$`r round(F.E * usd.per.h100e / 1e9)`B and $F_B$ is \$`r round(F.B * usd.per.h100e / 1e12, 1)`T.

  **Three reasons the figure is low, and what they come to together.** The construction charges private evaders frontier-lab utilization, counts only training and no inference, and — the least obvious of the three — treats every violation as happening at a single size. The aggregate $C_T \cdot \min_{x \ge 1} x\,V(x)$ is the *cheapest* way to breach the treaty, reached by concentrating all the illicit compute at one multiple $x$ of the ceiling. Real violations would be spread over a range of sizes, and every one of them consumes hardware.

  Suppose the sizes are Pareto with exponent $\theta$ on $[1, \infty)$, so that $\Pr(X > x) = x^{-\theta}$ and the number of violations above $x \cdot C_T$ is $V(x) = V(1) \, x^{-\theta}$ — the worked example $V(x) = 100/x$ is exactly $\theta = 1$ with $V(1) = 100$. Holding $V(1)$ at the count that undermines the treaty, the compute actually deployed is $V(1) \cdot \mathbb{E}[X] \cdot C_T$ rather than $V(1) \cdot C_T$. Writing $u$ for the evaders' utilization relative to the frontier and $s$ for the share of their compute spent on inference,

  $$F_P = \frac{\rho_P \, \beta_T \, C_F \, V(1)}{U_F} \cdot \frac{1}{u} \cdot \frac{1}{1 - s} \cdot \mathbb{E}[X], \qquad \mathbb{E}[X] = \frac{\theta}{\theta - 1}.$$

  At $u = 1/2$ and $s = 1/2$ the first two corrections contribute a factor of four, so the fleet is $4\theta/(\theta-1)$ times the figure above.

```{r fp-pareto}
x.max <- C.E / C.T                                                  # above C_E the violation is covert state evasion, not private
EX       <- function(a) a / (a - 1)                                 # Pareto(theta) mean on [1, Inf)
EX.trunc <- function(a, X = x.max) ifelse(abs(a - 1) < 1e-9, log(X) / (1 - 1 / X),
                                          (a / (a - 1)) * (1 - X^(1 - a)) / (1 - X^(-a)))
u.p <- 0.5; s.inf <- 0.5                                            # utilization relative to the frontier; share of compute on inference
pp <- data.frame(theta = c(1, 1.25, 1.5, 2, 3))
pp$E.X        <- EX(pp$theta)
pp$E.X.capped <- EX.trunc(pp$theta)
pp$F.P.M      <- F.P / (u.p * (1 - s.inf)) * pp$E.X.capped / 1e6
pp$usd.B      <- pp$F.P.M * 1e6 * usd.per.h100e / 1e9
pp$pct.of.F.E <- 100 * pp$F.P.M * 1e6 / F.E
print(format(pp, digits = 3), row.names = FALSE)
c("factor from utilization and inference alone" = 1 / (u.p * (1 - s.inf)), "cap on x used above, C_E / C_T" = x.max)
```

  The correction is largest at $\theta = 1$, the tail of the worked example $V(x) = 100/x$. At $\theta = 1$, $\mathbb{E}[X]$ diverges: a distribution with $V(x) = 100/x$ puts equal compute in every octave of model size, so the total is unbounded unless something caps it. The natural cap is the covert evasion threshold, since a private actor training above $C_E = 10^4 \cdot C_T$ is the state-scale case of §S.4, not this one; capping there gives $\mathbb{E}[X] = \ln(10^4) = `r round(log(x.max), 1)`$ and a fleet of **`r round(pp$F.P.M[pp$theta == 1], 1)`M H100e**, about \$`r round(pp$usd.B[pp$theta == 1])`B and `r round(pp$pct.of.F.E[pp$theta == 1])`% of the covert evasion fleet $F_E$. Thinner tails are milder: $\theta = 1.5$ gives `r round(pp$F.P.M[pp$theta == 1.5], 1)`M and $\theta = 2$ gives `r round(pp$F.P.M[pp$theta == 2], 1)`M, or \$`r round(pp$usd.B[pp$theta == 2])`B.

  All three corrections push the same way, so `r round(F.P/1e3)`k is a floor; with the tail of $V(x) = 100/x$ the fleet is more than an order of magnitude larger. A larger $F_P$ is the regime-favorable direction, so the printed figure is the cautious one. What the exercise cannot do is pin $\theta$, which is a claim about how illicit model-building would be distributed in a world that does not exist.
